Of the ventilating motion that is always consumed by the incident motion.

Ventilating motion is a certain flexible motion that is generated in bodies constrained to be unable to follow the impulse attached to them by the aspect from which it was created; but it moves now here, now there, converting the refracted motion into incident motion, and the incident motion into refracted motion; and so it continues successively until the impulse, dispelling the body in which it is created, is consumed and dies together with the motion of that body.

[Five figures.]

In the right margin of the page is a figure with letters.

Although ventilating motion always arises from the impulse, it is generated in different ways and in different bodies; and this will sometimes be seen in a heavy body suspended from one or more ropes or other supports above or below it, sometimes in the arms of a balance around its pole, sometimes in a boat placed on water, and often in water within its vessels or in the wind reflected off the walls. We see the same thing in fires in their furnaces, and we see the same thing happening at sea and in various river inlets.

Ventilatory motion is of two kinds: straight in itself and circumvoluble. Straight motion occurs when the motion occurs between only two aspects, that is, it will move between north and south, or between east and west, or the like. Circumvoluble motion occurs when the rope is wrapped around the axed wheel, which rope has one end fixed at one height, and the other end is fixed with the wheel; then, letting this wheel fall along a perpendicular line, it will continue to unwind from this rope until it is completely unwound; then, by the momentum it has acquired, it will turn again and rise up near the place from which it divided, and will continue in this way until its end.
Ventilating motion is divided into three parts: simple, compound, and decomposed. Simple is that which occurs between two identical objects; compound is that in which one ventilator joins another ventilator; decomposed is when several bodies are apposed to one another and one below the other by degrees.

The ventilating motion in dense bodies will never be straight unless constrained by channels or other guides; and if it is constrained, it quickly dies out of itself.

The ventilating motion in rare bodies, such as air and fire, can be both straight and curved; and this is because they rarefy and condense and can penetrate one another. Water can act similarly within water, that is, the faster one penetrates the surface of the slower one.

Compound motion quickly dies out, and decomposed motion dies out even more quickly.

Of any two equal triangles, the center of gravity is halfway along the line that starts from the center of one triangle and ends at the center of the other triangle.

Let there be two triangles a b c and d e f; let the center of a b c be g; let the center of d e f be h. Now let the line from the center g to the center h be g h; and let the line g h be divided equally at the point K. I say that if they weigh equally, they will weigh equally, being equal; because the line g h that issues from their centers is divided equally at the point K, so that the ratio from g K to K h is the same as that from one triangle to the other. Therefore, K is the center of gravity of the two triangles because they are in the same proportion to each other as their distances from the point K, the balance of their equilibrium g h suspended at the pole K. First of the first of Archimedes's De Ponderibus.

Equal quantities placed at equal distances weigh equally; and if equal quantities weigh equally, they are placed at equal distances. And if unequal quantities weigh equally, they are placed at unequal distances, the greater at the lesser distance and the lesser at the greater distance. And if equal quantities do not weigh equally, they are placed at unequal distances; the one that weighs more is at the greater distance. If two quantities at equal distances weigh equally, every equal quantity placed at those distances will weigh equally. And every flat space has its center of gravity on the surface within its terms.

Every triangle has its center of gravity at the intersection of the lines starting from the angles and ending at the midpoint of their opposite bases.

For example, let the triangle a b c have equal sides, and b d be the leg that contains the center of the weight of the triangle, and divides it into two equal parts, making two similar and equal triangles, so that they weigh equally. That this is so, I prove. a b, side of the triangle a b d, is equal to side b c of the triangle b c d, and a d, side of the triangle a b d, is equal to c d, side of the triangle b c d. And so b d is an equal side common to both triangles. So, from what has been said, it is proved that the two triangles are similar and equal to each other. And the same conclusion is concluded by the second of Euclid's first. Now draw the line to angle a, so that it ends in the middle of side b c at point e. And then draw the line from point b to the middle of side a c at point d, and from e at point g. I say that the center of gravity is on the line a e. Then draw the line from angle c to the middle of the side a b at point e2, which will pass through g, which I say is the center of gravity. And since each of these lines divides the entire triangle into two parts similar and equal in weight and measure, and in each is the center of gravity of the entire triangle, which, although it is on the two lines, it can only be one; hence it is concluded that this center necessarily lies at the intersection of the two aforementioned lines, that is, at the point g. And if this triangle has 12 sides on each, then d g will be the root of 12, which is 1/3 of b d, which is R of 108; and b g is R of 48, which is 2/3 of b d, by the 18th of the 14th of Euclid; etc.

This same conclusion is concluded for triangles with different sides. Prove it. You have that the lines drawn from each of their angles to the center of the base divide the triangle into two equal parts in each direction, and on each line is the center of the triangle's entire weight; and since there can be only one center, it must be at the intersection of these lines.

The sides of mountains cut by rivers are steeper toward the obliquity of the rocks that slope down toward the river than toward the obliquity of the slopes that descend toward the river.

River banks, being concave, will be worn down more by the flow of the water in their shallows than in places near the surface.

And this happens because the water flowing toward the concave edge of the embankment descends with the force of the hill interposed between this concavity and the concavity of the opposite embankment, and in descending this hill it follows the straight course to the roots of the opposite embankments, and thus, continually striking and rubbing, wears away these concave roots of the embankments.

The concave edges of river embankments are struck at their roots by different types of water currents; some of which strike at equal angles, rise into the air, and fall, penetrating the other water to the bottom, and displacing it, leaving the material hollowed out around the struck spot. The other water strikes the embankment at an acute angle and bends obliquely toward the bottom; And what the first water left behind around the edges of its concavity, this second percussion carries with it with its refracted motion, leaving a large part of it beneath the arc of refractory motion.

When the faces of the mountain stones are exposed to the rain, that mountain will undoubtedly absorb a great deal of water; and the river that will arise from the obliquity of that slope will be abundant with water, but not lasting, because that slope will quickly be penetrated by its waters.

Mountains, in addition to being continually disturbed at their roots by the course of rivers, are washed on their sides by the rains that pour down upon them; which become larger the further they descend, thus becoming faster and more turbid, and with greater force and weight they wear away the sides of the mountains, and the peaks, due to their lesser wear, always remain higher in relation to the valleys.

A very short way to measure a distance.

Let the distance b n be, where the measuring eye is at b, and a target is placed at n, from which its distance from the eye is to be judged.

Now to make this measurement, I will stand with my feet at b, and I will place a rod between the eye and the target n, and this rod will be held upright. Then I will move a distance from b to a, which can be a lot or a little, or whatever you like; but say that from a to b is 4 braccia; and once I reach a, I will do the same with another rod placed perpendicularly between the eye b and the target n. Having done this, I will see the difference between the length of line a b and line c d, which we will say is 1/2 braccio shorter than a b, the base of the triangle a b n. If a b, the base of the pyramid a b n, is 30 braccia, the cut of that triangle, made one braccio distant from that base, is one braccio narrower than the base, which will remain 29. Now say: if the base of the triangle, which is 30, in a space of one braccio squeezes another braccio, by how much distance will it squeeze me, 30 braccia? You will say: 30 times 1 is 30. Divide this 30 into units, and you will get 30 units; and so you will find that the base of the 30 will have consumed its pyramid in 30 braccia of distance.

Again, if b were 4 braccia, and it confines me to a space of one braccio at c d 1/8 of a braccio, always multiply the base by the part of the decrease, and the result will be the number of braccia in which those 4 braccia of the base will be consumed.

Then you will say: 4 times 8 is 32; and 32 braccia you will say is the length of the pyramid.

And just as you move from here to there transversally, so you can measure altitude from up to down in the same way I told you above; and it is shorter, because you do not have to move from site.

On progression.

Say: 8 times 8 equals 64 for its entire square; taking away half of it, you're left with 32 squares, of which there are 28 whole squares and 8 half squares. Adding another 8 half squares will make 8 whole squares, and so you'll have 36 squares. And this rule applies to the numbers of progressions, saying: I want to know how many units there are from 1 to 8. Multiply 8 by itself, and take away half of the resulting sum; then add half of the multiplier, which was 8; and so you'll have made 36, as you did before in the other rule.

River courses between mountain cuts have valleys of varying widths. This is because several rivers flow into these cuts, each with its own valley. Between this first and second river are two angles formed by the mountains that enclose it; and it is much easier for the course of two rivers to consume a corner of a mountain between them than for a single river to consume a mountain's side. Thus, the valley widens more at the junction of two rivers than at the junction of each river alone or of the two rivers joined together.

The ruins of the banks arise from their globular shapes that impede the straight course of the floods, or from the course of the water that does not follow the straight course of the floodwaters.

The water in straight and narrow channels will have a higher surface in the middle and on the sides than in any other part of its width. It is higher on the sides because, striking the bank, it rises high and refracts backward, striking the bottom and sinking; Then it refracts from the bottom and rises upward, colliding in the middle with the oncoming water of the opposite direction. This water, striking it, rises upward, and returns in the opposite direction to respond to its own impact on the bank, and so on.

The water that flows through straight channels passes only from the bank to the middle of the channel, and the same thing happens along the other half of the channel's width. It follows a long course before the water, having struck one bank, passes to the opposite bank; but if it is swift, it will not pass the middle.

There are many mountains whose rocks do not pass the roots of such mountains; but, following the same order of the strata, they are converted into tuff, and beneath the tuff is a beach. The water that moves strongly has its backwaters that erode the bottom; and this happens because the backwater's course follows the obliquity of the surface, so that its motion directs it to strike the bottom, continually boring with its front, and thus continues to wear away the bottom.

Gravity is an invisible power created by accidental motion and infused into bodies that are removed from their natural place.

Division of the greater inequality, which is of two kinds, namely simple and composite. The simple has 3 members, and the composite has 2 members. The three of the simple are these: multiple, superparticular, superpartient. A multiplicity occurs when the larger term contains the smaller term precisely more than once, such as 1 to 2, 8 to 4, or 6 to 2. Therefore, if the larger term contains the smaller term precisely twice, this will be a kind of multiplicity, called a dupla, such as 1 to 2; and if the larger term contains the smaller term precisely three times, this will be called a triple, such as 6 to 2; and if it contains 4 times, it is called a quadruple; and if 5 times, it is called a quincuple.

1. 2. Dupla; 2. 6. Triple.

The superparticular is when the greater contains the lesser more than once, and some aliquot (multiplicative) part, as 2 is an aliquot part of 6, and 4 is an aliquot part of 12. The non-aliquot (agregative) part will be 2 with 5. And if the aliquot part is exactly half of the lesser term, it will be called the sexquialtera proportion; and if the said aliquot is 1/3 of the lesser term, it will be called sexquitertia; and if the aliquot part is a quarter of the lesser term, it will be called sexquiquarta; and if it is the fifth, it will be called sexquiquinta.

The simple superpartient is when the larger term contains the smaller term once and a non-aliquot part composed of aliquot parts, such as the proportion from 5 to 3, for which 5 contains 3 once, and also 2, which is not an aliquot part of 3, even though it is composed of two aliquot parts of 3, that is, two units.

Of the moveable and its mover.

The motions of moveables are infinitely variable from the motion of their mover, but such motions can never be caused without the motion of their mover.

The first motion will be when the moveable has an equal motion with the motion of its mover. And this can vary in two ways, the first being when the moveable moves with equal motion along its own line and with the same amount of motion as that of its mover. The third is when the aforementioned motions, even if they are along the same line, are not of equal length, because that of the moveable is longer than that of the mover; and this can proceed along the same line. Also, along the same line and aspect, the motion of the mover can be longer than that of the moveable; and this, along the same aspect, can only be parallel. The fourth way is when the moveable moves in a straight line opposite to the motion of its mover, such as the mover to the east and the moveable to the west; and this can be equal to the motion of the moving body, or greater or less. The fifth motion is a right-angled transversal, that is, if the mover goes east, the moving body goes north. The sixth mode is a transversal of acute angles, that is, if the mover goes east, the moving body goes north. The seventh is a transversal of an obtuse angle with the motion of the moving body; and this is when the mover goes east and the moving body goes east. Now the lines made by the aforementioned motions can be caused by the mover and the moving body in such a way that they will create infinitely variable angles, greater or less than right angles. And that is what has been said.

Excessive force exerted on the same resistance has no effect on the moving object. But if the force of the mover is proportional to its moving object, then the motion produced by the moving object will be the primary factor. For example, if I wanted to push a bladder full of wind against the air, if it were moved by excessive force, the air, when struck by it, would, through its condensation, create such resistance that the bladder, struck inside, would be thrown backward, just as if it were slammed against a wall. But if this bladder is moved by a mover whose force and motion are proportionate to the lightness of the aforementioned moving object, then the moving object will move forward as far as its force is able to push the air that opposes its course with slowness.

And just as the sun strikes hollow mirrors, and from there rises up in a pyramidal confluence, so that the smaller the portion of the pyramid, the hotter it becomes than its base, so too when this humidity contracts: the hot vapor that was mixed with it becomes more powerful the more it unites, and the smaller the space it shrinks, the greater the heat it generates. Thus it often ignites and multiplies, turning the cloud into a bombardment; and thus the cloud crashes with thunder and thunderclaps. The small grains of water, when the cloud is constricted by the cold, grow together and fall under their weight. And in this way the clouds dissolve, and thus, in the rain, return to their base.

This consumes the high peaks of the mountains. This strips and removes the great rocks. This one drives the sea from its ancient shores, because with the earth it carries it raises its bed. This one shatters and ruins the high banks; no stability is ever seen in it that does not immediately corrupt its nature. This one with its rivers searches every slope of the valleys, and where it raises and where it places new soil. Hence we say that many rivers are those through which all the element has passed, and many times the sea has returned to the sea, and no part of land is so high that the sea was not already at its foundations, and no depth of the sea is so shallow that very high mountains were not already founded. And so it is sometimes bitter and sometimes strong, sometimes pruning and sometimes bitter, sometimes sweet and sometimes coarse or subtle, sometimes harmful or pestilential, sometimes salutary or tosculpable. Hence they say that it changes into as many natures as the places through which it passes are varied. And just as the mirror changes to the color of its object, so this changes to the nature of the place through which it passes: salutary, harmful, dissolving, stitious, sulfurous, salty, bloody, melancholic, quivering, choleric, red, yellow, green, black, blue, greasy, fat, lean. When it catches fire, when it extinguishes it, hot, cold; when it raises or raises, when it hollows out or elevates, when it ruins or stabilizes, when it fills or empties, when it rises or sinks, when it rushes or subsides, when it causes life or death, when it generates or deprives, when it nourishes and when the opposite, when it salts or sips, when it submerges broad valleys with great deluges.

With time, everything changes.
When it twists toward the north, gnawing at the bottom of its own bank; when toward the south it collapses the opposite bank; when it turns toward the earthly center, consuming the ground that supports it; when it leaps toward the sky with roaring boils; when with a circular revolution it confuses its course; when from the west it widens, stripping the crops from their comrades; when from the east it unloads its plundered land. And so when it digs and when it fills, where it takes and where it places. Thus without any respite it always removes or consumes those who border it. Thus when turbulent and destructive it rages, when lucid and tranquil it frolics with its gentle course among the fresh grasses. When with rain or snow or hail it falls from the sky, when with thin mists it composes heavy clouds. When it is moved by itself, and when by the force of another, when it increases the things born with vital humor, when it appears fetulent or fragrant. Nothing among us is found without it. When it is infused with the hot element and, vaporizing, mixes with the air, and drawn upward by the heat, it rises where, having found the cold region, by its contrary nature it constricts itself together, and the minute particles are apical together. And just as the hand under water presses the sponge, when it is well soaked, and when it is enclosed in water it pushes it among the other water and, with the swaying of its place, drives it away through the cracks, so does the cold that constricts the warm humidity, that when it has reduced it to a denser form, the air enclosed within it bursts by force into its weakest parts, and actually blows as if it were coming out of nowhere, when pressed by an excessive weight. And so through various places it drives away the lighter clouds that are between its opposing courses.
The spur placed at the beginning of the water torture breaks the back of its shoulders and depth; the spur placed at the end of the torture acquires wood, roots, and other light objects; the spur placed after the torture acquires mud and useful soil. Thus, placed in various places, the water discharges or removes various things after it, such as rocks or small jars, sand, and other types of material.
And always consuming and removing whatever is confined to it, when it is driven by the air, and when it carries air and earth with it.

The cause that moves water through the veins against the natural course of its gravity is the same as that which does the same to all humors, in all kinds of animate bodies. And as the lowly blood rises high and falls back through the cracks in the forehead, so from the lowest depths of the sea the water rises to the summits of the mountains, where, finding its veins broken, it pours through them and returns to the shallow sea. Have you ever seen the water descend from the severed branches of the vine and fall back upon its roots, which, penetrating them, rise again? Thus does the water that falls back into the sea, which penetrates through the earth's canals, and returning to the power of its mover, where it again rises with violence and descends by its usual descent, then returns. Thus, simultaneously apposed and conjoined, in a continuous revolution between within and without, it continues to revolve: sometimes by accidental motion it surges, sometimes by natural free descent. Thus between up and down, within and without, no rest ever rests it, not only in its course, but in its substance; and just as a mirror changes according to the color of the objects through which it passes, it has nothing of itself, but moves or captures everything, and changes into as many different natures as are the places through which it passes.
That cause which moves the humors against the natural course of their gravity in all kinds of living bodies, so moves the water through the earthly veins and with constant solicitude assists it in all those places that necessity directs it.

And that which is seen falling from a high place, which gives rise to the course of every river, acts like the blood that rises from below to above and pours out through the cracks in the forehead.

This demonstration separates natural perspective from accidental; but before proceeding further, it will define which is natural and which accidental. Natural perspective says this: of things of equal magnitude, the more remote one appears smaller, and conversely, the closer one appears larger; and this proportion is from diminution to diminution, as it is from distance to distance. But accidental perspective places unequal things at various distances, reserving the smaller one closer to the eye than the greater one, with such a distance that the greater one appears smaller than all the others. And the cause of this is the wall, where this demonstration is depicted, which has an unequal distance from the eye along every part of its length. And this diminution of the wall is natural; But the perspective depicted in it is accidental, because it does not accord in any part with the true diminution of the said wall; hence it results that, by removing the eye somewhat from that perspective, everything depicted appears monstrous. This does not occur in natural perspective, which is defined above, etc. Therefore we will say that the square a b c d depicted above is a foreshortened square seen from the eye placed at the center of the width of its front; but the accidental perspective mixed with the natural one will be found in the square called elmain, that is, e f g h, which appears to the eye that sees it similar to a b c d, with the eye fixed at the first position below c d; and this will be shown to have a good effect, because the natural perspective of the wall ensures that the wall will hide the lack of such monstrosity.

Motion arises from excess or deficiency.

The motion of a moving object toward its object can be varied by the moving object itself in two ways: simple motion and compound motion. Simple motion is that motion in which the object never moves its axis outside its original being: compound motion occurs when, in addition to the straight motion the moving object makes toward its object, there is added the voluble motion of itself. Volatile straight motion can be varied in two ways: direct voluble motion and lateral voluble motion. Direct voluble motion occurs when the upper part of the moving object turns toward the object, and its lower part returns toward its mover. Lateral voluble motion occurs when the object turns around the central line of its motion. These are the ways in which the mover displaces its moving object: the first is when it is moved by a simple impulse; The second is the impulse compounded with other impulses; the third, when the mover follows its movable with equal motion; the fourth, when the movable is driven by the percussion.

There are three modes of motion for the sites that receive the percussion, one of which is capable of resisting, the other of yielding. There are two modes of motion: direct or circumvoluble. The circumvoluble varies in three main ways: direct, equi-subjective, or oblique. The mover of the circumvoluble can be of two kinds: counterweight, spring, or blow. The counterweight varies in two ways in circumvolubles: augmentative or diminutive: augmentative is when the counterweight that moves moves away from the center of the circumvoluble, and diminutive is that of the counterweight of the bricules.

There are two natures of percussion: simple and compound. Simple is that which the moving object makes in the motion incident upon its object; it is called compound when this first percussion passes through the support of the object first struck, as would be the blow given on the sculptor's chisel, and is then passed through to the marble being carved. This blow is also divided into two others, namely, the simple blow and the double blow. The simple blow is said enough; but the double blow is when the hammer descends suddenly by natural motion, and flees, leaping from the upper blow, and falls when the lower blow is created, and this percussion is made in two places by the two opposite parts of the hammer. And this blow is diminished as the number of objects interspersed between the blow and the final resistance, like someone who beats a book on the first pages; even though all of them touch, the last one feels little damage.

Refractive motion.

Motion arises from two different causes, the first of which is called inpetus, the second is called percussion. The motion arising from inpetus is that which leads the moving body to the point of percussion. The motion arising from percussion is that which arises from the point struck between two right angles. Now we will say in the above figure that, moving a moving body from a to b, that the moving body is only moved to b by the simple power of inpetus; and if this mobile is moved from c to d, then this mobile will be rebounded by refracted motion from d to n: which motion from d to n is born from the simple power of percussion.

Now having defined the two natures of motion, we will proceed by these definitions to prove why the angle of the refracted motion is necessary to be equal to the angle of the incident motion.

There are three principal motions of heavy bodies: violent, transverse, and natural.

Transversal is that which falls away from the mover and is divided into two: natural and violent.

There are two actions of these motions: incident motion and refractory motion. Incident motion is that motion which separates the moving body from the mover and carries it to the point of its percussion; and refractory motion is that motion which separates the moving body from the percussion and raises it to its highest height.

Percussion is the impediment of motion, that is, the end of incident motion and the beginning of refractory motion.

There are two qualities of motion, namely, augmentative and diminutive: augmentative is when a heavy body moves toward the center of the universe, which at each degree of descent acquires gravity and velocity of motion; diminutive motion is when such a heavy body is removed from the center of the universe, which at each point of motion acquires degrees of lightness and slowness.

There are three differences in the lines that can be traversed by the inrush or motion of heavy bodies: direct line, line of equality, and oblique line. A direct line is one that extends from a given point and directs itself to the center of the universe; equidicent, or equal, is one whose ends are equally distant from the center of the universe; oblique is one that is included between the equidistant and direct lines. And these can be infinite, because such space is divisible into infinity; and they only vary in greater or lesser obliquity. The more oblique is the one that comes closest to the equilateral line, the less oblique is the one that comes closest to the direct line.

Of the moon.

The moon has no light of its own, except as much as the sun sees—that is, its alumina. We see as much of this luminosity as we see. And its night receives as much splendor as our waters lend it in refracting the image of the sun, which is reflected in all those that see the sun and moon.

The surface of the water that makes up the sea of ​​the moon and the sea of ​​our earth is always wrinkled, whether slightly or considerably, more or less; and this wrinkling causes the innumerable images of the sun to dilate, which are reflected in the hills and hollows and sides and fronts of the innumerable wrinkles—that is, in as many different locations on each wrinkle as there are different locations on the eyes that see them. This could not happen if the sphere of water that largely covers the moon were of uniform sphericity, because then the image of the sun would be one in each eye, and its reflection would be particular, and it would always be a spherical splendor, as the golden balls placed at the tops of tall buildings clearly show us. But if these golden balls were wrinkled or globular, like blackberries, black fruits composed of minute round globules, then each part of these globules, seen by the sun and the eye, would display to that eye the lustre generated by the image of the sun. And so in the same body one would see many tiny suns, which often merge at a long distance and appear continuous. The lustre of the new moon is brighter and more powerful than when it is at full moon; And this is because the angle of incidence is much more obtuse in the new moon than in the old, where such angles are very acute, and the moon's waves reflect the sun both in their valleys and in their hills, and the sides remain dark. But on the sides of the moon the depths of the waves do not see the sun, but only the tops of the waves see it, and for this reason the images are rarer and more mixed with the shadows of the valleys. Landscapes have a more beautiful blue when the sun is at midday in fair weather than at any other time of day, because the air is diluted with moisture. Looking from that angle, you see the trees beautiful toward their ends, and the shadows darkening toward the middle. And at long distances, the air between you and them becomes more beautiful when it is darker, and therefore the blue is most beautiful.

Things seen from the direction the sun shines on them will not show you their shadows. But if you are lower than the sun, you will see what the sun never saw, and that will be all shadowy.

The leaves of the trees between you and the sun are of five primary colors: that is, a beautiful green lustre and reflection of the air that illuminates those who cannot be seen by the sun, and the shadowy ones that only see the earth, and the darkest ones that are surrounded by anything but darkness...

The trees among the reeds that are between the sun and you are much more beautiful than those you stand between the sun and them. This is because those that are toward the sun show their transparent leaves at their tips, and those that are not transparent, that is, at the tips, are shiny. It is true that the shadows are dark, because they are not filled with anything.

The trees between which you stand between the sun and them will not show themselves to you except with their clear and natural color, which in itself is not very excessive; And, in addition to this, some trees, which, because they are not too different from their brightness, are of little clarity, and if you are lower than them, they can also be seen to you with those parts the sun did not see, which are shaded.

But if you are on the side where the wind blows, you will see the trees much brighter than you would from other sides; and this happens because the wind reveals the undersides of the leaves, which on all sides are much whiter than on the tops; and above all, they are very bright if the wind blows from the region where the sun is, towards which you have turned your back.
All trees seen from the sun are dark toward the middle; this darkness is the shadow of the tree's shape when it is separated from the others.

The secondary shadows of trees seen from the sun are as dark as that of the middle of the tree.

The secondary shadow of trees is never less than the height of the tree itself; but it will be greater the more oblique the site where it is cut is toward the center of the universe.

That shadow will be narrower toward the middle of the tree, than which its tree will have more sparse ramifications.

Each branch has the middle of the shadow of any branch, and consequently of its entire tree.

The shape of any branch or tree's shadow will be clothed in a luminous part from that side whence the light comes; This illumination will be the shape of the shadow, and this will be for a distance of a mile from the direction of the sun.

If a cloud happens to cast shadows on some part of the hills, the trees on them will change less than their spaces or planes; for the trees on the hills have thicker branches, so they produce fewer branches per year than on the planes. Therefore, because they are naturally dark and filled with shadow, the shadows of the clouds can no longer obscure them, and the planes between the trees, which have not lost any shadow, are greatly changed in brightness, especially those that are different from green, such as cultivated land or mountain ruins or their barrenness or rocky nature.

Where the trees border the air, they appear to be the same color, unless there are many nearby and have thick leaves, like pines and similar trees.

When you look at the trees from the side illuminated by the sun, you will see them almost as clear as the sun, and the shadows within them will be filled with the illuminated leaves that lie between your eye and the shadow.

Nearby trees.

The trees that lie between the sun and your eye, after the shadows that expand toward their center, will show the green of their transparent leaves. This transparency will be interrupted in many places by the shaded leaves and branches that lie between you and them, and in their upper parts by many gleams of leaves.

The trees in the hemp fields are of various kinds of green; some are black, such as firs, pines, cypresses, laurels, box trees, and the like; some are yellow, such as walnuts and pears, vines, and young greens; some are yellow with darkness, such as chestnuts, oaks, and the like; some are reddish toward dawn, such as rowans, pomegranates, vines, and cherries; some are white, such as willows, olives, reeds, and the like.

And this will appear when one of the eyes remains stationary and the other is removed with the finger.

The eye that looks into a lit candle will appear to see a round splendor around its light, even though it is elongated.

The reason for this is that, since the surface of the eye receives the reflection of the light, that reflection illuminates and illuminates that hole of the eye filled with transparent fluid. Since the reflection of the light is in the middle of the surface of that hole, the power of the understanding that sees that light sees it surrounded by the roundness of that illuminated hole. And if other circles are seen around that light, they will arise from the circular parts furthest from that hole, which contain some transparency, which are incorporated into that light.

Given that the natural center of gravity of a body is known, it is not possible to find the natural center of its parts.

Even if the accidental center of gravity of a body is known, it will not be possible to find the accidental center of gravity of that body using it.

Given the accidental center of gravity of the parts of a body, it is possible, using them, to find the accidental center of gravity of the entire body.

Given the natural center of gravity of each part of a body, it is possible, using this knowledge, to find the center of natural gravity of the entire body.

With the natural center of one part of a body and the accidental center of the other part, it will be impossible to investigate either the natural center or the accidental center of gravity of the entire body.

With the center of the natural or accidental gravity of a body alone, the center of the natural or accidental gravity of that body will never be found.

With the natural center of the part and of the whole of a body the center of its accidental gravity will not be investigated.
A pyramid with a triangular base has its center of natural gravity in the line extending from the center of the base to the center of the side opposite it, equidistant from the junction of the base and the aforementioned side.

Every solid having its opposite parts similar and equal to one another will have the center of its natural gravity concentric with the center of its magnitude.

Uniformly dissimilar bodies have within themselves three centers, one of which is the center of magnitude, the other is the center of accidental gravity, and the third, less known, is the center of natural gravity.

The center of magnitude of bodies is placed midway between their length, width, and thickness.

The center of accidental gravity of these bodies is placed midway between those parts that resist one another, remaining in equilibrium.

The center of natural gravity is that which divides a body into two parts equal in weight and quantity.

With regard to the centers of accidental gravity of the whole and of the part of a body, the center of natural gravity of that body will not be investigated.

Force is generated by famine or abundance: this is the daughter of material motion and granddaughter of spiritual motion, and the mother and origin of weight; and this weight is finite in the element of water and earth, and this force is infinite, because with it infinite worlds would move, if instruments could be made where this force could be generated.

Force through material motion and weight through percussion are the four accidental powers by which all mortal works have their being and their death.

Force originates from spiritual motion, which motion, sliding through the limbs of sensitive animals, swells their muscles, so that these swollen muscles come to contract and pull back the nerves that are connected to them, and hence the force in human limbs is caused.

The quality and quantity of a man's strength will be able to generate another strength which will be proportionally greater the longer the motion of one is than that of the other.
Gravity, force, along with material motion, and percussion are the four accidental powers by which the human species, in its wondrous and varied operations in this world, seems to demonstrate a second nature. For with these powers, all the evident works of mortals have their being and their death.

Material motion, along with gravity, force, and percussion, are the four accidental powers by which all the works of mortals have their being and their death.

The motion between these powers is the cause that each of them can regenerate itself, and likewise each of the others, and also this motion, without which one of these cannot regenerate.

Gravity is a power created by motion, which, through force, transports one element into another, and this gravity has as much life as that element struggles to repatriate.

Force and gravity have much similarity in all their powers, but only in the motions of their birth and death are they different. For simple weight alone dies, that is, toward the center. And force arises and dies with every motion.

Many philosophers, with common opinion, affirm that force is accidental weight, almost calling it accidental, as if gravity itself were not accidental.

Here the question arises: whether weight is generated by itself or by force, or force by itself or by weight.

The spirits of sensitive animals move along the limbs of their bodies, and finding the muscles within them equal, they prepare to grow; and as soon as they grow, they contract, and as they contract, they draw back the nerves that are connected to them. And from here arise the force and motion of human limbs. Therefore, material motion arises from the spiritual.

By lowering or raising the pyramid, one seeks the increase or decrease of its base.

The proportion of the shrinkage of the cylinder will be the same as the shrinkage of its base; the similar occurs in the pyramid. And so the proportion of the increase in thickness of the cylinder is the same as the shrinkage of its length. The similar I mean of the pyramid is the increase of its base.

It is similar to square tables increased in length, or length increased in width, because as you shrink it in one direction, it increases in the other, which is according to its law, and as you thicken it, the narrower it becomes, and as you squeeze it, the more it thickens. 1. From a given cylinder with sides, make a cube; ask the height of this cube.

2. From a cube, make a cylinder of a given distance; ask its thickness.

3. Transform the cube into a cylinder of a given thickness; then ask its length.

4. Change the length of a cylinder into a shorter one; ask how much it thickens.

5. When a cylinder is stretched to a given length, ask how much its thickness decreases.

6. When a square board is reduced to a given length of a cylinder, ask how much the board narrows.

7. From a cylinder, make a square board of a given depth; ask how much the cylinder widens.

8. From two given unequal cubes, make a single cube; its height is asked.

9. I want to draw a cube of a given thickness from another cube, and let the remainder remain a cube.

10. Make a single cube of two equal cubes.

11. Square a rectangular table that is longer than it is wide, according to a given width; its thickness is asked.

12. Of a square table stretched to a given length without losing its width, the amount of its thickness is asked.

13. Of a square table stretched to a given distance without decreasing its thickness is asked how much it shrinks.

14. Of a long table stretched to a given greater length without decreasing its width, the amount of its thickness is asked.

15. A long board, when extended to a given greater length without decreasing its thickness, is determined by how much it narrows.

16. A long board, when shortened to a given shorter length without increasing its width, is determined by how much it thickens.

17. A board of greater length is shortened to a given shorter length without increasing its thickness, is determined by how much it widens.

Just as the northerly north wind rebounds with its storm.

The stormy sea does not roar so loudly when the northerly north wind rebounds with its foaming waves between Sulla and Charybdis; nor does Stronboli or Mongibello, when the sulfurous flames, being contained, burst by force and split open the great mountain, blasting stone and earth through the air, along with the escaping and vomited flame.

Nor when the fiery caverns of Mongibello release the poorly restrained element, regurgitating it and forcing it back into its region with fury, pushing forward any obstacle that stands in the way of its relentless fury.

Since the element of water remains confined within the increased banks of rivers and the shores of the sea, within the increased earth, it will be necessary that in the surrounding air, having to enclose and circumscribe the multiplied machine of the earth, its thickness, which existed between the water and the element of fire, will be greatly restricted and deprived of its needy water. The rivers will be left without their waters, the fertile earth will no longer send forth its flourishing leaves, the fields adorned with tumbling grain will no longer bear hay, all the animals, unable to find the fresh grass to graze on, will die, and food will be lacking for the rapacious lions and wolves and other animals that live by rapture; and after many refuges, men will be forced to abandon their life, and human generation will be lost. And in this way the fertile and fruitful earth, abandoned, will remain arid and sterile, and because of the locked-in warmth of the water enclosed within its belly and because of its lively nature, it will observe some of its growth, so much so that, once the cold and thin air has passed, it will be forced to end with the element of fire. Then its surface will remain a parched ash, and this will be the end of earthly nature.

O powerful and once animated instrument of ingenious nature, your great strength being of no avail to you, you were forced to abandon your tranquil life, obeying the laws that God and time gave to creative nature were of no avail to you.

The brawny and vigorous backs with which you, pursuing your prey, furrowed with your chest, parting the salty waves in a storm.

O how many times were the terrified flocks of dolphins and great tuna seen fleeing from your merciless fury. And you, with swift, branching wings, and with your forked tail, thundering, plunged into the sea in a sudden storm, with a mighty crash and the submergence of ships. With a great wave, you filled the exposed shores of the frightened and startled fish. And, taking themselves away from you by the sea, they remained dry, becoming abundant and plentiful prey for the neighboring peoples.

O Time, consumer of things, turning them back to you from their drawn lives, new and varied habitations. O Swift Time, predator of created things, how many kings, how many peoples have you undone, and how many changes of states and various events have occurred since the marvelous form of this fish died here.

Through its cavernous and twisted innards, now undone by patient Time, you have given us in this closed place, with its stripped, fleshless, and naked bones, a framework and support for the mountain above.

Contra. ― Because nature did not ordain that one animal should not live by the death of the other.

Pro. — Nature, being eager and taking pleasure in creating and continually producing lives and forms, because it knows that they are an increase in its earthly matter, is eager and quicker in its creation than time is in its consumption, and therefore has ordained that many animals be one another's food. And since this does not satisfy this desire, it often sends forth certain poisonous and pestilential vapors and a constant plague upon the great multiplications and congregations of animals, and especially upon men who cause great increase, because other animals do not feed on them, and if the causes are removed, the effects will be lacking.

Contra. — Therefore this earth, seeking to lose its life, desires continuous multiplication for the reason you assigned. Often the effects resemble their causes. Animals are an example of the life of the world.

Pro. ― Now see the hope and desire to repatriate or return to the original chaos, like the butterfly in the light, of the man who with constant desires always joyfully awaits the new spring, always the new summer, always new months, and new years, it seeming to him that the desired things, coming, are too late, and he does not see that he desires his own undoing; but this desire is in that quintessential spirit of the elements, which, finding itself enclosed for the soul of the human body, always desires to return to its mandate.

And I want this same desire to be found in that quintessential company of nature, and man is the model of the world.

The split parallels are universally generated in those buildings constructed in mountainous places, which are made of stones with oblique cleavage. And because water and other moisture, carrying a certain greasy and slippery soil, often penetrate this obliquity, and because these layers do not extend to the valley floor, these stones move due to their obliquity and never stop moving until they descend to the valley floor, carrying with them, like a boat, that part of the building that is separated from the rest. The remedy for this is to build thick pillars under the moving wall, with arches connecting one to the other and well-beamed, and these pillars should be built and fixed in layers that are not broken.

To find the stable part of the above-mentioned slopes it is necessary to dig a well under the foot of the wall with a great depth between these slopes, and to clean this well with a flat surface a span wide, from the top to the bottom on the side from which the mountain descends, and after some time this cleaned part that is made on the wall of the well will show a clear sign which part of the mountain is moving.

On the cause of the failure of public and private buildings.

Walls break through cracks that are direct, and some that are oblique. The cracks that have a direct connection are created by the new walls built in conjunction with the old walls, either straight or with clamps joined to the old walls, because such clamps cannot resist the unbearable weight of the wall joined to them, it is necessary for them to be lost and make way for the descent of the aforementioned new wall which lowers one arm for every 10 arm lengths or more or less according to the greater or lesser amount of mortar placed between the masonry stones, and with more or less liquid mortar. And note that walls must always be built first and then covered with the stones that will cover them, because, if this were not done, the wall would sag more than the outer crust, and it would be necessary for the joints made in the sides of the walls to be broken. This is because the stones that cover the walls, being larger than the stones covered by them, must receive a smaller amount of mortar in their joints and consequently sag less, which cannot happen if such a crust is built in once the wall is dry.

Of the smoke from an unlit candle.

The smoke from an unlit candle has its edges denser than the medium, because it refracts toward the medium, fleeing from the impediment of the cold air where it strikes as it expands. And because it can rarefy and condense, it becomes dense at its edges. In this case, it does not act like water, which, because it cannot rarefy or condense by itself, necessarily causes its part refracted from the site of the percussion to create a wave that moves upon the advancing water in a counter-motion.

Without wind.

Figure with letters.

A bird will rise to flight more easily if it takes the momentum of its motion with some descent at the beginning of its flight.

With the wind, that is, gaining momentum against the wind.

When the bird flies against the wind, it is necessary that the gain it makes against the wind be made on an oblique line toward the ground, entering leeward. And because its weight is more powerful than the amount of wind that strikes it at unequal angles, it would willingly push it toward the ground if it were not for the fact that the air in front of it, along the line of its motion, is much less in quantity than the air below it that is contingent and touches it. This motion only overcomes that air that resists it least, and that air that is of smaller quantity will resist it least. Therefore, from what has been said, we are certain that the bird will move against the least resisting air, which touches the shoulders of its wings, and not against that which touches the underside of the entire mass of said wings.

Rectilinear motion.

But when such a bird wants to rise, it will enter into the wind, and will make great use of the momentum it has acquired in its aforementioned descent, since at this acquired speed it will lower its tail and likewise the elbows of its wings, and will raise its shoulders. Then it will be above the wind, and such a wing, being forced neither to end nor to be consumed, its being is immediately forced to follow that line where the least air impedes it, the motion that will be along that line where the wings appear edged on the air where they strike, that is, along the line where the air that strikes will always be divided by the shoulders placed in the thickness of the wings, and never by the line of their latitude.

Therefore, once this is done, such a bird rises aloft without flapping its wings, because the wind that passes beneath it lifts it aloft like a wedge lifts weight, and for this reason it would make it return in the opposite direction, were it not that in this ascent the wing already acquired is retarded and consumed; And after this impulse is consumed, the bird would be overturned by the wind that carried it aloft, if it did not immediately lower the rudders of the shoulders and wings, enter to leeward, and lower its tail. Then the already finite motion begins, and, declining, it regains the already lost momentum, with which it then again rises upward with the refracted motion until it again loses the momentum it has already acquired. But if this motion were circular, then the bird would observe other rules, which will be defined in subsequent order.

How rivers widen valleys and wear away the roots of the lateral mountains.

In the right margin of the sheet is a figure with letters.

Next to the figure:

The rushing motion of rivers through their valleys strikes and wears away the roots of the lateral mountains.

The meanderings that rivers make through their valleys as they rise from one mountain to another create a rushing bank. This rushing motion moves with the flow of the water and over time searches the entire valley, if it is not impeded, increasing its length and depth, while decreasing its width.

Let the valley be a c k h through which the rushing river flows a c e g k. I say that the embankment is of the same speed as the river, and moves together with the flow of the water, that is, its part a c will wear away the lower embankment up to b d, and likewise the embankment c e up to d f, and 'l e g up to f h, and with this rule this meandering will search the entire valley, and will increase its length and depth, because the river continually wears away the roots of the mountain where it enters the valley, and the depth, because it carries with it the soil that muddies it, and narrows the valley floor, because, in submerging the lateral matter of the mountains, it falls back to the foot of the bare hills, and the lighter particles flee together with the water, and the heavier ones settle on the sides of that valley.

On the motion of the waves of the embankment opposite the course of the river.

When the first wave of the embankment departs toward the head of the river, the second wave is immediately generated, following the first, and so do the third and fourth successively; that is, when the wave of the bank c e has descended to d f, wave a c immediately has descended to b d, and so on.

Like the Abile and Calpe cut in the Strait of Gadeta.

The Abile and Calpe cut in the Strait of Gadeta greatly diminished the rivers that descend from the Alps and flow northward. And this is proven by the fact that before this cut of the Gadetani mountains was created, the Mediterranean Sea had a very high surface, which exceeded three-quarters of the height of the Alps, and the penetration that this sea made through the channels and veins of the earth was very high and abundant, whereas after this Gadetani cut the Mediterranean Sea lowered its surface, and the aforementioned high channels remained empty of their waters, and the rivers lost their abundant courses.

In the morning, the fog is thicker at higher altitudes than at lower altitudes, because the sun draws it upwards, so that even large buildings, even if their tops are as far away as their foundations, remain unknown to you. And for this reason, the sky appears darker at higher altitudes and toward the horizon, and not blue; rather, it is all smoke and dust.

The air infused with fog is entirely devoid of blue; but only appears the color of clouds that turn white when the weather is clear; and the further you look toward the west, you will find it darker and more lucid and clear toward the east. And the greenery of the reeds takes on a bluish hue in the middle of the fog, but turns black in the thickest fog.

Buildings facing west only reveal their luminous side, once the sun is revealed; the rest is hidden by the fog.

When the sun rises and chases away the fog, and the hills begin to clear in the direction from which it originates, they turn blue and smoke toward the fleeing fogs, and the buildings show light and shadow, and in the less dense fogs they show only light, and in the thickest none; and this is when the fog's motion begins transversally, and then the edges of the fog will be few and far between against the blue of the air, and toward the earth it will look like rising dust.

The thicker the air, the buildings of cities and the trees of the reeds will appear rarer, because only the most prominent and largest will be visible.

Mountains are rare, because only those with greater intervals are visible, because in such spaces the thickness multiplies in such a way that it creates such clarity that the darkness of the hills divides and spreads well toward its height. In the small and nearby hills, not so much darkness intervenes, and therefore they are less discernible, and even less so in their lowlands.

Darkness tinges everything with its color, and the more a thing distances itself from that darkness, the more it regains its true and natural color.

Describe the landscape with wind and water, and with the setting and rising of the sun.

All the leaves that hung to the ground, as their branches bent, turned upside down along with that branch, are oriented with the course of the wind, and here their perspective plays a contrary role, for if the tree is between you and the source of the wind, the tips of the leaves that are toward you make their natural projection, and the opposite leaves that were supposed to turn their tips in the opposite direction are, by their overturning, turned with their tips toward you.

The reed trees are not very distinct from each other, because their illuminated parts border on the illuminated parts behind them, and in these there is little difference between the lights and the shadows.

When clouds pass between the sun and the eye, all the edges of their spheres are bright, and the middle is dark. This happens because the upper edges of these spheres are seen higher by the sun and lower by you. The same thing happens at the top of tree branches, and both clouds and trees become partly bright because they are somewhat transparent, and greater subtlety is revealed at the edges.

But when the eye is between the cloud and the sun, the cloud does the opposite to what it did before, because the edges of its spheres are dark, and the middle is bright. And this happens because you see the part that the sun still sees directly, and because their edges are transparent and reveal to the eye the parts that are hidden behind them. These, not being seen by the sun like the parts facing it, must necessarily be somewhat darker. It may also be that you see the minute details of these globules from below, while the sun sees them from above. And because they are not positioned in such a way as to reflect the sun's brightness as they did before, they are therefore dark.

And black clouds that often appear above clear and sun-illuminated clouds are overshadowed by the other clouds that come between them and the sun.

Moreover, the globules of clouds that face the sun reveal its dark edges because they change color with the light; and that this is true, you will look at the top of the whole cloud which is clear, because it shines in the blue of the air which is darker than the cloud.
The point has no part, and every quantity of line is limited by points.

The instant is indivisible, and every distance of time is limited by these instants.

The point has no part, and this is contained in continuous quantity.

The point has no part in continuous quantity, and the instant is indivisible in time.

Although time is contained in continuous quantity, it cannot be composed into any figure to be imagined as incorporeal; nevertheless, the spaces of its divisible length can be proportioned together.

The point has no part. The line is limited by two points. The angle is the concurrence of two lines at a single point. And the instant has no time.

Although time is numbered among the continuous quantities, because it is incorporeal, it does not have the power to be divided into various geometric figures like other corporeal quantities, and it is only associated with geometry in three ways: point, line, and proportion. A point in time is called an instant, and a line, which in geometry is terminated by two points, similarly a space of time is terminated by two instants.

Because it is invisible and incorporeal, it does not fall entirely under the power of geometry, which divides it into an infinite variety of figures, as is seen in visible and corporeal things; but it is only associated with its first principles, namely, point and line. And this point in time is to be equated with an instant; and the line, which is terminated by two points, will be equal to a space of time that is terminated by two instants. And the continuous quantity of the line is infinitely divisible; thus the space of a time can be infinitely divided. And if the divided parts of the line fall under the power of proportion, you will find the same in the divided parts of that space of time. As for proportions...

Although time is numbered among continuous quantities, being invisible and bodiless, it does not fall entirely under the geometric power that divides it into figures and bodies of infinite variety, as is seen in visible and corporeal things. Rather, it is related only to its first principles, namely, to the point and the line. The point in time is to be equated with its instant, and the line is to be compared with the length of a quantity of time. And just as points are the beginning and end of the aforementioned line, so instants are the terminus and beginning of any given space of time. And if the line is infinitely divisible, the space of time is not alien to such division; and if the divided parts of the line are proportional to one another, the parts of time will also be proportional to one another.

The point is that than which nothing can be said to be smaller, and it is the terminus of nothingness and the beginning of all things without occupying space.

The line is a length created with the motion of the point and ending at the terminus of that point's motion; than which line nothing can be said to be narrower.

The surface is composed of width and length, which is generated by the transverse motion of the line, and its extremes are the lines; than which nothing can be said to be thinner.

The body is a length that has within itself width and depth, created by the motion of the width of the surface, and its extremes are the surfaces.

Every body always has quantity, but not always weight; because line and surface are incorporeal quantities and therefore have no weight; and similarly, earth, nor water, nor any other element in themselves have weight.

The line is an abstention generated by the motion of the point, than which nothing can be narrower; and the point is that which the mind does not divide, and no smaller thing can comprehend in its mind.

The point is the common boundary between the nothingness and the front of the line; neither is it nothing, nor is it a line, nor does it occupy a space between the nothingness and the line. Therefore, the end of the nothingness and the beginning of the line are in contact with each other, but not joined; and in this contact is the point. The nothingness is the brother of this point, because all imaginable points are equal to a single point, just as all the zeros of arithmetic are in value equal to a single zero. And therefore it does not follow that many imagined points in direct contact with one another compose a line, and consequently many lines joined together by their sides, one after the other, will never form surfaces, nor will many equal surfaces placed integrally one above the other ever form a body; because among us, a body cannot be composed of incorporeal things.

The times for dividing things successively in half are equal, both in the one who begins to divide the universe with the mind and in the one who begins at the same time to divide the natural point with the mind. Therefore, from the natural point to the mathematical point, there is an infinite proportion in terms of division. As in dividing the infinite in half, one will make two finite parts, and the same will be done in the same time as the natural point; because in both divisions made in equal numbers successively, one will never arrive at the mathematical point. Therefore, things of almost infinite proportion have an equal number of divisions made in equal time with the mind, because they cannot be done in actuality; and there is no other difference except that the infinite has greater parts than the natural point.

Every continuous quantity is divisible into infinity; therefore, the division of this quantity will never reach the point, which is given as the extreme of the line. It follows that the width and thickness of the natural line are divisible into infinity.

The question is whether all infinites are equal, or one greater than another. And that cause which moves it through the veins against the natural course (desire) of heavy things is like that which moves the humors in all species of animate bodies, and if...

And just as from the lower part of the vine the water is driven to its severed branches and then falls back to its roots, penetrates them and rises again, so from the lowest depths of the sea the water rises to the tops of the mountains and through the broken veins falls downward and returns to the sea and resurfaces again; thus between below and above, so between within and without without rest, sometimes with accidental and sometimes with natural motion, sometimes of its own free will and sometimes by the force of its mover, and returning by the force of its mover, it resurfaces again and again falls; Thus when one part rises, the other descends.

Just as from the lowest depths of the sea, water rises to the tops of mountains and falls downward through broken veins, at which time other water rises; thus the entire element revolves and has often flowed through royal rivers.

So, joined together within and without, it continues to vary in constant revolution, taking on the likeness of the places through which it passes. Sometimes it rises with accidental motion, sometimes it descends with natural freedom.

Sometimes it transforms into very high clouds, and then it encloses itself in the low caverns of the earth.

It has nothing of itself, but it moves and takes everything, as it reveals itself through its clear drippings.

Thus it flows hither and thither, up and down; no peace ever rests it, it always succors where humor is lacking.

When it takes away the soil and when it gives it, to some it dumps wood to some it dumps stones, to some it offers sand to some it offers mud, it maintains firmness in its depths or in its banks; when it courses with a crumbling course, when it descends with a calm motion, when it shows itself with a turbulent face, when it appears clear and serene, when it mixes with the air in a thin fog and when it falls with the crumbling rain; when it turns into snow or blustery hail, when it wets the air with fine rain, sometimes cold and sometimes warm; but it maintains firmness in its company; when it rises in a thin fog on high, where the air, restrained, presses and moves among the other air like a sponge pressed under water, which pushes the enclosed air among the other water.

The heavy liquid moves the light liquid, that is, water moves air. And this is proven in the vessel of water and air, c d, where the air a was in d and the water was in c, the vessel c d being upside down; and thus, when the vessel was turned, the air separated from d and rose to the position b. Let the proportion of half a circle be divided into eight similar and equal triangles, finding the centers of which first. Then draw a line from center to center and you will have four lines that each terminate in the centers of two triangles, which are a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h; now take the middle of line c d and line e f, which will be r, s, and draw the line from r to s; then draw line x u from the middle of line a b and line g h; then draw line n t from the middle of line r s and from the middle of line x u. Now conclude the center of gravity of the portion be at the middle of line n t at point m.

In the margin of the last lines of the text, it is shown with letters.

Of every portion of a rectangle, the center of gravity is found in its diameter dividing it in sexquiter proportion, residing in the smaller part toward the base.

Let the portion a b c and a c be the base, which is divided equally at point d, and above d the perpendicular b d, which is the diameter of the portion, in which portion the triangle a b c is drawn. Now divide b d, the leg of the triangle a b c, at point K, which is the proportion from b K to K d, which is the ratio from the triangle to the remainder of the portion. It will follow that just as the triangle and the remainder consist of this portion, so the leg consists of the triangle and the remainder of the portion, which is b K and K d. Therefore, since the said quantities are in one proportion, as has been proven, I say that K is the center of the portion a b c, and b K is sexquiter to K d. Furthermore, divide the diameter of the two portions, called the residue, in sexquitertial proportion, and the diameters are L m and o p. Because the intersection n, being composed of two compound derivative shadows, will be a compound shadow and not a simple shadow, as the other composite shadow intersections do. This arises from the second of this, which says: the intersection of the derivative shadow, born from the intersection of the shadowy columns illuminated by a single luminous sun, will not be a simple shadow. And this arises from the first, which says: the intersection of the simple derivative shadows never acquires darkness, because all the supreme obscurities joined together do not acquire greater darkness than a single one, for if the many supreme obscurities increased in darkness in their duplications, they could not be called supreme obscurities, but rather parts of darkness. But if such intersections are illuminated by a second light placed between the eye and the intersected bodies, then such shadows will be composed shadows and will have uniform darkness both in the intersection and in the remainder.

Book One on Waters.

The lowest depth of the elements is their center. The common center is that which is equally distant from the extremes or opposite weights of the elements, and nothing can be imagined to be smaller than the center, and this is what mathematicians call a point.

2. Depth and Height.

That thing is said to be lowest which is closest to the center of the elements; it follows that that which is furthest from that center is highest.

3. Gravity.

Gravity is an accident generated by the force of one element pulled or pushed by another.

Levity is called that thing which is less heavy, because in the elements all is heaviness, but one is more or less heavy than the other.

5. Elements.

No part of an element has heaviness or lightness in the same element.

6th Water does not acquire weight unless it unites with an element or other liquid lighter and lower than itself.

Water does not move by itself unless it descends; it follows that, if it moves, it descends, and this occurs by the 6th. And if you were to say that in the refractory motion it makes after its descent, it rises upward by itself, this is not true; it is due to the weight it acquires, which is an accident, as is proved in the 3rd of this article. This accident is not part of water nor has any similarity to it, nor does it remain with it, because it is short-lived.

Water does not rest by itself unless it is contained or is contained at an equal height.

The center is that which is equally distant from the opposite ends of anything. The center is not a part. Center is that which occupies no space nor is a part of any. The center is that which is equally remote from the opposite extremes and opposite weights of anything, and nothing can be smaller.

The point is that than which nothing can be smaller. Its width, length, and depth are zero, and its ends are nothing.

The short is created by the motion of the surface toward the part seen. Its space and its ends are the surfaces, than which nothing can be thinner.

The body is created by the motion of the space of the surface, and this has width, length, and depth, and its ends are the surfaces.

The line is created by the motion of the point, and this has length without width and depth, and its ends are two points.

The point has no middle, and its ends are nothing.

The line is created by the motion of the point.

A line is a length formed by the motion of a point, and its endpoints...

Earth is in contact with water and air, and it acquires as much weight from the water as from the air; which is nothing if they have no motion. And this is taught to us by the leaves of the grasses that grow at the bottom of the water that rests on the meadows, and by the leaves and branches of the trees, and similarly by the grasses that grow at the bottom of the waters, which, since they do not bend downward, clearly do not contribute weight to the earth.

On the weight of water.

Either water has weight or it has no weight. And if it has weight, why does it not bend the leaves that grow at the bottom where it rests? And if it does not bend them, it does not impart weight to the bottom of the water. And if it does not impart weight, what supports it? It supports its own bottom, but receives no weight, because water has been proven to have no weight except over a liquid lighter than itself, such as air and fire and other liquids, such as oil and the like. And if this is so, why does a vessel filled with water weigh more in the air than a vessel filled with air? The water does not weigh on its sides, but the full vessel weighs in the air, which it will not do under water except by the weight of the material from which the vessel is made. The sea does the same thing over its vessel on earth, and the edges exposed to the air are the lips of the vessel that receives it. This vessel, being joined to the other earth, gives off its weight over the air of its antipodes as the sea rises, because these antipodal seas correspond in weight to one another because they are opposite. and the inequality of their weights, and because of this the sea is continually changing position, the centre of gravity that the earth has together with the water, also changes position.
Example of the center of the world.

Imagine the earth being drawn to the moon's position along with the water, and that the element of air fills the void of air that leaves the earth separated from itself, and that from the air a vessel filled with air is drawn. Certainly, after many ventilated motions—that is, incident and refractory motions—this vessel will come to rest around the center of the elements. And the center of the elements will remain in the air within the vessel and will not touch the vessel. Or imagine the earth concave like a ball filled with wind, then you will be certain that this center will not be in the earth, but in the air clothed by the earth.

The course of the winds changes and becomes the motion of any other wind through the openings of the valleys, where it enters and where it exits, and this happens more with low winds than with high ones, and this makes it flexible and pliable by any line, except that which is against its arrival. And if one wishes to clear and give space to the new wind, it must act like water that enters a reservoir by a line and then pours out through various conduits, but more along the line that follows the motion created by its entry, and less along the line that is furthest from that entry.

The wind gathers above the places where it strikes, and more so at the tops of mountains than at the shores they strike, because all the refracted winds end up there, that is, at the tops of the straight sides of the mountains where they strike. These winds do not then all extend transversely to follow the shape of the mountain top, but many of them go upwards in a straight line, especially those that strike closer to the bases of the mountains, although once they are above the top of the mountain they begin to curve, and after this curve they direct themselves with the course of the other wind that struck them and which had previously curved them.
Many times the course of one wind changes into the course of the other, and this arises from the percussions they make when their courses collide, which, unable to penetrate each other, force them to strike in opposite directions.

But if the aforementioned winds are not of equal strength among themselves, their refracted motions will not follow the motion of their percussive partner, but the angle of percussion of the more powerful wind will be greater than that of the lesser wind, the greater the excess of the greater wind over the lesser wind.
