Winds blowing in the same direction can be simple or mixed with other winds. That is, at one end of its latitude, it can be a narrow wind striking the broad wind, and it blows backward at equal angles, but never against its source, because it would have to re-enter itself.

And the motion of two bodies cannot intersect. It then follows that the part of the larger wind struck by the smaller wind would return backward and follow the line of the smaller wind that struck it, but it collides with the remainder of its width, which gradually bends it until it has returned to its original course.

Thus, a wind, striking itself, generates different motions and different qualities of power, because that part which is called its latitude, which pushes forward the part that was fleeing, also takes on motion refracted by the wind it strikes, and so does the part which, having been struck, flees; and the fourth which strikes the third, so that in these places it becomes denser. But the first density is greater than the last, similar to two bodies of water that strike each other, as I demonstrated in the fourth of the seventh book of the Elements of Machinery, which forms an angle at the place of its first percussion, which causes the water that is struck first to leap higher than any other part of it.

The pyramid of one mile is given a base of 4 arm lengths, and each arm length is divided into 12 ounces, so that the 4 arm lengths equal 48 ounces. I divide the length of this pyramid into 15 equal parts, so that since the mile is 3,000 arm lengths, each of the said 15 parts is 200 arm lengths. Now I want to give a rule for a pyramid of one mile up to a pyramid of 100 miles, based on the same base of 4 arm lengths, by how much it narrows at the end of 200 arm lengths above the base. That is, if the base, as has been said, was 4 arm lengths, then its pyramid will be narrowed at the end of 200 arm lengths. and so I will continue from the 200-arm end of the one-mile pyramid to the 2-arm end of the 100-mile pyramid, always subtracting the width of the pyramid 200 arm lengths from its base.

Above the 4-arm base, build 100 pyramids with equal variation from one another, with the first being one mile, the second two miles, the third three, and so on up to a hundred miles. Let each be given how much it narrows and its diameter is 200 arm lengths above the base. This makes 200 arm lengths in the first 200 arm lengths, and it will make 100 arm lengths in all the other 200-arm lengths. Since the base is 4 arm lengths, and each arm length is 12 ounces, all 48 ounces.

Let the one-mile pyramid narrow at the end of 200 arm lengths from the base. Here we will give a rule that serves all pyramids, given that the base is 4 arm lengths and each arm length is divided into 12 ounces, so that the 4 arm lengths give 48 ounces. The mile is made of 3000 arm lengths, into which the 200 arm lengths mentioned above fit 15 times; therefore, to find this narrowing at the top of 200 arm lengths above the base of 48 ounces, divide that base by 15 fifteenths of a mile, that is, by the 200 arm lengths, which equals 1/15 of the entire base. That is, you will divide these 48 ounces by 15, which equals 3 1/5 ounces, and this is how much the pyramid narrows at a distance of 200 arm lengths beyond the base. And if the pyramid were 2 miles long beyond the base, which is 30 hundred-foot cubits, divide the 48 ounces of the base by that 30, which is 1 ounce and 3/5. And so on, for a pyramid of 3 miles and 45 hundred-foot cubits, and you would divide the 48 ounces of the base by that 45 hundred-foot cubits.

The thread p q is what moves the cloth toward the scissors when the scissors open; and when the scissors close and cut, the cloth stops. Invisible before restoration; 293 x 198 mm; columns spaced 21 mm apart; watermark ('wheel') in the center 28 mm. Following the report by C. Pedretti (An "Arcus Quadrifrons" for Leo X, in "Raccolta Vinciana" XX 1964, p. 248), the restorers of the Codex Atlanticus have reassembled this folio, which in the old codex was divided into four fragments. It is likely that when Leonardo wrote on it, it was already divided into three parts, one of which was folded into four small pages, in whose precise measurements he placed drawings and notes. The current recto, which in the old codex was visible or intuited only through the transparency of the paper, has now been brought to light and reassembled. The drawing, not by Leonardo, depicts a hermaphrodite with wings instead of arms, the male and diabolical right side with a bird's claw instead of a foot, and hairy skin; the female side has pale skin, an eye on the knee, and a large V on the chest. The head ends in a long, straight horn.

If you want to shoot accurately with a blunderbuss, here's the method.

Stop the blunderbuss for the first shot; then draw it a short distance, and aim it at a wall, a door, or wherever you like; and where the bullet hits, a mark remains. From top to bottom:

The bombard with its tail between two trumpets will not be moved by the fire. The powder that is most attractive to the fire will drive the bullet more, and the more the bombard will resist.

If you fire a bombard with its hole at the end of the tail, it will escape less, because it ignites from the point of the fire forward. If you fire midway along the length of the tail, the fire would take two opposite courses and ignite twice as much powder, and the bullet would travel very quickly, causing great damage to the shelter.

If you fire a pointed tail, the bullet will escape little.

The reason why the bombard gives direction. The fire that multiplies within the body of the bombard, not finding itself in a vacuum sufficient or capable of holding its quantity, with sudden fury seeks a receptive place; This space and the air are joined by a violent repercussion. Since the air is a larger body than the fire, it resists the flame and gives way to the heavier pellet. The flame, finding itself recalcitrant to the body of the air, and the part that remains in the body unable to be disposed of, seeks to create a space capable of its growth, and pushes the body of the bombard backward. Like a rocket, which, unable to create a space for its effect, creates the cause; and therefore, the powder that ignites more quickly gives the air less room to evacuate, and that which ignites more slowly gives the air room to find space.

This flame that issues from the bombard is clearly recognized to be of marvelous power, as is evident in the expulsion of the pellet. And since this flame cannot absorb the vacuum with the speed that is its multiplication, and instead finds resistance in the air it creates, it makes of the condensed air that surrounds it a resistant body similar to the bombard; and with the flame that remains inside, which is joined to that outside, and wanting to multiply, being prevented by the resistance of the aforementioned air, it pushes the bombard as it first did the bullet, as appears in the drawing above. And this flame creates between the bombard and the percussion of the air, similar to that of a strong green spear thrown by a jouster into a resistant wall, which what the spear cannot hit with the point, does with the pedal, knocking the jouster to the ground with its resistant hardness. And that path that the bullet makes through the air is filled over a long distance with the fire that drives the bullet. Or if you were to place a man in a short wine jar, and the bottom of the jar where the feet of the enclosed man are placed were next to a wall, you would see the man, stretching out his feet, act like the burning powder of a bombard, because, unable to stretch out completely, he carries the jar backward with his head.

Four things can be deduced from this instrument: first, that wheel n, making continuous motion by the cause of wheel m, will be so slow that nothing on earth so slow could be found that its motion would not seem like lightning. Secondly, that wheel m, because of wheel n, will have such a rapid course that every other course, whether of the sun or of other planets, will appear very slow, as appears in the proof below figured by arithmetic, which, as you see, 1 leva 20 and 20 leva 400 and 400 leva 8000 and so on. The proof of the slowness of wheel n you will do as follows: there are 1000 times per hour, and when the first wheel, that is, m, will turn in one time, the second will do the same in 20, the third will complete its full turn in 400, the fourth in 8000; and thus you can see, since the fourth turns in 8 hours, in how many hours will wheel n have turned. Third, that by giving wheel n once, the third after it will give 400, and whatever touches its pole that is capable of igniting will immediately ignite. * What is the difference between a spring and a counterweight? Of the spring and the counterweight, the spring is always the most powerful, since its power is pyramidal and its greatest power is at the beginning of its motion. The counterweight has composite powers, one of which is columnar and the other pyramidal. The columnar power is that the weight is always equal in itself and pulls with equal power both at the beginning of the motion and at the end, but the pyramidal power is zero at the beginning and a lot at the end.

There may be four motions in the same body suspended from a string in a direct line, namely: hesitant from right to left, incident and refracted, and self-circulating, and also circular motion. Let us prove: let the string be be strongly twisted within itself and placed at a great obliquity. Then, being left free, it immediately generates three different motions, of which the first is circular and declining motion. The circular motion is caused by the mobile body which itself makes a circumvoluble motion around its center in the unwinding of the string which was forced to twist. The second motion is of double obliquity, of which the first is in the incident motion, the other is in the string which is lengthened in its unwinding, and this is a motion composed of two obliquities; and up to this point we have three motions. The fourth is the refracted motion; the fifth will be the circular motion that the mover can give it at the beginning of the motion. The sixth will be made in leaps, when the mover throws the body upward, which returns downward and then leaps up, and thus continues leaping in this circular motion; the first being, as has been said, the thin cord, well wound and twisted by force within itself. 1)

Every triangle cut equidistant from one of its sides separates another triangle whose sides are in the same proportion as the sides of its whole. It follows that the triangle ab e, which has side b c 10, is double its side a c 5; hence it follows that the triangle cut d f 8 is double its side a f 41); and similarly the triangle cut b e 2 is double its side d e 1. Therefore we have here 1 2 4 8 in continuous proportion; hence it follows that of four proportional numbers beginning with 1, the second is always the cube root of the fourth number.

A board of uniform thickness and weight, dropped from a point of equilibrium at an equal time, will fall through an equal and quiet medium along a perpendicular line to a point of equilibrium at the same time.

If the given board were found to have air of uniform resistance and its opposite ends were equally distant from the center of the universe, and if these ends, along with their entirety, were allowed to descend through the air at the same time, it would undoubtedly descend along a perpendicular line onto the plane beneath it and would strike and stop on that plane at the same time. The bird will never descend backward, because the center of its gravity is closer to the head than to the tail.

The bird will always descend, with all or part of its motion, along that line where the center of its gravity is closest to the extremes of the bird's latitude.

Descent, as I said, occurs entirely toward that part closest to the center of its gravity when only one part is close to that center of gravity and the extremes of the other parts opposite remain equally distant from that center. Not content with simply flying through the air, the vain and wandering parrot, overcome by the delightful flame of the candle, decided to fly into it. Its joyful movement was the cause of sudden sadness; for in the said light its thin wings were consumed, and the wretched parrot, falling all burned at the foot of the candlestick, after much weeping and repentance, wiped the tears from its moist eyes and, raising its face, said: "O false light, how many like me must you have miserably deceived in times past! When the nut was carried by a crow to a high bell tower, and was freed from its deadly beak through a crack where it fell, it prayed to the wall, by the grace that God had given it, being so eminent and great and rich in such beautiful bells and of such honorable status, to help it. For since it could not fall under the green branches of its old father, and lie in the rich earth covered with his falling leaves, it would not want to abandon it. For, finding itself in the fierce beak of the fierce crow, it declared that, escaping from it, it wanted to end its life in a small hole. At these words, the wall, moved with compassion, was happy to shelter it in the place where it had fallen. And in a short time the nut began to open and put down roots between the cracks in the stones, and these began to spread out and send out branches out of its cavern. And those, having soon risen above the building and swollen the twisted roots, began to open the walls and expel the ancient stones from their former places. Then the wall slowly and in vain lamented the cause of its damage and, soon opened, collapsed a large part of its limbs.

The monkey, finding a nest of small birds, joyfully approached them, and, as they were already ready to fly, could only catch the smallest. Filled with joy, she went to her lair with it in her hand. And beginning to consider this little bird, she began to kiss it; and out of undying love, she kissed it so much, twisted it, and squeezed it, that she took its life. It is said of those who, through not punishing their children, come to harm.

The forager, being stung in its slender branches, overflowing with new fruit, by the sharp claws and beaks of the importunate blackbirds, complained with pitiful regret to the blackbird, begging her, after she removed them and her beloved fruit, not to at least strip it of the leaves that protected it from the scorching rays of the sun, and not to strip it of its tender skin with her sharp claws. Seeing the laurel and myrtle cutting down the pear tree, they cried out in a loud voice: "O pear tree, where are you going? Where is the pride you had when you had your ripe fruit? Seeing the chestnut tree on the fig tree, the man bent its branches toward itself and plucked the ripe fruit, which it placed in its open mouth, undoing and tearing them apart with its hard teeth, shaking its long branches and saying in a tumultuous murmur: "O fig tree, how much less obligated are you to nature than I am! Then the fig tree began to laugh together with his children and, stopping the laughter, said: "You know that man is of such ingenuity, that he knows how to make you poor of your fruit with poles and stones and twigs, drawn from between your branches, and trample the fallen ones with feet or stones, so that your fruit comes out torn and mangled outside the armed house. The wretched willow, finding itself unable to enjoy the pleasure of seeing its slender branches grow to the desired size and rise toward the sky—because of the vine and whatever other plants were nearby, it was always crippled, branched, and ruined—and gathered within itself all its spirits, and with them opened and flung wide the doors of its imagination. And remaining in constant thought and searching with it the universe of plants1), to which of them it could connect without needing the aid of its ties; and while dwelling for a while in this nourishing imagination, the pumpkin suddenly came to mind. And it toppled all its branches in great joy, seeming to have found companionship for its longed-for purpose—since it is better suited to tying others than to being tied itself—and having made this decision, it raised its branches toward the sky. He was waiting for some friendly bird that would be the intermediary for his desire. Among them, seeing the magpie near him, he said to her: "O gentle bird, I pray you by the help you found these days, from the morning, in my branches, when the hungry, cruel and rapacious falcon wanted to devour you, and by those reposes you often used on me, when your wings asked for rest, and by those pleasures you have already used among my branches, playing with your companions in your lovemaking, I pray you to find the pumpkin and obtain from it some of its seeds, and tell those that, once they have been born, that I will treat them no differently than if I had generated them from my body; and similarly use all those words that are persuasive with a similar intention, although you, teacher of languages, need not be taught. And if you will do this, I am happy to receive your nest on the birth of my branches together with your family without paying any rent. " Then the magpie, having made and confirmed some new agreements with the willow, and even if she never accepted snakes or martens on her, raised her tail and lowered her head and threw herself from the branch, she returned her weight to her wings; and beating them in the fleeting air, now here now there curiously with the rudder of her tail, she came to a pumpkin, and with a nice greeting and some good words she obtained the requested seeds. And having led them to the willow, she was welcomed with a happy face; and having scratched the ground near the willow a little with her feet, with her beak, in a circle around it, she planted the seeds. Which in a short time, growing, began with the growth and opening of her branches to occupy all the branches of the willow, and with her large leaves to take away the beauty of the sun and the sky. And not satisfied with such evil, following the pumpkins, he began, with an unseemly weight, to pull the tips of the tender branches toward the ground, to their strange tortures and discomfort. Then, shaking himself and collapsing in vain to make the pumpkins fall, and wandering in vain for several days in a similar deception, because the good and strong connection denied such thoughts, seeing the wind pass, he implored it, and it blew strongly. Then the old and empty willow stem split in two down to its roots, and, having fallen in two, he wept in vain and recognized that he was born to never be happy.

A surface is that which separates bodies from the air, or, I mean, air from bodies; that is, the area between the body and the surrounding air. If the air touches the body, there is no space left for another body to be placed. Hence, the surface is concluded to have no body, and therefore has no need of space.

A surface is that which divides bodies from the surrounding air, or, you might say, that which divides and defines the air from the things incorporated in it. And if the air and the bodies included in it are in continuous contact, no space remains between them. Since the surface is that which displays the shape of bodies, it is a surface which has being within itself. And if the air and the body touch, there is no space left; hence, it is concluded that the surface has being but no space. Therefore, the surface is equal to nothingness, and all nothingness is equal to the smallest part, if it could have a part. Therefore, we would say that surfaces, lines, and points are equal to each other, and each in itself is equal to the other two combined.

Left column:

Surface is the division made by the body of air with the bodies included in it, and it is not a division of the body that surrounds it, nor of that which surrounds it; rather, it is the contact that the two bodies make together. Therefore, if these bodies are in constant contact, it is necessary that nothing intervene between them, and therefore the surface included therein is nothing. This surface has a name and not a being, because that which has being has a place; having no place, it is similar to nothingness, which has a name without being. Hence the part of nothingness, having only the name and not the being, this part is equal to the whole, so that the point and the line are concluded to be equal to the surface.

Every body resists its friction with a force equal to a quarter of its weight, since the motion is in a plane plane and the surfaces are dense and smooth.

Multiply the arm of the counterweight by as many times as it receives the arm of the friction of the pole, and subtract one from the sum, and with the remainder divide the friction of the pole, and multiply this by 4, and the sum will be the counterweight of the friction of the weight of itself and of the aforementioned pole. The multiplication1) of the arm of the counterweight, made by as many times 4 as it receives within itself the arm of the friction, is done so that the calculation of the weight of the pole divided by 4, as I said in the penultimate2), is easy in its calculation. And from the sum subtract one. This one is the true friction of the counterweight, that is, its quarter. And with the remainder divide the friction of the pole. This partition serves no other purpose than to find the denomination of the parts being calculated. Therefore, that one that you subtracted has taken the name of one: that is, whether it is a whole, a half, or a quarter. Then this one, multiplied by 4, makes this multiplication the counterweight of the friction of the pole, and also the counterweight of this one multiplied by 4, which becomes the friction of the counterweight itself. And thus, the powers remain equal to the resistances. Multiply the arm of the counterweight by as many times 4—this is defined in the penultimate section3)—as the number of times it receives its opposite arm. That is, if the arm of the counterweight receives the arm of the friction once, multiply that arm of the counterweight once by 4; and if it receives 2, multiply it twice by 4, that is, multiply it by 8; and if it receives it three times, multiply it three times by 4, that is, by 12, and so on to infinity, and subtract one from the sum. This subtracted unit does not yet have a name, but is set aside and will be the friction of the counterweight from which we seek the quantity of the weight. And with the remainder divide the friction of the pole. At the top right, I draw with the spheres of fire and air, clouds, and rain:

Element of fire. - Half region of air. Water, placed between fire and water, participates in both water and fire, but more so in one than in the other the closer it is to one than the other. It follows that it participates less in each the more remote it is from them; this separation occurs in the middle of the region of air. Therefore, this half region is in the first degree of cold. From this it follows that the part of the cloud that comes closest to this half region cools more. Therefore, the heat of the sphere of fire, the attractor of this cloud, is less potent, and for this reason it follows that the motions of the moist grains, which compose clouds, are slower. And for this reason it happens that in the elevation of the grains of moisture, that which rises most to the vicinity of this half-region, the more it is slowed down, and that which follows it is faster than it, so it catches up with it, and often happens that it strikes it from below and is incorporated into it, increasing its quantity and weight. And for this reason the air, unable to support it, gives way to its descent, which strikes all the droplets that impede its motion, and incorporates many of them into itself, and by acquiring heaviness, acquires speed of descent. Therefore, once its entire cloud has been penetrated, with each degree of descent it will acquire degrees of diminution, and many times these grains will not be brought to the ground. But if these grains, at the highest point of their height, acquire such gravity that their weight causes them to descend rapidly, this motion will undoubtedly increase in size, since it will reach the droplets descending from below with such velocity, and will incorporate them into itself; and this will be the increase in weight at each stage of its descent.

Here the two streams of water meet along line a b and in this percussion they completely revolve around each other, so that they strike each other from the surface to the bottom. And once this revolution is created, it is pushed out of the place where it was created by the impetus of the overflowing waters; and in this transformation, this revolution has acquired two motions: its natural one around its center, and the second one it acquires from place to place. Therefore, this will be a straight, circumvoluble motion, which, when it occurs in water or air, removes the soil with great excavations and scrapings.
When the streams of water are not equal, the revolutions are caused by the counteraction of these waters along a straight line. But if these water courses are not equal, their collisions will carry the waters' vortices toward the shore of the less powerful water, and, boring beneath it with its duplicated motions—that is, straight and convoluted—they go on digging out the banks below, where the upper parts supported by these, undermining their missing foundations, are again consumed by it.
When the waters are unequal, their collisions become vortices, and the less powerful water enters with the branches of the lower backwaters under the branches of the higher backwaters, that is, those born from the more powerful waters. When the water of greater power strikes the water of less power, then the line of the backwaters curves, entering with its convexity into the body of the water of less power. When the curvature of the line of the backwaters enters with its convexity into the water of lesser strength, then this lesser water remains at that boundary without motion, where it swells and rises and acquires gravity; then, due to the weight it has acquired, it multiplies in strength and exerts an impetus against the water that previously exceeded it, so that the line of the backwaters bends in the opposite direction, and where previously it was convex, it becomes concave. And so the lesser water is often pushed by the greater water, and the greater is pushed by the lesser, but the lesser is pushed all the more the lesser it is of lesser strength.

Why the bird is supported on the air.
The air that is struck with greater velocity condenses with greater concentration of itself.
This is proven because the least dense fluid body will never support the densest, as we see from experience with the anvil resting on molten bronze, and molten gold and silver resting on molten lead. And because air is a body capable of condensing within itself, when it is struck by a motion of greater velocity than its flight, it condenses within itself and forms itself among the other air like a cloud, that is, of that density.
But when the bird finds itself caught in the wind, it can support itself on it without flapping its wings, because the same function that the wing performs against the air, while the air is motionless, the air moved performs against the wings, while the latter are motionless.

The echoic voice is continuous and discontinuous, alone and accompanied, of brief and long continuation, of finite and infinite, sudden or distant. Experiment of the force that an iron wire of various lengths can exert.
I remember how you must experiment with holding, or how much a wire can support. You will use this method for this experiment. Attach a wire about two arm's length long to a strong place. Then attach a basket or a hopper, or whatever you like, into which you will pour a hopper of fine sand through a small hole. And when the wire can no longer support and breaks, attach a small clamp that immediately closes the hopper's hole, so that no more sand falls into the basket, which will fall on its feet, because half a finger will fall from above. And note how much weight the wire broke, and note in which part of itself the wire breaks, and repeat this test several times to confirm whether it always breaks in the same place. Then make this thread half as short as before, and note how much more weight it supports. And then make it 1/4 of the original length, and gradually make it in different lengths, noting the weight that each one breaks and the place where it breaks. And you will do this test with each metal and wood, stones, ropes and everything that is capable of supporting. And make a general rule for each thing. And you will do the same with earthly supports, that is, those that support one end of themselves fixed on the ground or towards the earth.

The greater the declination, the faster the motion of water.

A wave is the impression of a repressed percussion, which will be greater or lesser in proportion to the greater or lesser percussion. A wave is never alone, but is mixed with as many other waves as there are inequalities in the object where the wave is generated. At the same time, innumerable other waves, moving in different directions, will move on the greatest wave of a sea. If you throw a stone into the sea from different sides, all the waves that strike those sides will refrain from the impact and, in the collision of the others, will never impede one another's course. Waves of equal size, motion, and power, when colliding with opposite motions, will refrain from each other's impact at equal angles. The wave that arises from the greatest percussion will be of greater eminence, and so on. The wave generated in small seas will often return to and from the place it struck. The more often the wave will return and return, the smaller the width of the sea where it is generated, and so on. In the greatest sea only the waves move without refraction; In small seas, the same percussion gives rise to many incident and refractory motions. The largest wave is clothed with innumerable other waves, which move in different directions. These waves deepen more or less, depending on their greater or lesser power. The largest wave is clothed with various waves, which move in as many different directions as the places from which they are divided were varied. The same wave, generated in a small sea, acquires a greater number of other waves above itself, the more it experiences percussion and refractory motion on opposite shores. The motion of the wave is greater than the motion of the water of which it is composed. Many waves facing different directions can be generated between the surface and the bottom of the same body of water at the same time. Revertiginous motions can follow the straight motions of each wave. All the impressions of percussion made on water can penetrate one another without destroying them. One wave never penetrates the other, but only refracts from the site of their percussion.

Common sense is that which judges things given to it by the other senses.

* Common sense is moved by things given to it by the five senses. And these senses are moved by objects, and these objects, sending their likenesses to the five senses, are transferred from them to the understanding and from there to the common sense; and there, being judged, they are sent to the memory where they are, by their power, more or less reserved.

* The five senses are these: seeing, hearing, touching, tasting, and smelling.

Ancient speculators concluded that that part of man's judgment is caused by an instrument, to which the other five refer through the understanding. They called this instrument common sense, and said this sense is in the middle. And they use this name of common sense only because it is the common judgment of the other five senses, namely: seeing, hearing, touching, tasting, and smelling. The common sense is moved by the understanding, which is placed between it and the senses. The understanding is moved by the likenesses of things given to it by the superficial instruments, that is, the senses, which are placed between external things and the understanding; and similarly the senses are moved by objects. The likenesses of surrounding things send their likenesses to the senses, and the senses transfer them to the understanding, the understanding sends them to the common sense, and from there they are established in the memory and are retained there more or less according to the importance or power of the given thing. That sense is swifter in its function, which is closest to the understanding, which is the eye, superior and prince of the others, of which alone we will treat and leave the others aside so as not to stray from our matter. Experience tells us that the eye extends to ten different natures of objects; namely: light and darkness—the one cause of the other nine, the other privation—color and body, shape and location, repulsion and proximity, motion and rest.

Of the nature of seeing.

I say that seeing is operated by all animals through light. And if anyone should allege against this the sight of nocturnal animals, I will say that these too are subject to a similar nature, since clearly understood (4) the senses, receiving the likenesses of things, do not send out any virtue of themselves, but rather, through the air that is between the object and the sense, incorporates into itself the species of things and by the contact it has with the sense, it transmits them to it, if the objects either by their nature or by their smell are sent by the spiritual powers to the ear or nose. Here light is not necessary nor is it used. The forms of objects do not enter into the air by likeness, unless they are luminous; this being so, the eye cannot receive it from that air which does not have it and which touches its surface. If you wanted to speak of many animals that prey at night, I would say that when they lack the little light that their eyes naturally provide, they rely on the power of hearing and smell, which are not impeded by darkness and far surpass man. If you consider a cat leaping between many vessels during the day, you will see them remain safe, and if she does the same at night, she will break many. Nocturnal birds do not fly unless the moon shines, in whole or in part; rather, they feed between the setting of the sun and the complete darkness of night.

No body can be complete without light and shadow. Light and shadow are caused by light.

The 12 portions of the included subdouble circle weigh the 6 portions of the circle that includes it; and this arises because the two circles are double one another, and the number of these portions increases as their figures diminish, which, by having diminished by half their figures, have increased by half their number; that is, the double portions are 6, and the subdouble portions are made up of 12 and are equal to the value of these six. From what is said above, always assume that the number of the 6 maximum portions is an aliquot part of the number of portions into which they must be divided. As if the six maximum portions above had to divide the number of the 12 internal portions, which the divider enters twice into 12; therefore, six, which enters twice into 12, is an alicota part of that twelve, because it divides it into two parts similar to itself; and the 18 is divided from it by 6 into 3 equal parts, and the 24 into 4, and so on infinitely.

Here the 6 largest portions are the aliquot part, or you could say the multiplicative part, of the 18 portions included by them. And this arises because the two circles are in triplicate proportion to each other. Therefore, the numbers of the portions of the circles have in themselves the same proportion as the proportions of the circles including each other have in themselves.

Subtracting 12 from 84 is as much as 72. Let us prove it this way. I have here the 84 portions of the first figure and the 72 of the second figure, which quantities exceed each other by a seventh of their number. If we want to equalize these numbers with the quantities, it is necessary to reduce the real quantities by the greater sum by a seventh of their real quantity; that is, if 84 exceeds 72 by a number of 12, then 72 exceeds 84 by 12 of real quantity. 1) Therefore, we will reduce the 84 portions into 42 bisangles and the 72 portions into 36 bisangles. And we will do this to avoid confusion.

And for this reason we will increase each of the 36 bisangles by the seventh part of their size, which will be 42, or we will decrease each of the 42 bisangles by the seventh part of their size, and so that they will be 36. Where the science of weights is deceived by practice.

The science of weights is deceived by its practice, and in many respects it does not accord with that science, nor is it possible to harmonize them. And this arises from the poles of the scales, through which the science of such weights is made. These poles, among the ancient philosophers, were placed in the nature of mathematical lines and in some places in mathematical points, which points and lines are incorporeal, and practice places them corporeal, because necessity so dictates, wishing to support the weight of these scales together with the weights judged upon them. I have found that the ancients were deceived in this judgment of weights, and this deception arose because in much of their science they used corporeal poles and in a large part mathematical poles, that is, mental or incorporeal; these deceptions I set out below.

The black face on the first object is very horrible and frightening to look at, especially the swollen, red eyes, set under the fearful, dark lashes, which make time shudder and the earth tremble. And believe me, there is no man so fierce who, wherever he rolled his fiery eyes, would willingly not put on wings to escape, for Lucifer of hell seemed an angelic face compared to it. The nose was wrinkled with broad anuses, from which protruded many large bristles, under which was the wrinkled mouth with thick lips, at the ends of which were hairs like those of cats and yellow teeth. It advances over the heads of the men on horseback, from the backs of the feet up. And being displeased by the great stooping and being overcome by the importunity of the pretext..., her anger turned to fury, and she began to enter the crowd with her feet, driven by the fury of her powerful legs, and with her kicks she threw the men into the air, who fell no differently on the other men, as if it had been a heavy hailstorm. And many were those who, dying, said[r]2) death. And this cruelty lasted until the dust stirred up by the hailstones, raised into the air, forced this infernal fury to retreat backwards. And we continued our flight. Oh, how many vain attacks were used against this devilish creature, to whom every offense was nothing! O wretched people, impregnable fortresses are of no avail to you, nor are the high walls of cities, nor are multitudes, nor houses or palaces! Nothing remains for you except small underground holes and caves; like crabs or crickets or similar animals, you find salvation and escape. Oh, how many pitiful mothers and fathers were deprived of their children! Oh, how many miserable women deprived of their company! Certainly, my dear Benedetto, I do not believe that, since the world was created, a public lament, a public weeping, was ever seen made with such terror. Certainly in this case the human race has reason to envy every other generation of animals, since, if the eagle surpasses other birds in power, they are not surpassed in swiftness of flight, so that swallows with their swiftness escape the prey of scallop, dolphins with their swift flight escape the prey of whales and great sperm whales; but we, wretched creatures, no flight avails us, since this, with its slow pace, far surpasses the course of any swift steed.
I do not know what to say or do, and yet I seem to find myself standing with my head bowed in the great throat, and remaining buried in confused death in the great belly.

How many ways are there for a bird to turn its straight course into a curved path?

Figure of a bird in flight:

The bird that wishes to turn its straight course into a curved path without rising or falling from its height beats its wing on the convex side of its curved motion more times than the wing on the concave side of that motion.

Figure of a bird:

The wing of a bird that flaps its wings raises the shoulder of those wings more forward than backward. And this is done to acquire motion, because if the wings moved equally from high to low, the bird would not move from its original position.

Figure of a bird:

The bird bends its straight course toward the side from which the wing is lowered most; and it is as if this wing were struck more by the wind than the other.

Figures of birds on a wavy line:

Of the bird that flies in leaps.

The bird that flies in leaps acquires impetus in its descent because, by closing its wings, it acquires weight, thus becoming swift. Hence it follows that the refracted motion is more powerful, to which, by adding the flapping of the wings, it doubles the power of the simple refracted motion. By this doubling, the refracted motion becomes longer than it would have been without the addition of the flapping of the wings. And this is the very reason why the refracted motion is equal to its incident motion and why the sum of the flight is equal in its lowness and also in its highness.

Figure of a Bird:

When a bird descends at a great angle without flapping its wings, all the tips of its wings and tail bend upward, and this motion is slow, and the bird is not supported solely by the air below it, but by the lateral air, to which the convexity of its feathers, bent between equal angles, is visible.

On the Motion of the Fingers.

The motions of the fingers are principal (1), namely, ascending and bending. The stretching and bending vary in ways: sometimes it bends all in one piece over the first joint, sometimes it bends or straightens half over the second joint, and sometimes it bends entirely in itself, and at the same time bends at all three joints. And if the first two joints are prevented from bending, then the third joint will be bent more easily than before, nor will it ever be able to bend by itself alone, since the other joints are free, and unless all three joints are bent. In addition to the aforementioned motions, there are four other principal ones, two of which are up and down and two others from here and there, and each of these is performed with its own simple chord. From these, infinite other motions follow, always performed with two strings, and, releasing one of the strings, it continues to take up the other. The thick strings were made inside the finger, and the thin ones with holes. The strings were made inside each joint, but without holes.

Of Motion and Weight.

For equal motions performed at equal times, the mover will always have greater power than the moving body. And the mover will be more powerful than the moving body the more the motion of the moving body exceeds the length of its mover's motion. But the difference between the mover's power and the moving body will be smaller the less the length of the motion performed by the moving body exceeds the motion of the mover. But understand, reader, that in this case we must take into account air, which condenses more in front of the moving body the greater the velocity of the moving body; for this air is condensable toward infinity. This cannot apply to motions performed by moving bodies in water, which is incondensable, as is demonstrated by placing it in a narrow-mouthed vessel, which, lacking the ingenuity of any mover, will be filled with more than the vessel's natural capacity requires. And the opposite is true of air, which, when forced into vessels with very narrow openings containing some water, and the vessel is bent so that the enclosed water is interposed between the perforation of the vessel and the condensed air, the force of the condensed air then drives the water out of the vessel with such force that it penetrates the air for a long time, until the air, which remains in the vessel, returns to its original natural rarity. But to return to our purpose, we would say that among bodies of equal gravity, that which occupies more air with its front dividing the air will have the slowest motion; and conversely, when it occupies less air, it does the opposite, but not by extending itself to such a thinness that it loses weight, because where there is no weight, there is no local motion within the air.

No local motion can occur within the air unless it is due to a density greater or lesser than the density of the air itself. And if, for the adversary, it were said that the same density that the condensed air acquires in relation to the moving object acts similarly in relation to the mover, and all the more so in relation to the mover the more it is in contact with a greater quantity of air, impacted and condensed, than its moving object, as we see in the hand when throwing a stone through the air,—here (4) one responds that it is impossible for the motion of the mover combined with the motion of the moving object to be faster or slower than the motion of the moving object, nor ever between any part of accidental motion that is equal to the velocity of the motion of the mover. And this is proven in accidental motion, where the moving object acquires degrees of slowness at every degree of motion, although the impact of the moving object is greater when somewhat distant from the mover than when nearby.

And we see this in the arrow of the bow resting with its point on the wood, which, even if the string pushes it with all the power of the bow, penetrates very little into the wood, while the opposite does, having some motion. Some say that as the arrow moves, it prepares a wave of air in front of it, which wave, through its motion, does not impede the arrow's course. But this is false, [because] every moving object strains and impedes its mover. Therefore, the air flooded before the arrow is flooded by the motion of the arrow and gives little or no help in motion to its mover, which must be moved by the same mover; rather, it impedes and shortens the motion of the moving object. * Among the powerful causes of earthly disasters, it seems to me that rivers, with their disastrous floods, hold sway, not fire, as some have claimed, since fire ends its abyss where it lacks nourishment.

Among the irreparable and harmful furies, the flooding of disastrous rivers must certainly be considered superior to every other horrible and terrifying movement, and not, as some have claimed, that the conflagration of fire surpasses it. I find the opposite, since fire consumes those who nourish it and is consumed along with the nourishment. The movement of the water, maintained by the sloping valleys, also ends and dies together with the lowest depth of the valley; but fire is caused by the nourishment, and the movement of the water by the depth. The fire's nourishment is disunited, and the damage will be disunited and separated, and the fire dies where nourishment is lacking. And the declension of the valleys is united, and the damage will be united with the ruinous course of the river, until, in company with its valleys, it ends in the sea, the universal lowliness and sole repose of the wandering waters of rivers. But with what words can I describe the nefarious and frightening evils against which no human remedy avails? But with its swollen and proud waves it undermines the high mountains, undermines the strongest embankments, uproots the deep-rooted plants, and with its rapacious waves, roiling the cultivated fields, it carries with it the intolerable toils of wretched and weary farmers. It leaves the valleys denuded and vile due to the poverty it has abandoned.

Among the irreparable and harmful furies, the inundation of destructive rivers must certainly be ranked above every other horrible and terrifying damage. To melt pearls.

If you want to make a paste of small pearls, take some lemon juice and put them in a tong, and let them melt overnight. Once they are set, throw away that juice and add new water, and do this two or three times until the paste is very thin. Then wash the paste with clean water many times until all the lemon juice is released. Once this is done, let the paste dry until it turns into powder. Then take some well-beaten egg white and let it sit. With this, soften the powder until it turns into paste. From this, make pearls as large as you like and let them dry. Then place them on a small lathe and burnish them, either with a toothpick or with a crystal or chalcedony burnisher. Burnish them until they regain their original luster. I believe that mother-of-pearl is the same process as pearls.

Of muscles.

Nature has arranged in man the official muscles that direct the nerves, which can move the limbs according to the will and desire of the common sense, similar to the officers distributed by a lord throughout various provinces and cities, who in their ranks represent and obey the will of that lord. And the officer who has obeyed the verbal commands given to him by his lord more than once in a single instance will then do for himself in the same instance something that does not deviate from the will of that lord. Thus we often see the fingers, which, learning with the utmost obedience the things on an instrument commanded by their judgment, after having learned them, will play them without that judgment attending to them. Do not the muscles that move the legs also perform their function without man's knowledge?

Vessel with a perforated bottom:

Here the question is: if a vessel has its bottom perforated with equal holes like sieves, which of the holes will pour out more water in the same amount of time. To experiment and establish a rule, you will do this: unplug only one hole at a time and weigh its water against it for the distance of a fall of one arm, or more or less as you prefer. But make sure that other water restores the vessel, which pours, without any percussion, so that it does not force any part of the bottom of the vessel receiving it and that the vessel always has the same weight of water; and to do this, it is necessary that the vessel receiving the water be separate from the one pouring it.

All cases of perspective1 are understood by means of the five terms of mathematics, namely point, line, angle, surface and body. Of these, the point is alone in its generation2, and this point has no height, nor width, nor length, nor depth; hence it is concluded that it is indivisible and has no place. Line is of 3 natures, namely straight, curved, and flexible. It is that which has no width, nor height, nor depth; hence it is indivisible, except by its length; its terms are 2 points. Angle is the terminus of 2 lines at the point, and they are of 3 natures, namely straight, acute, and obtuse. Surface is called that which is the terminus of bodies, and has no depth, rather it is indivisible in the said depth, like the line or point, and is only divided by length or width. These are of as many kinds as there are bodies that create them. Body is that which has height, breadth, length, and depth, and is divisible in all directions. These bodies are of infinite and varied forms. Visible bodies are of only two kinds, the first of which is figureless, or has some distinct or finite ends; and [if] they exist, they are insensible, so that their color is barely discernible. The second kind of visible bodies is that whose surface terminates and distinguishes their figure. The first kind, which is without surface, is that of those bodies which are subtle or liquid, which easily melt and mix with other subtle bodies, like mud with water, like fog or smoke with air, like the element of air with fire and other similar things, which with their outer parts are mixed with their neighboring bodies, so that through this mixture their edges are confused and insensible, so they are found without surface because they enter into one another's body, hence such bodies are said to be without surface. The second kind of bodies is divided into two other natures, namely transparent and opaque. Transparent is that which on every side shows its whole and occupies nothing after itself, like glass, crystal, water and the like. The second kind of bodies whose surface shows and defines its shape is called opaque. This is the one that must be discussed at length, since infinite cases arise from it.

The air is filled with infinite similarities of things, which are scattered within it, and all are represented in all and all in each. Thus it happens that if two mirrors are turned so that they look at each other along a straight line, the first will be reflected in the second and the second in the first. The first, which is reflected in the second, carries with it its own similarity with all the similarities represented within it, among which is the species of the second mirror, and so on from [similarity] to similarity they go on to infinity, so that each mirror has within it infinite mirrors, each smaller than the other, and within one another. Thus, by this example, it is clearly proved that each thing sends its likeness to all places that can see that thing, and conversely that that thing is capable of taking in all the likenesses of the things represented before it. Therefore, the eye sends its likeness into the air to all the objects that are opposite to it and receives them within itself, that is, on its surface, from where the common sense takes them and considers them, and sends those that please it to memory. If the eye sees something too close, it cannot judge it well, as happens to someone who wants to see the tip of the nose. Therefore, as a general rule, nature teaches that a thing will never be seen perfectly unless the distance between the eye and the thing seen is at least similar to the size of the face.

The air is filled with the particles caused by the objects surrounding it. Let us consider the stars that appear at night: there is no part in this hemisphere of ours where the radiant lines caused by them are finite that does not encompass all the objects, the cause of those radiant lines; and so they are all in the air and all appear in the part, and each star is entirely in the part and entirely in the air. I say that objects fill the air with their likenesses.
This second reason is proven in the sun, which sends forth from itself two kinds of reasoning: the first luminous, the other heat. The luminous all...
That the air attracts to itself like a magnet all the likenesses of the things that surround it, not only the forms of bodies but also their natures, is clearly seen in the sun, which is a hot and luminous body. All the air that is its object is entirely embodied with light and heat and all receives within itself the form of the cause of the heat and splendor and in every minimal part does the same.
The north wind demonstrates this same thing through the magnet, and the moon and other planets do the same without diminishing its own nature. Among terrestrial things, musk and other odors do the same.

Painting, or rather, painted figures, must be made in such a way that those who view them can easily discern the concept of their minds through their attitudes. And if you have to make a good man speak, make his actions accompany the good words; and similarly, if you have to depict a bestial man, make him with fierce movements, throwing his arms toward the listener, and his head and chest, extended from his feet, accompany the speaker's hands. Like the mute man, who, seeing two speakers, although deprived of hearing, nevertheless understands the theme of their dispute through the speakers' actions and gestures. I once saw in Florence a man who was accidentally deaf, who, if you spoke to him loudly, did not understand you, and if you spoke softly without a sound, he understood you only by the movement of his lips. Now you might ask me: does not someone who speaks loudly move his lips as if he were soft? And if one person lip-synchs like the other, will the other not be understood as if he were the one? In this matter I leave the verdict to experience: make one speak softly and then loudly and pay attention to the lips.

All falcate pyramids of equal sides, uniformly unequal, that arise on the circumference of a circle and end at its center are equal, even if they are of varying lengths, because the space from the center to the circumference is parallel, and the straight lines that pass through it are equal.
Geometric proportions will not be changed by increasing the greater and lesser extremes of each of their parts equally. Let 6 be 12, that is, double. Now increase the third of 12, which is 4, and you will obtain 16; and increase the third of 6, which is 2, and you will obtain 8; so that you see that the same proportion is observed, because it doubles as before.

So, according to geometrical rules, adding and decreasing is understood according to their parts; that is, if you add a quarter to one, you will also add a quarter to the other, and so on equally according to the said parts. And if you subtract a third from one, you also subtract a third from the other; but in arithmetic, increasing and decreasing is understood according to the equality of differences. When the lesser and greater extremes of each geometrical proportion increase equally, the same proportion always remains unchanged.

When both the arithmetical extremes of any proportion are increased equally, the geometric proportion always diminishes. Let the proportion be double between 6 and 12, to which extremes you add 2, and then it will be 8 and 14, and they will have increased equally arithmetically; but the geometric proportion, which was double, is diminished because it has been made 2, because between 8 and 14 it is a proportion super tripartiens quartas, that is, one is double and the other is 1 and 3/4, so that it lacks 1/4 from the geometric one.

When both the extremes of each proportion are decreased equally arithmetically, the geometric proportion that was before always increases. Let 6 and 12 be equally arithmetically removed from their extremes, that is, 2 for each; there will remain 4 and 10. I say the proportion between 4 and 10 is greater than the double that was previously between 6 and 12.

How painting declines and disappears from age to age, when painters have no other source of excellence than the finished painting.
How painting...
The painter's painting will be of little excellence if he takes the paintings of others as sources of excellence; but if he learns from natural things, he will bear good fruit, as we saw in painters after the Romans, who always imitated one another and, from age to age, always went, that art, in decline. After these came the Florentine Giotti, who (not content to imitate the works of his master Cimabue, not having...) was born in lonely mountains, inhabited only by goats and similar animals. Nature, inclined by this art, began to draw on the rocks the actions of the goats for which he was a keeper, and thus began to paint all the animals found in the country, in such a way that, after much study, he surpassed not only the masters of his age, but all those of many past centuries. After this, the art fell back, because everyone imitated the paintings made, and so from century to century it continued to decline, until Thomas of Florence, nicknamed Masaccio, showed with a perfect work that those who took anything other than nature, the mistress of masters, as excellence, labored in vain. Thus I wish to say of these mathematical matters, that those who study only the works of nature and not the works of nature are by art grandchildren, not children, of that same nature, the mistress of good masters. O, the utter folly of those who blame those who learn from nature, leaving aside the works of nature, her disciples!

harmful marvel, which serves to advance our purpose. This Mount
Taurus is what many say is the yoke of Mount Caucasus; but having
wanted to clarify myself, I wanted to speak with some
of those who live above the Caspian Sea, who show that, although their

of greater height, and therefore confirm that it is the true Mount Caucasus, because Caucasus in the Iscitic language means supreme height. And indeed there is no news that the east, nor the west, has a mountain of such great height, and the proof of this is that the inhabitants of the countries that lie to the west see the rays of the sun, which illuminates, up to a quarter of the night, a large part of its summit, and the same happens in those countries that lie to the east.
Quality and quantity of Mount Taurus.
The shadow of this Taurus ridge is so high that when the sun is at noon in mid-June, its shadow extends to the beginning of Sarmatia, which is 12 days, and in mid-December it extends to the Hyperborean Mountains, which is a month's journey towards the north. And its side opposite the blowing wind is always full of clouds and fog, because the wind that opens up when the rock strikes, closes up after the rock itself and thus carries the clouds with it from all sides and leaves them in their percussion. And it is always filled with the percussion of arrows because of the great multitude of clouds that are lodged there, so that the rock is completely shattered and full of great ruins. This 4 at its roots is inhabited by very rich peoples and is full of beautiful springs and rivers, and fertile and abundant in every good thing, especially in the parts that face south; But when you ascend about three miles, you begin to find forests of large firs, pines, beeches, and other similar trees. After this, for another three miles, you find prairies and very large pastures; and all the rest up to the rise of Mount Taurus is eternal snow that never leaves for any time, extending to a height of about fourteen miles in all. From this rise of Taurus to a height of one mile, clouds never pass, which are 15 miles here, which is about five miles high in a straight line and about the same height as the top of the horns of Taurus, in which from the middle upwards one begins to find warming air, and no blowing winds are felt, but nothing can live there for long. Nothing grows here except a few birds of prey, which nest in the high clefts of Taurus and then descend beneath the clouds to hunt their prey on the grassy mountains. This is all simple rock, that is, from the clouds on up, and it is very white rock, and one cannot reach the high summit because of its rugged and dangerous ascent.

To the Diodarius of Syria, lieutenant of the sacred Sultan of Babylon.
The new event that has happened in these northern parts of ours, which I am sure will terrify not only you but the entire universe, will be told to you successively in order, showing first the effect and then the cause.
Finding myself in this part of Erminia, lovingly and diligently carrying out the office for which you sent me, and in making a start in those parts that seemed to me to be most suited to our purpose, I entered the city of Calindra, near our borders. This city is located on the shores of that part of Mount Taurus that is divided by the Euphrates, and looks towards the horns of the great Mount Taurus to the west. These horns are of such a height that they seem to touch the sky, for in the universe there is no terrestrial part higher than its summit. And always four hours before day it is struck by the rays of the sun in the east, and because it is of very white stone, it shines brightly and performs its function for these Hermini, as a beautiful moonlight would in the midst of darkness. And because of its great height it surpasses the highest heights of the clouds by a distance of four miles in a straight line. This peak is seen from a large part of the west illuminated by the sun after its setting until a third of the night, and it is what in clear weather among you has already been judged to be a cumulate, and to us in the darkness of the night it appears to change into various shapes, and sometimes divide into two or three parts, and sometimes long, sometimes short. And this arises because of the clouds that on the horizon of the sky intervene between part of this mountain and the sun; And to cut off these solar rays, the mountain's light is interrupted by various spaces of clouds, and therefore its splendor varies in shape.

The Friars Minor have a certain Lent during which they do not eat meat in their convents, but when traveling, so that they may live on alms, they are allowed to eat whatever is placed before them. During these journeys, a couple of these friars happened upon an inn in the company of a certain merchant, who, being at the same table, was not brought anything except a cooked chicken because of the innkeeper's poverty. The merchant, seeing this as not enough for him, turned to the friars and said: "If I remember correctly, you do not eat any kind of meat in your convents on such days." At these words the friars were forced by their rule, without further ado, to say that this was the truth; whereupon the merchant had his wish, and so he ate that chicken, and the friars did the best they could. Now, after this dinner, the three companions departed, and after a while of traveling, having found a river of good width and depth, all three being on foot, the friars out of poverty and the other out of greed, it was necessary for the custom of the company that one of the friars, being barefoot, should step over the merchant's shoulders. Whereupon the friar, giving him his wooden shoes to keep, took upon himself the burden of the man. It happened that, as the friar was in the middle of the river, he again remembered his rule and, stopping like Saint Christopher, raised his head towards the one who was weighing him down and said: "Tell me, do you have any money on you?" "You know well," he replied, "how do you think that a merchant like me would go about otherwise?" "Alas, said the friar, "our rule forbids us to carry money on our persons," and immediately threw it into the water. The merchant, knowing facetiously that the injury already done was avenged, with a pleasant laugh, peacefully, half blushing with shame, endured the revenge.

If you find the distance of the sun, you will find its size by this means: take the hour of midday in the equinox, which is 12 hours per day, or whatever length you want, just measure the sun's path in one hour, and see how many suns it enters in the course of one hour, and then multiply by 24, for the 24 hours in which the sun makes the entire circle. And to know how many suns it enters along the path it takes in an hour, do this: put a rod and, like an ancient sun clock, observe the shadow of the rod at its origin, where it is most swift, and mark the limits of an hour. Then look: as many times as this shadow enters that space of an hour, that many times the sun will enter in the course of an hour. Then calculate all the miles of the circle the sun makes in 24 hours. If the shadow entered in that hour 20 times, you will say: 20 shadows in 24 hours make 480 suns in its entire course between day and night. And so, having the distance, you will have the semidiameter of that circle and then the diameter and then the true miles of the circle and the true miles of the diameter of the sun and so on for its entire body.

Doubt.

A doubt arose here, and that is whether the Flood that occurred in the time of Noah was universal or not. And here it will seem that it was not, for the reasons that will be given. We have in the Bible that the aforementioned flood was composed of 40 days and 40 nights of continuous and universal rain, and that this rain rose ten elbows above the highest mountain in the universe. And if it were so that the rain was universal, it clothed our earth with a spherical shape, and the spherical surface has each of its parts equally distant from the center of its sphere. Therefore, since the sphere of water is in the said condition, it is impossible for the water above it to move, because water itself does not move unless it descends. The bird that makes a shorter revolution prepares for the final extension of its wings with less obliquity, and therefore the rotation of its revolution is more curved the shorter the revolution. Very large rivers flow underground. Rains wear away the roots of mountains more than their summits for two reasons. The first is that the impact of rain is more powerful when falling from the same height, at the roots of mountains than at their summits. This is due to the seventh reason: heavy water becomes faster the further it descends through the air, and the faster it travels, the heavier it becomes. Therefore, since there is a greater distance from the roots of mountains to the clouds than from the clouds to the summit of the mountain, rain is, as has been said, heavier and more powerful at the roots of mountains than at the summit of the same mountain; and so it gradually wears away less as less falls. The second reason is that a greater amount of water descends from the middle of the mountain to its roots than from the summit of that mountain to the said middle. And so we have concluded our purpose. Valleys widen at every degree of time.

Valleys are shallow because the rain returns to the valley almost as much soil as the river carries away, and in some places more and in others less.

Water, carrying a subtle and imperceptible turbulence, generates stone on the side where it is delayed.

No impetus generated by any motion can be immediately consumed, and if it encounters an object of great resistance, it is consumed by refractory motion.

The impetus acquired by the flapping of wings in the oblique descent of birds is the cause of their descending for a long distance without flapping their wings and because of the said obliquity. Define what is impetus and what is oblique motion, what is greater or lesser obliquity, and how the refractory motion of birds becomes more or less oblique according to the greater or lesser opening of the tail and wings. The impetus acquired will be more premanent than the descending motion will be of lesser obliquity.

If bird a departs with impetus from a along the line a b, it has lost impetus in f; And if the impetus is applied along the line c, the impetus will end at g; and along the line d, it will end at h; and if it is applied along the line c, it will pass 7/8 of the incident motion beyond the center of the universe. Impetus is the power of the mover applied to its body, which is the cause of the motion of the body once it is separated from its mover. There will never be impetus where the resistance of the body is not greatly exceeded by its mover, especially when the dense friction of the moved bodies resists the body. This is seen in the beam pulled by oxen, which moves only as long as the motion of the oxen persists, and when the cause ceases, the effect ceases, namely, that the motion of the beam ends together with the motion of the oxen.

When the friction of the moving body upon the place where it moves is of little density, then the power of the mover will join with the moving body for a space as long as it is separated from the mover, even though the friction is of less density. Just as a boat pulled through water, after it is separated from the power of its mover, moves of its own accord for a certain space; and a bird, after it has beaten its wings upon the condensed air, moves for a long distance without further flapping of its wings, carried by its impetus.

Moving bodies and movers are of three kinds: one moves for a space equal to the motion made by its mover, and this is only slightly exceeded by the power of the mover; the other moves for a much smaller space than that through which the mover moves, and this in itself has greater resistance than the power of its mover, not to mention the medium interposed between the mover and the moving body. There are three winds that bend to the west the rivers that flow into the Mediterranean Sea from shores facing south. Let us try this. The sand that the winds push into the water is no longer in the power of the winds because it is burdened by the water that covers it and shields it from the winds. Therefore, the river n m, which flows into the sea at midday, will begin to move from the west, with the winds called Greek, Levant, and Sirocco blowing, which at different times push the dry sand from the shore and throw it into the sea, where it submerges and settles on the seabed; but the north wind, called Greek, throws it to the south-west and the sirocco to the mainland. But the southern waves, striking the shore, throw this sand toward the river, and the river refracts it toward the sea. Where the waves refracted by the shore collide with the waves coming toward the shore, there the motion of these waves stops, and therefore their power of motion ceases. Therefore, the sand that turbids the water sinks to the bottom, and this is the sand that forms a dam and bends the aforementioned river to the west. Why does the course of the aforementioned river not bend both to the east and to the west? Because the sea has been proven to flow west and not east. Of liquid impetus, that is, of air and water and other kinds, etc.

The impetus at every degree of time acquires degrees of diminution, and the prolongation of its essence arises from the air or water that closes in behind the body, filling the vacuum left by the body that penetrates it. This air is more powerful in striking and impacting the body with percussion than the opposite air, which, by its condensation, resists the penetration of the body. And the condensation of air is what diminishes the fury of the aforementioned impetus in the said body. Why is a fish in water swifter than a bird in air, which should be the opposite, since water is heavier and denser,

that air and a fish are heavier and of lesser weight than a bird?

This is why fish are not moved from their position by swift currents of water, as birds are by the fury of winds in the air. And furthermore, fish are seen running upward along their own straight line through the sudden falls of water with a very swift motion, like lightning through thick clouds, which seems a marvelous thing. And this happens because of the immense speed of such a moving object, which exceeds the motion of the water itself, that it remains immobile with respect to the motion of the fish. And the ratio of the aforementioned motions is as one to ten, and the motion of the water has a speed of one and that of the fish is ten, which ten exceeds one times nine. Therefore, the fish, having a force of ten, remains with a force of nine, with which force it rises above the force of ten that has fallen, and the water takes one from it, leaving nine.

This happens because water itself is denser than air and consequently heavier, which is why it fills the vacuum left by the fish more quickly in the place from which it departed. Furthermore, the water it strikes in front of itself does not condense like the air does in front of the bird; rather, it forms a wave that, with its motion, prepares and increases the motion of the fish, thus making it faster than the bird whose air condenses in front of it.

Right margin.

Impetus is the impression of local motion, transmuted from the mover to the moving object and maintained by the air or water as it moves in the direction of the prohibition of the vacuum.

The impetus of a body under water is different from that of a body under air; and these differences result from the varieties of the aforementioned liquids, because air is condensable toward infinity, while water is not.

The impetus of water is divided into two parts, being of two natures, one simple and the other composite. The simple one is entirely under water, the other is composite, that is, between air and water, as seen in boats. The simple impetus does not condense the water before the motion of the fish, but moves the water toward the motion of the fish with the same velocity as its mover, and the wave of water in front of it will never be faster than its mover.

Fable.
One day, when the razor was removed from the handle with which it sheathed itself, and placed itself in the sun, it saw the sun reflected in its body. At this, it was filled with great glee and, turning its thoughts backward, began to say to itself: "Shall I ever return to that shop from which I have just emerged? Certainly not; may the gods forbid that such splendid beauty should fall into such cowardice of spirit! What madness would it be, to lead me to shave the soapy beards of rustic peasants and perform such mechanical operations! Is this body fit for such exercises? Certainly not! I want to hide myself in some hidden place and there spend my life in tranquil repose." And after being thus hidden for several months, one day, returning to the air and emerging from its sheath, it saw itself transformed into the likeness of a rusting saw, and its surface no longer reflected the shining sun. In vain repentance he wept in vain over the irreparable loss, saying to himself: "Oh, how much better it would have been to exercise my lost cutting edge with the barber! Where is the lustrous surface? Certainly the annoying and ugly rust has consumed it!"
The same thing happens to minds that, in exchange for exercise, give themselves over to idleness, which, like the aforementioned razor, loses its sharp subtlety and the rust of ignorance spoils its form.
Fable.
A stone, newly exposed by the water, of a fair size, stood in a certain raised place, at the end of a delightful grove, on a stony road, surrounded by little grasses, adorned with various flowers of different colors, and saw the great mass of stones that were placed in the road below it. She felt the desire to let herself fall down there, saying to herself, "What am I doing here with these grasses? I want to live in company with these sisters of mine." And, letting herself fall among her desired companions, she ended her fickle course. After a while, she began to be continually tormented by the wheels of the carts, the feet of the shod horses, and the travelers: some turned her, some trampled her, sometimes a piece of her body would lift off, when she was covered in mud or some animal's dung, and she looked in vain back to the place from which she had come, in the place of solitary and tranquil peace.

So it happens to those who wish to come from the solitary and contemplative life to dwell in the cities, among the people full of infinite evils.
