Of the simple shadow.
Why is a simple shadow generated at the intersections a b of the two compound shadows e f, m c, and similarly at a 1) h and m g, and no such simple shadow is generated at the two other intersections c d, made by the same compound shadows mentioned above?
Answer:
Compound shadows are mixed of light and dark, and simple shadows are simple darkness. Therefore, of the two lights, one sees the compound shadows on one side, and the other sees the compound shadows on the other, but neither light sees the intersections a b, and therefore it is a simple shadow; but in the compound shadow, one or the other light sees. And here a doubt arises for the opponent, because he says: "In the intersection of the composite shadow, of necessity, one sees the two lights, the cause of these shadows, and for this reason such shadows must be cancelled out, since where one does not see the two lights, we say the shadow is simple, and where one of the two lights is seen, we say such a shadow is composite, and where one sees the two lights, it is a cancelled out shadow; because where one sees the two lights, no shadow of any kind is generated, but only the brightness of the field surrounding the shadows is composed." Here one responds that the opponent's saying is true, since he only mentions that truth which is in his favor, but if he adds the rest, he will conclude that my proposal is true. And this is that if, in seeing the two lights, such intersections would cancel out the shadows, I confess this to be true even if the two shadows were not seen in the same place. For, if where one sees a shadow and a light, a composite shadow is generated, and where one sees two shadows and two similar lights, that shadow cannot vary in any way, since the shadows are equal and the lights are equal. And this is proved in the eighth proposition, where it says: "Such a proportion has simple power with simple resistance, as has double power with double resistance."

Air is inherently capable of timelessly absorbing and discarding every species and resemblance of any body it sees.
The sun, appearing on the eastern horizon, timelessly penetrates and fills our entire hemisphere with its luminous likeness.
All the surfaces of dense bodies turned toward the sun or toward the air illuminated by it are clothed and stained with the light of the air or the sun. Every dense body is surrounded and clothed in light and darkness.
A body whose entire shaded part or only the luminous part is seen will be poorly recognized within its boundaries.
The long interval between the eye and dense bodies is the cause of the luminous part increasing or the shadowy part decreasing in quantity.
The figure of that body will be poorly understood, whose ends will end in a color similar to itself, the eye being in the middle of the shaded or luminous part.
[The] [figure] of that body will be better complex2), of which the eye [is] [placed] [i]n] between the shaded and luminous part.
All bodies have infused and mixed all their species and similarities into the entire quantity of the air opposite to themselves.

The species of each point of the corporeal surfaces is in each point of that air. All the species of bodies are in each point of that air.

And the entire part of the similarity of the air is in each point of the surfaces of the opposing bodies.

Therefore, the part and the whole of the species of bodies appears in the whole and in the part of the air opposite to itself. The body of the air appears in the whole and in the part of the surfaces of these bodies. Hence we can clearly say: the similarity of each body is, whole and in part, in each part and in the whole reciprocally of opposite bodies, as is seen in mirrors opposite to one another.

Air in its uppermost element takes on weight in itself, and in the lower element it gives weight to that element.
* The part of the element does not weigh as a whole, if it does not move.
*    The part of the element weighs in its element when it moves.
*    The part of the element that moves in its element becomes denser or less according to the slowness or speed of its movement.
*    That part of the air that moves within the air will be heavier the denser it becomes.
*    That part of the element that is without motion in its element will also be without density or weight.
*    E2) that part of the element will become so much more dense and heavy in its element the greater its motion.
*    The element within the element does not weigh if it does not move, and if it does move, it weighs as much as it would in a similar time in a similar space.
*    Air within the air does not condense or weigh if it does not move, and the faster it moves, the denser and heavier it becomes.
*    And the more it condenses, the more it resists weight.
*    Air has the potential to become dense, but it does not condense if it does not move.
Air within air moves, and as it moves it condenses, and the faster it moves, the denser it becomes, and as it condenses, it acquires heaviness, and the heavier it becomes, the greater its impact on its object. Moving the object against the still air is as difficult as moving the air against the motionless object.
Therefore, the bird, beating its heavy wings on the thin air, condenses it and makes it resist its descent.
And if the air moves against the still wing, this air supports the weight of the bird within the air.

Life of the Painter 1) in Landscapes.
The painter needs the mathematics pertaining to painting and the freedom from company that is alien to their studies; and a mind changeable according to the direction of the objects that oppose it, and remote from other concerns. And if in the contemplation and definition of one case a second case is interposed, as happens when the object moves the sense, then of these cases one must judge which is more laborious to define: the one to pursue to its ultimate clarity and then continue the definition of the other. And above all, one must have a mind equal to the nature of the surface of the mirror, which transmutes into as many different colors as there are colors of its objects. And his companions must have similarity with him in such studies and, failing to find them, accustomed to himself in his contemplations, until finally he will no longer find useful companions.

Of colors.
Of colors of equal whiteness, that which is on a darker background will appear more candid, and black will appear more tenebrous than on a background of greater whiteness.
Red will appear more fiery when it is on a more yellow background, and so will all colors surrounded by their directly opposite colors.

Figure of a tortuous water current:

The bends created by river banks are destroyed in great river floods, because the longest current pushes the water in a straight course, but as it diminishes, it resumes a meandering course, refracting from one bank to the other. This diminution of the water concaves the river banks, but in this diminished depth, the water does not have an equal flow, because the largest current leaps from one concavity to the other of the opposite banks, and the sides of the water bordering the bank have a very short flow.

There are four kinds of friction between bodies, the first of which occurs when two bodies are smooth and flat, as shown here. Of the study and its order.
I say that first one must learn the limbs and their labors, and once this knowledge is complete, one must follow the actions according to the accidents that happen to man. Third, compose the stories, the study of which will be made from natural actions done at random, through their accidents, and place them in mind in the streets, squares, and countryside, and note them with brief descriptions of lines, that is, that for a head one draws an o, and for an arm a straight or bent line, and the same is done for the legs and torso, and then, returning to the house, make such memories in perfect form.
  The opponent says that to become practical and produce many works, it is better to spend the first part of the study in copying various compositions done for paper or walls by different masters, and in these one gains quick practice and good habit.  Water has motion only through its own weight and lightness, and these are its accidents, because it has neither weight nor lightness in itself, but it acquires weight when it is above or within the lateral boundaries of air or another liquid lighter than itself, and it acquires lightness when, in vaporizing, it is thinned by heat, and then it rests above the cold water.

n - S - b - a - m f
 The arid and dry are almost of the nature of vacuum and attract the moist with as much weight as their power. In this elevation of moisture, a weight of the moisture is generated equal to the power of attraction of the dry matter, and so, making the two powers equal, these powers are finite, because, since one does not overcome the other, the moisture remains in the air and the power of the dry matter resists the descent of the moisture. And the experiment is at the edge, where a strip of old, dry linen, which is n m f, is placed with its face downwards at f, under the water of the vessel at f, and this strip of linen attracts to itself as much water as the power of its attraction, that is, from a to b, and when it can no longer draw this water, it always holds it in place, and as much of it diminishes as it tries to dry, so much of the other rises up until the linen and the water have durability. And this is necessary because if the weight of the water were to decrease, the power of the dry matter would increase and would necessarily withdraw as much water as the power had acquired in strength. Therefore, it is concluded that the water will never decrease in height, because its weight would decrease, and the power of attraction will never be lacking, since the attractive matter of this moist substance is not lacking, etc.
  It follows that when the water loses the levity it has in its rising, it gradually loses its power, and the dry matter has lost the power of its attraction, which power is lost at the same rates as the levity of the water, which is drawn by the dry matter.
  It is true that, as the height of the water in its vessel decreases, the height of the wet substance in the cloth also decreases.
 But if the cloth is wetted from a to n and to S and then submerged as before, that is, from a to f, then the water at S will descend somewhat downwards without drawing any part of the water at n with it. Therefore, the abstention of the water at S will make it thinner and lighter, and the more it descends, the more it becomes lightened and consumes the power of descent in consuming its weight. This descent of water arises for two reasons: the first is that the weight of the water descends by itself; the second is that the dryness of that dry cloth attracts it to itself. But if, according to the adversary, the abstention of the water at S were to descend lower than the surface of the water, it would then have a continuous motion until the water in the vessel is consumed. This is false, because such extended water is thinner than the water at n and weighs less. Where it cannot descend, but part of it evaporates and part of it returns backwards, as will be proven.

These are the modes of friction of three kinds:

one is caused by a straight plane, the other

by a curve, as are the poles, and the third is made in a flat circle, like the millstones of a mill. And of these, two are created, mixed and composite, that is, they can participate in the first and third, the other in the first and second. There is the intersecting friction, which is two long bodies moving in a cross, and there is another, which moves the plane against the moving object that rubs them together.

The frictions of bodies are of as many different powers as there are varieties of lubricity of the bodies rubbing together. The friction of bodies is divided into two principal natures: liquid with liquid and dense with dense. From these arises a third nature that participates or is composed of the two aforementioned, that is, liquid can rub against dense, and dense against liquid, that is, frictional.

There is a fourth friction, between which is the wheel of a chariot moving on the earth, which does not rub but touches, and which can be said to be of the nature of walking with steps of infinite smallness or smallness.

Frictional motions are of two kinds: plane and oblique, and never toward the center of the universe except by accident.

Just as water escapes through various channels from a pressed sponge, or as air from a cloak, so the rare and porous mists are driven upward by the heat of the breeze. That first part, which is above, is the one that reaches the cold region and there stops against the cold and dryness and there awaits its companion. The part below, which rises toward the still one, acts like a spout with the air that is in the middle, which escapes through the cross and downward; it does not go upward, because it finds the cloud so thick that it cannot pass. And for this reason all the winds that fight the surface of the earth come from above to below. And if they strike the opposing earth, they cause a refractory motion there, which, wanting to rise upward, encounters another wind there that descends and opposes its ascent; whereby the said elevation is forced to break its natural order and, taking a transverse path, follows a violent course, which continually scratches the surface of the earth. And when the said winds strike the salt waters, there clearly ends the angle created by the incoming and refracted wind, from which results the proud, threatening, and submerging waves, which most often cause the one to cause the other. Here someone might think they can rebuke me by arguing against my proof of the winds, saying that they cannot be generated by clouds, since it would be necessary for one to remain stationary and give motion to the other, and this is not apparent because, when the north wind blows, the clouds all rush away in unison before the said wind.
  To this the answer is that when the air is at rest and a full province of clouds rises high up and, as has been said, closes up there, they squeeze out so much air that, due to the force given, it takes on such a motion in the air that it gives motion, as you see, to the other, smaller clouds. And by spitting out air, they also give themselves a similar cause for greater flight. For if a cloud is found among or in part among the others, if it generates wind in its direction, the air between it and its nearest neighbor begins to multiply, and by multiplying, it acts no differently than dust bombards it, which drives from its neighbor the less ponderous and lighter body. This being so, the cloud, by expelling the wind toward the other resisting clouds, causes itself to flee. And if it sends said pressures of wind in its direction, it also increases the wind in the other clouds. And if it sends wind across, some clouds form a backward circle and then return to a league with the others.

At the edge.

Just as the natural heat diffused through the human limbs is driven back by the surrounding cold, its opposite and enemy, and, returning to the lake of the heart and liver, strengthens there, making these its fortress and bastion, - so 6) clouds, being composed of heat and moisture and, in summer, of certain dry vapors. And these, being found in the cold and dry region, are similar to certain flowers and leaves attacked by the cold frost which, pressing together, create greater conflict. Thus these, in the first contact they have with the cold air, begin to resist and not want to pass further; the others below observe the continuous rising. The upper part, being stationary, begins to swell, the heat and dryness retreat 7) to the middle. The upper part, abandoned by the heat, begins to freeze or actually dissolve. The clouds below, rising still further, bring the hot closer to the cold, so that the hot, forced to reduce itself to a pure element, immediately bursts into flame and becomes entangled in the dry vapor. At the center of the cloud, it grows greatly, and, igniting within the cooled cloud, it makes a noise similar to water falling into pitch or boiling oil, or molten copper thrown into cold water. Thus, driven by its opposite, it shatters the opposing cloud and, flowing through the air, shatters and shatters all opposition. And this is the thunderbolt.

Lake Corno. Ciavenna Valley.
Up from Lake Corno, towards Lamagna, is the Ciavenna Valley, where the Mera River flows into the lake. Here are barren, very high mountains with large rocks. In these mountains are the water birds called maragons. Here are fir, larch, and pine trees, deer, imbue, chamois, and terrible bears. You cannot ride on them except on all fours. The peasants go there with great ingenuity during the snowy season to make the bears swarm down these banks. These narrow mountains cut across the river. They are on the right and left for a distance of 20 miles, all in the same way. Good inns are found every mile. Along the said river are waterfalls of 400 fathoms, which are a beautiful sight.  Having repeatedly congratulated you in letters on your prosperous fortune, I now know that as a friend you will support me in the miserable state in which I find myself. And this is that in recent days I have been in so many troubles, fears, dangers, and misfortunes together with these wretched villagers that I began to envy the dead. And certainly I do not believe that after the elements by their separation destroyed the great chaos, they would gather their strength, indeed their rage, to inflict such harm on mankind as has been seen and experienced by us at present, so that I cannot imagine what could further increase such evil. First we were assaulted and battered by the force and fury of the winds; to this was added the ruins of the great mountains of snow, which filled all these valleys and destroyed a large part of our city. And not content with this, fortune submerged the entire lower part of this city with sudden deluges of water. To this was added a sudden rain, or rather a devastating storm, full of water, sand, mud and stones together entangled with roots, twigs and hooves of various plants. And everything, flowing through the air, descended upon us, and finally a conflagration of fire, which seemed to be carried not by winds, but by 30 thousand devils who carried it, has burned and destroyed this entire country, and has not yet ceased. And the few who remained were left with such dismay and fear that, like fools, we barely dared to speak to one another. Having abandoned all our cares, we are gathered together in certain ruins of churches, mixed together, male and female, small and large, like herds of goats; and if it were not for certain people who have helped us with provisions, we would all have died of hunger. Now you see how they find us, and all these evils are nothing compared to those that are shortly promised to us.
  I know that as a friend you will be saddened by my misfortune, as I have already shown you in my letters, with the effect of rejoicing in your goodness.

Why the Spanish current is always greater towards the west than towards the east?
The reason is that if you put together the mouths of the rivers that flow into this Mediterranean Sea, you will find a greater amount of water than that which this sea pours through the straits into the ocean. You see Africa emptying its rivers, which run north, into that sea, among which is the Nile, which lines 3,000 miles of Africa, there is the river Bragada and the Mauretanus and others like it; Europe1) empties into it the Tanais and the Danube, the Po and the Rhone, the Arno and the Tiber; so that it is clear that these rivers, together with an infinite number of rivers of lesser fame, have a greater width and depth and course than the sea, eighteen miles narrow, which at the furthest western land divides Europe from Africa. And if you wanted to say that the rivers that flow into the ocean were as many, certainly the aforementioned rivers have almost all their origin in the mountains near the ocean, and if these mountains do pour any river into it, it will not be because of its proximity to such a course as the Nile and the Danube; And if there is any similarity, consider that these rivers, flowing into the ocean, can give it little increase that restores the easterly current, without always raising a greater amount of water in the clouds than the rivers add. For all the kinds of objects which have to pass from one surface of spherical and transparent bodies to another, it is necessary for them to make a path through the center of that body, and it is necessary that the kinds be turned upside down. Since the center is indivisible, no thing so small can pass through it that it does not become indivisible there and that it does not fall into intersection. Therefore, since the surface of the eye gives to the impressing body the kinds sent to it by the opposite objects by means of a spherical body which is situated in the middle of the eye, it is necessary that the kinds make intersection and turn upside down on contact with the impressing body. And this reason seems to confirm that there was another intersection in front of the spherical body, which first turned the particles upside down, and the second intersection of the spherical body turned them upside down, and in this way the object sees them upright.
  If you place a glass ball filled with water before your eyes, all the particles of the objects that pass inside it will appear to be upside down. And if you place two of them, one after the other, the particles in the first one toward the eye will appear to be straightened in their natural direction.

Wherever flame is generated, there a wind is generated around it, the course of which serves to nourish and increase that flame.

Second. - The motion of that wind will be more impetuous the greater the quantity of flame it has to nourish.

Third. - That flame will be hotter, which will be more splendid. The converse follows: and the one with greater heat will be more splendid.

And the flame that is generated in air of faster motion will be of greater splendor; and the one with the fastest motion will be more splendid.

The flame that is generated in air of greater heat will extend to a greater length, and, through the converse, it will become shorter in length, which is generated in a site of greater cold.

b c a
The motion of the flame in the company of the wind generated by it will be circular, if it is nourished by matter of uniform nourishment, and this circulation will be parallel, or this circle will be of empty circulation, that is, annular. Therefore, the growth of the fire moves against the wind that nourishes it, but the opposing wind that is generated around the center of this circulation jousts against the wind that is generated outside this circle, and within their collisions they enclose and strike the flame, and the percussion, refracted by them, rises toward the sky, carrying the generated flame with them.

The wind that is generated within the annular fire descends from above and not from below, and that which is generated outside this ring moves from below and from above, as will be demonstrated.

The element fire continuously consumes the air that partially nourishes it, and would remain in contact with the vacuum if the succeeding air did not help to fill it. But the place from which this assistance was separated would still remain empty, and so it would continue if the succeeding air did not continuously fill the space left by the preceding motion of the air, and so it would continue up to the sphere of the water. But the air that borders the water is so thick with its exhalation, or vaporization, that it would continuously sufficiently restore all sorts of vacuum that could be generated above it, etc.

What is heavy and light?

[Gravity] is an action or accident caused by one part of an element extracted from another, which, being heavier, cannot be supported by it; and if it is lighter, it cannot support the parts of the heavier one that rest on it. If the heavy body is a liquid and continuous body, it will descend into the lighter one in a pyramidal shape, until the opposite part, after this pyramid, intersects and forms an opposite pyramid, which, although discontinuous, will observe the same shape, incorporating air, and with each degree of descent will acquire degrees of width at its base.

If the course of the air's penetration is from the bottom to the surface of the water, since it is continuous, it will still form a pyramidal shape, but it will be opposite to that formed by the water falling through the air, because that of the water turned its angle to the center of the world, and this of the air turns the pyramid to the opposite side of its origin, so that with each degree of motion it acquires degrees of width at the base.

Why does the air under the water acquire, at each degree of motion, width at the base of its pyramid?

* This happens because the water that covers the origin of the air rests on top of it, so that, being heavier, it comes to press on it, and this action comes to widen and dilate its edges from its center with equal distances, and the higher it rises, the more it multiplies, because a greater amount of water is placed on it.

* This happens because the water that surrounds the origin of the air comes to remain with...

* The water that surrounds the air that accidentally enters it weighs down toward its center, and if it has a long shape, by pushing it laterally it will push it and displace it from its place, because the weight of the water that surrounds it laterally will be greater than that which forms a lid. Therefore, being narrow at the sides, it pushes into the lid, which, striking and overcoming that as the weaker resistance, it comes to expand, and thus, at each step widening in the upper parts, it comes to take on a pyramidal shape.

The water circumscribing the air that accidentally enters it either immediately gains weight, causing it to prey and collapse toward the center of the air; by successively pushing and displacing the air from its position, or by being evacuated and filled by a body lighter than itself, it immediately gains weight. By its nature, air does not escape from beneath the water, but the water that rests upon it preys upon and dispels it.

On navigation.

If the north wind blows, the ship cannot sail between the north and the west, but must pass halfway between the west and the north, and the sail must be lateen, not square. And if the ship is a caravel, it will sail with 5½ winds from the north and west, that is, one and a quarter winds.

Group of piles driven into the ground:

To drive piles: and that the blow will always be equal, because it falls equally.

The north wind is cold and dry: cold because it rises in cold places, dry because the cold constricts and locks the waters in perpetual ice, so that this wind cannot draw out the trapped humid vapors, and therefore it draws pure and clean vapors, and thus flows over the high mountain peaks, traversing all of Europe.

Right column.

* The southern wind is hot and humid not by its nature, but by the places it passes through, namely the southern3) countries, which are hot and dry. Therefore, as it passes through warm countries, it becomes hot, and because heat opens and resolves moisture, which comes from the Mediterranean Sea and over which it flows, it is therefore hot and humid.

* Every wind by its nature is cold and dry, but the southern ones are hot and humid. The heat comes from the southern regions over which it flows, which are hot and dry; and because heat opens and resolves moisture, it resolves dew and opens the water of the Mediterranean Sea and the earth, except for moist vapor,4), which makes it hot and humid; and the more it draws, the more powerful it becomes in driving turbulent and water-laden clouds, which generate heavy rain, and for this reason its percussion is more powerful than that of the southern wind.

* Every wind by its nature is cold and dry, but the southern wind is warm and humid. The heat comes from the southern parts it passes through, which are warm and dry; and because the heat is a catalyst and resolver of moisture, it resolves the dew, and in flowing over the great Mediterranean Sea, it opens the water and then the land of the European coasts and excepts the humid air, whereby it becomes warm and humid; and the more it moves, the more powerful it becomes at carrying turbulent clouds laden with water, which generate very heavy rains.

Southern winds are stronger in the northern parts than in the southern ones in summer than in winter. And this is because the sun resolves all the moisture it raises from the Mediterranean Sea, which it cannot resolve in the cold of winter, of which it lifts little vapor and resolves what little it does into water; but when the sun passes beyond the equinoctial circle, then here is our winter and there their summer, whereupon the sun resolves all the vapors that it raises, which flow with an airy wave up to the beginnings of Europe, where, finding it cold in the summer, they make rain and in the winter they condense and fall as snow5), and thus the aforementioned winds are gradually annihilated by their blowing.

I have been so happy, my most illustrious Lord, with the almost complete restoration of Your Excellency's health—with the desired recovery of your health—that my own illness has almost escaped me. But I am greatly sorry that I have not been able to fully satisfy Your Excellency's wishes due to the malice of this deceiver, to whom I have left nothing behind that I could have helped him with—that has not been done for him. And first, his allowance was paid to him before the immediate due date, which I believe he would willingly deny—denied—if I did not have the written attestation from the interpreter's hand. And seeing that I was not working except when he lacked the work of others, of which he was a diligent investigator, I begged him to eat with me and work with me, because in addition to the account - the works as well - he would acquire the Italian language (he always promised it and never wanted to do it.) 1) - And I did this also because that young German who makes the mirrors was in the shop every day and wanted to see and understand what was being done, and he published throughout the city blaming and reviling what he did not understand. And I did this because he ate with the Pope's guard, and then went off in company, with his guns killing birds for these antiquities, and continued like this from after dinner until evening; And if I sent Lorenzo to urge him on the work, he would get angry and say that he didn't want so many masters on his head and that his work was for Your Excellency's wardrobe. Two months passed and it continued like this. One day, finding Giannicolò in the wardrobe, I asked him if the German had finished the Magnificent's works, and he told me it wasn't true, but that he had only given him two small guns to clean. Then, when I urged him on, he left the shop and began to work in his room, wasting a lot of time making another vice and files and other screw tools; and there he made reels for twisting silk and gold, which he hid when none of my friends went in, and with a thousand curses and scoldings, so that none of my friends wanted to go in anymore.

I have been so happy, my most illustrious Lord, at the desired recovery of your health that my illness has almost disappeared from me. But I am greatly sorry that I have not been able to fully satisfy Your Excellency's wishes due to the malice of this German deceiver, for whom I have left nothing undone that I thought would please him. And first, I invited him to live and dwell with me, through which I would continually observe the work he was doing and easily correct his errors, and in addition to this, he would learn the Italian language, in which he could easily speak without an interpreter. And first, his money was always given to him ahead of time, and that was it. Then his request was for the finished wooden models of how they were to be made of iron, and how he wanted to bring them to his country. Which I denied, telling him that I would give him a drawing of the width, length, thickness, and shape of what he had to do; and so we remained reluctantly. The second thing was that he built another shop with new vices and tools in the room where he slept, and there he worked for others. Then he went to dine with the Swiss guard, where there were idle people, in which he outdid them all. From there he went out, and most of the time two or three of them would go off with their guns, killing birds in the antiques, and this would last until evening.

Finally, I discovered that this master Giovanni delli specchi is the one who did it all for two reasons. And the first is because he said that my coming here had deprived him of the conversation and favor of Your Lordship, which always sees... 6); the other is that this blacksmith's room is said to be suitable for him to work on mirrors, and this is demonstrated by the fact that, in addition to making this man an enemy, he made him sell all his ... and leave his shop to him, in which he works with many workers on many mirrors to send to the fairs.

* Having discussed the nature of shadows and their percussion, I will now discuss the places touched by these shadows, and their curvature, obliquity, or straightness, or whatever quality I can find.

Since I have considered the nature and various qualities of original and derivative shadows and their percussion, it seems time to demonstrate the various effects of the various places touched by these shadows.

Shadow is the privation of light.

Shadows seem to me to be of the utmost necessity in perspective, because without them opaque and cubic bodies are poorly understood—whatever is placed within their boundaries—and their boundaries are poorly understood unless they terminate in a field of a different color from that of the body. Therefore, in the first proposition on shadows, I propose and explain in this way how every opaque body will be surrounded and superficially clothed by shadows and lights, and upon this I build the first book. Furthermore, these shadows are in themselves of various qualities of darkness, because they are abandoned by varying quantities of luminous rays, and these I call original shadows, because they are the first shadows that clothe the bodies where they are attached: and upon this I will build the second book. From these original shadows result shadowy rays, which continue to expand through the air and are of as many qualities as there are varieties of the original shadow from which they derive. For this reason I call them shadows derivative shadows, because they arise from other shadows. I will write a third book on this. These derivative shadows, too, in their percussion produce as many different effects as the places where they strike are varied. Here I will write a fourth book. And because the percussion of the derivative shadow is always surrounded by the percussion of luminous rays, this, by reflected concurrence, rebounding back toward its cause, encounters the original shadow and is sorted and converted into it, somewhat varying its nature. I will build a fifth book on this. In addition to this, I will write the sixth book, in which I will inquire into the various and many diversifications of the reflected rays, which will vary the original by as many different colors, as the places from which these reflected luminous rays originate are varied. I will also make the seventh division of the various distances that will be between the percussion of the reflected ray and the place from which it originates, as varied as the similarities of the colors that it imparts upon the opaque body upon percussion are varied.
Those similarities will be more evident in the eye that originates from a brighter body.

Of lightning.

Just as the point of the pyramid made of a mirror with the rays of the sun lights the fire, for the same reason the fire itself lights up among the clouds. The reason is that the more often the point of the said pyramid enters the plane, or surface, of the mirror, the hotter it is than it; so the element of fire, infused among the clouds and constricted by its opposite, the more often it shrinks into less space than before, the hotter it is and therefore lights up in the dry vapor that rose with it among the clouds.

The stone, being struck by the steel of the fire, marveled greatly and said to it in a stern voice: "What prudence moves you to trouble me? Do not trouble me, for you have taken me instead: I have never displeased anyone." To which the steelmaker replied: "If you are patient, you will see that marvelous fruit will come from you." At these words, the stone, resigned itself, patiently stood firm before the martyr, and saw the marvelous fire arise from within itself, which through its power worked in infinite ways.

Said for those who frighten the principles of studies, and after they themselves prepare themselves to be able to command and patiently devote continuous effort to those studies, from them one sees things of marvelous demonstration result.

As the painted parrot wandered and wandered through the darkened air, he saw a light, which he immediately turned towards and, circling it in various circles, was greatly amazed at such splendid beauty and, not content merely with seeing it, he set out to treat it as he was accustomed to do with the fragrant flowers, and, directing his flight, with bold courage he passed through that light, which consumed the ends of his wings and legs and other ornaments, and falling at its feet, he considered with wonder what had happened, not being able to imagine that any harm or damage could come from so beautiful a thing. and having somewhat restored his failing strength, he took another flight and passed through the body of that light, immediately falling, burned, into the oil that the light nourished. Only enough life remained to him that he was able to consider the cause of his ruin, saying to it: "O cursed light! I thought I had found my happiness in you! I weep in vain for my mad desire, and to my own harm I have come to know your consuming and harmful nature." To which the light replied: "So I do to those who do not know how to use me well." And immediately, having fallen to the bottom, he ended his life.

Said for those who, seeing these lascivious and worldly pleasures before them, like the parrot, run to them without considering the nature of those who, after long practice, are recognized by them as men, to their shame and harm.

When the light of a long figure generates the derivative shadow in rectangular conjunction with the primary shadow, then the derivative shadow diminishes its initial darkness at every degree of its length. And this is proved by the fourth of this, where it says: "The derivative shadow loses as much darkness as it becomes more distant from its primary shadow." The greater the angle generated by the conjunction of the derivative shadow with its primary shadow, the less darkness will the end of the derivative shadow be. And this arises from the aforementioned fourth, because the greater the angle created by the conjunction of the derivative shadow with the primary shadow, the further the opposite ends of these shadows will be from each other, and according to the fourth, the derivative shadow will be less obscure. The converse of this follows: The darker the end of the derivative shadow will be, the more acute the angle created by the conjunction of the primary shadow with the derivative shadow. And this is proved by the converse of the fourth, which says: 'That part of the derivative shadow will be darker which is closest to its primary shadow.' 'Therefore, since the angle of greater sharpness causes its sides to come closer together, it is necessary that the original shadow and the derivative shadow, of which the sides of these angles are composed, also become closer to each other. Of the limits of the derivative shadow. The limit of the derivative shadow will be darker and more visible, the one closest to its original shadow. Prove it by the fifth of this, which says: "in the contact that the derivative shadow has with its original shadow, there the conjunction of simple shadows with compound ones is imperceptible", because starting at an angle they begin at a point, as is proven in the definition of the angle, where it says: "an angle is the concurrence of two straight lines at the same point". Although the opponent claims that the lines composing the angle could be curved, this is partly accepted and partly denied, because the lines could be of the same curvature and equally distant from the center of the circle surrounded by them, so that the contact of these two lines would form a single line and would be like the contact of two straight lines in the same straight line, which would also compose not an angle, but a single straight line. But we would call an angle the contact of two straight lines situated outside the same straight line; and of curves, we would call a curvilinear angle the angle composed of curved lines at various distances from the center of their circle.

If the darkness of the night is 100 degrees darker than in the evening, and a man's eye doubles its pupil in this darkness, this darkness diminishes by half for that eye, because its visual power has doubled by half. There remains, therefore, 50 degrees of darkness.

And if the owl's eye increases its pupil a hundredfold in the aforementioned darkness, its visual power increases a hundredfold, which is 100 degrees of visual power acquired; and since equal things do not exceed each other, the bird sees in the darkness with its pupil multiplied a hundredfold in quantity, just as in the daytime with its pupil diminished by 99/100.

On the consumption or vaporization of the water of the Mediterranean Sea.

The Mediterranean Sea, the largest river between Africa, Asia, and Europe, contains about three hundred royal rivers and, in addition to these, receives the rains that descend over a distance of three thousand miles. This returns to the great Ocean Sea its own and other received waters, and undoubtedly gives less to the sea than it receives, because many veins descend from it, which flow through the bowels of the earth to vivify this terrestrial machine. And this is necessary because the surface of the Mediterranean is further from the center of the world than the surface of the Ocean itself, as is demonstrated in the second part of this book. And furthermore, the heat of the sun continually vaporizes much of this Mediterranean water, and therefore the sea can acquire little increase from the said rainfall or little decrease from the pouring of the received waters into the Ocean or from being vaporized by the heat of the sun or by the course of dry winds.

On the motion of flame

The flame that is born has a rapid birth and a rapid life and death. Its first principal motion is upward; its second principal motion is at the point of its exhalation; its least is downward. And it approaches no dense material, except scorching hot, except by impetuous motion, which brings it to contact with opposing objects, and from them it emerges, but not between equal angles, as is seen with many other powers. Flame is infinitely condensable, as shown by the flame that condenses in bombards, which contract to such a density that it exceeds that of the matter of the bombards, with an excess that is greater the more the matter of the bombard exceeds the air. We may say better: flame is infinitely condensable, as demonstrated by the condensing of bombs, which becomes denser the more dense the material it bombards, which surpasses it with such power that it causes it to fly to pieces through the air, as something of greater lightness than fire, the more light fire is than air, etc. The free motion of fire, the more it moves upward, the faster it becomes, just as a heavy object moves downward. And it can be deflected along any tortuous path without loss or diminution of equal velocity; and if this were not the case, it would follow that where it were continually retarded, the antecedent quantity would separate from the succeeding quantity, and thus a vacuum would be generated between these separations, which is impossible. Therefore it is necessary that this motion of flame be uniform along every part of its length; But it need not have uniform motion throughout any part of its thickness unless the width of the conduit is itself uniform. A flame that moves through a conduit of varying widths will have various motions within itself—tortuous, circumvolutory, retrograde, and straight—which motions it will exhibit throughout the thickness of the flame. And as one side slows down, the opposite side becomes proportionately faster, so that an equal quantity of flame passes through every part of the conduit at the same time. The flame will be brighter the denser it is, and the converse will be less bright the thinner it becomes, etc.

Where the air is not proportionate to receive the flame, no flame can live there, nor any terrestrial or aerial animal.
If all the bases of an equal quantity of flames were contingent on each other throughout, they would form a continuous flame, which, having sufficient and continuous nourishment, would form a pyramidal fire, similar in shape to each of the aforementioned flames, separated from the others. But it seems that such a flame must be of equal thickness from below to above, and this is proven with certainty, because if all such flames clothed the sphere of the earth with themselves, given that it were of perfect sphere, then it would be necessary for this garment of flame to clothe the earth with itself with equal thickness, because each flame escapes in a straight line from the surrounding sphere of fire.
There is no science of the heat and color of fire, nor of its nature, nor of the colors of glass and other things generated within it, but of its motions and other accidents, and of its increasing and decreasing power and the transmutation of colors in its flames in as many different ways as there are varieties of materials that nourish it or that are infused into it. Whether hail has a circular motion in descending through the air or not.
Hail that descends through the air does not have a circular motion, because if it is round, its descent is straight in parts of equal weight, and if it is not round, its descent is also straight, because in heavy objects that descend through the air, the heavier part becomes the guide of the motion.

And if you say that such hail, in descending, is largely resolved into water, this is denied, because every heavy object that descends, the more it descends, the faster it becomes, and that which is more rapidly cools and consequently freezes. Therefore, due to the increased motion, the hail condenses and therefore does not resolve into water. Of the heat that escapes to the center of the cloud it raises.
The heat infused into the cloud levitates it with greater lightness than the air, and therefore it rises upward toward the cold region of the air, where the heat, repressed by the cold, retreats toward the center of the cloud and settles at that height where the cold resists the elevation of the heat and the heat prevents the penetration of the cold. Therefore, the two contrary powers of heat and cold are made equal, and since equal things do not surpass each other, it is necessary that this cloud be resolved by the heat infused into it, and then its destruction will follow. But if we have assumed these powers to be equal, namely, heat and cold, it is necessary that one not be consumed by the other, and for this reason we would have to conclude that the situation and shape of such a cloud were eternal. However, since such eternity is not granted to us by experience, because no cloud has premanence of its own, shape, or quantity, we must find the true cause of its destruction. This will be the wind, which, striking, will break and envelop the parts of such a cloud and will mix together the heat and moisture along with the cold, and generate a furious discord of water, rain, hail, and wind, etc.

The higher the motion of smoke, the more it is retarded, and the opposite seems to be true, since the closer heat approaches its natural location, the faster it moves. But this happens because the heat, which generates the smoke, at each degree of elevation of the smoke acquires degrees of diminution for two reasons: and one is that the more it rises, the colder it finds the air; the second is that the more it rises, the more it loses of the impetuous motion with which it was converted from flame to smoke; and still a third cause can be produced, namely: the more it rises, the more the time of its creation is prolonged. The central part of the smoke rises to a greater height than any other part, that is, the part of the middle of its thickness. The following converse follows which says: the lateral parts of the smoke are all the slower, the further they are from the middle of the thickness of that smoke; and this happens because this central smoke, being protected from the cold by the thickness of the smoke which covers it, remains warmer than the external parts of the same smoke.

Of heat and cold.
That thing cools more, the more it is removed from the heat that has the potential to warm. That heat is of lesser potential that is further from the incident and refracted potential of that heat. That part of the body heats more, the closer it approaches the heat; and conversely, it heats less, the more it is removed from that heat. The cloud freezes above and not below, and more from the sides than from the bottom or in the middle, because the heat extends more upward than from the sides and more from the sides than from the bottom. The more it heats, the lighter it becomes, and the more it cools, the heavier it becomes; but the more it condenses, the more it heats up. The following proposition follows: the less it heats up, the more it becomes rarer. But the more it heats up, the closer it approaches heat, and the less it cools down, the more it is removed from that heat. Contrary opinions.

Again, if one were to say that the eye, like the ear, is only capable of receiving the likenesses of things without transmitting any power toward them, one could prove this by the example of the spiracle made in a window, which transmits within it all the likenesses of the bodies that are its object; thus one could say that the eye did so.

Refutation.

If the aforementioned spiracle, without transmitting anything other than its own form, without spiritual power transmits within the dwelling the species of objects in color and shape and there renders them upside down, then the eye would have to do the same, for everything seen would appear to it to be the opposite.

Counterproof.

The circle of light that appears in the middle of the white of the eye is of a nature apprehensive of objects. And this same circle contains within itself a point that appears black, which is a perforated nerve that leads to the intrinsic virtues, which is full of the understanding and judgmental power that reaches the common sense. Now the objects that are opposite the eyes act with their missiles like many archers who want to shoot through the hole of a gun. The one among the archers that is located along a straight line to the hole of the gun will be the one best able to hit the bottom of that hole with his arrow. Thus, the objects opposite the eye will be more easily penetrated by the senses, the more they are along the line of the perforated nerve.

The water that is in the light around the black center of the eye acts like the pointers in the hunt, which are the cause of the wild animal's release, and the leewardess then captures it. So this, because it is a humor that possesses the power of understanding and sees many things, but does not grasp them, but immediately turns its mind to them, which goes by line to the senses, and that takes the spices, and imprisons those that please in the prison of memory.

Operation of the compound shadow.
The operations of compound shadows are always of contrary motion. That is, if the confluence of the luminous rays is touched by an opaque body, before they reach their intersection, all the shadows of that body which breaks the upper ray will be shown beyond that intersection in the percussion of the lower ray, and just as the upper ray becomes inferior after the intersection, so the motions that the shadowy body makes within that upper ray will show themselves to be of opposite motion after that intersection. And this will be demonstrated in the percussion of the shadow cast upon the pavement or upon the wall struck by the sun or another luminous body. But if the luminous ray is impeded by an opaque body somewhat after its intersection, then the percussion of the shadow deriving from the opaque body will cause the motion to be similar to the motion of its own opaque body. And if these rays are prevented from their proper intersection, then the shadows of the opaque will be two and will move with opposite motions toward each other before they merge.
The compound derivative shadow is because the percussion of the solar ray, which passes through any angle, does not impress those angles, but portions of circles, which are greater or smaller the more remote or nearer these impressions are to those angles.

How the eye does not discern the figures of bodies within their boundaries except by means of shadows and lights; And many are the sciences that would be nothing without the science of shadow and light, such as painting, sculpture, astronomy, and to a large extent perspective and the like.
It is proven that the sculptor does not work without the aid of shadow and light, because without such shadow and light the sculpted material would remain all one color. And by the ninth of this it is proven that a flat surface, illuminated by an equal light, does not vary in any way the brightness or darkness of its natural color, and by this equality of color the equality of the flatness of that surface is proven. It follows, therefore, that if the sculpted material were not clothed in shadows and lights such as the reliefs of the muscles and the concavities interposed between these reliefs require, the sculptor would not continually see his work as the work he sculpted requires, and such an operation would be done during the day almost as if it had been worked on in the dark night.

The point has no middle, and its boundaries are nothingness.
The opponent says that nothingness is the vacuum, and that vacuum does not exist in nature; and if the point were the vacuum, it would not have being, and, not existing, the point is not in being. The answer is that if vacuum existed, it would be a place occupied by space, and the point that is in place without occupying space is not the vacuum—and the point that exists is in place without occupying space, and therefore the point is not the vacuum.
* The point has no middle, and its boundaries are nothingness.
* The opponent says that nothingness would be the vacuum, and that vacuum does not exist in nature, and not existing, and therefore the point would not exist.
* It is answered that if vacuum existed, space would exist with occupation of space, from which it follows that the point, which is in space without occupation of space, is not vacuum, for if it were vacuum, it would have a middle and be divisible.
* From which it follows that nothingness, because it is in space without occupation of space, cannot be vacuum.
* The nothingness, the terminus of the point, being located in space without occupation of space, cannot be vacuum.
* The point has no middle and its terms are nothingness. The opponent says that nothingness and vacuum are similar and that, since vacuum does not exist in nature, nothingness does not exist either.
* Nothingness has no middle and its terms are nothingness.
* The opponent says that nothingness and vacuum are one and the same thing with two names, which are said and not given in nature. The answer is that if there were a vacuum, there would be a space surrounding it, and nothingness exists without occupying a space. It follows that nothingness and vacuum are not similar, because one is infinitely divisible, and nothingness is not divided, because nothing can be less; and if there were a part of it, it would be equal to the whole, and the whole to the part.

On the gait of a man.

The gait of a man is always in accordance with the universal gait of four-footed animals, since just as they move their feet in a cross, like a horse at a trot, so a man moves his four limbs in a cross; that is, if he puts his right foot forward to walk, he puts his left arm forward with it, and it always continues in this manner.

Of the Grazing of Oxen on Tall Plants.

Oxen graze on the foliage of tall, slender plants, such as small poplars and the like, by climbing on them—that is, riding with their front legs on the top of the plant and always pushing forward—so that, since the plant itself cannot resist the undue weight, it must yield and sink with its height.

Of the Government of Rivers.

For every large river to remain within its banks, it is necessary to have an officer with the authority to command the people near it and to always repair any breaches.

Of the Maintenance of Rivers.

The river that flows straightest will remain within its banks.

The imperceptible fluttering of the wings, without their further flapping, keeps the bird balanced and even in the moving air.
The refractory motion against the onset of the wind will always be greater than its incidental motion, and the refractory motion, made together with the course of the wind, will be increased by the wind and will become equal to the incidental motion. The ways in which birds ascend without the flapping of their wings, but with the help of the wind, performed in a circle, are of two kinds: simple and composite. Simple are those that with incident motion proceed against the flight of the wind, at the end of which they turn against the oncoming wind, receiving its percussion under themselves, and end with a refracted motion against the wind. The compound motion of the ascent of birds is similarly circular and has incident and refracted motion against the oncoming wind in the course made in a semicircle, and has incident and refracted motion that follows the course of the wind. The simple circular motion of ascent without flapping its wings will always be performed in the strong motions of the wind: and that it is true (2) the bird is very much carried in this ascent together with the course of the wind. The compound motion will be performed in light winds, because experience shows that in such compound motions the bird rises through the air without being carried too far by the wind towards the places where it is walking. 3) The feathers and plumes under the wings are very useful. 4) The flexible, or bendable, ends of the wings and tail are very good, and the front is hard where the air is split.

The opponent claims that he could not deny that the bird cannot fall either backward or head down along a perpendicular line, but that it appears to him that it can descend by an edge, holding its wings completely open and placing one of the wings, together with the head, under the center of its gravity: that is, it will descend along the line a b, with the wings d and d remaining completely extended with their natural extension. To this part the same answer is given as to the previous one, namely, that if this bird in this position, without any other aid, were to descend perpendicularly, it would be contrary to the fourth part of the second book of the Elements, where it was proved that every body that descends freely through the air will descend in such a way that the heavier part will become the guide of the motion. and here the heavier part is found between the ends of the open wings, that is, between the two lighter parts; which, as has been proven, is impossible. Therefore, we have proven, with the bird standing with its wings open and its head slightly raised, that it is impossible for it to ever fall or descend along a perpendicular line, but will always descend along an oblique line, which2) line every small movement of the wings or tail converts the oblique motion and descent into refractory motion.
Nature has given all large birds to stay at such a high altitude that the wind that increases their flight is straight and powerful, so that their low flight among the mountains, where the wind roams and is always full of backlash and dizzying motions, - where, due to the fury of the condensed wind, it could not shield itself through the gorges of the mountains at its own discretion and govern itself with its large wings from the percussion of the beaches and high rocks and trees, - would not sometimes be the cause of their destruction; so that on the great heights, if by some accident the wind should turn it, it always has time to straighten itself and safely restore its flight, which will always be swift everywhere. But it always passes above the clouds, so as to avoid wetting its feathers. On the speed of motion made by the tip of the jointed rod.

It is clear that if the head q of the upper rod lowers one cubit, the head r, which is further away, will lower 2 cubits, and K, which is twice as far away, will lower 4 cubits, since the rod is made of a single piece. The motion of a heavy body through air.
There are two motions that can be caused by a heavy body through air, one of which is called simple and the other compound. Simple is that motion in which the surface of the body moves as much as its center. Compound is that in which the surface of the body moves faster than its center.
Simple is the cause that causes compound motion. And this is manifested in any wheel where a circumvolutionary impetus is given, which is maintained for a short time and is always diminishing.

I suspect that my modest remuneration for the great benefits I have received from Your Excellency has made you somewhat angry with me; and this is because of the many letters I have written to Your Lordship, I have never received a response. Now I am sending Salaì there to let Your Lordship know that I am almost at the end of my affair with my brothers, and that I believe I will be there at Easter and that I will bring with me two paintings of two Madonnas of various sizes, which are made for our Most Christian King or for whomever Your Lordship pleases. I would be very pleased to know, upon my return there, where I will be staying for my request, because I would not want to cause Your Lordship any further trouble; and, since I have also worked for the Most Christian King, whether my provision is going to be made or not. I am writing to the president about the water that the king gave me, of which I was not given possession, because at that time there was a shortage of it in the Navilio due to the large droughts and because its nozzles were not regulated, but he promised me that, once such a regulation was made, I would be given possession of it. So I ask Your Lordship, in the displeasure that now that these nozzles are regulated, to remind the president of my expedition, that is, to give him possession of that water, because upon my arrival I hope to make instruments and things for you that will be of great pleasure to our most Christian king. Nothing else happens to me. I am always at your command.

Stucco to be molded.

Take 6 parts of biturro (biturro), 2 parts of wax, and enough volatile flour to make the two pieces firm, like wax or molding clay.

Figure of a section of a ceiling:

If you want to make a beautiful ceiling at a low cost, you will take your stringers (biturro) that are 1/4 wide, 1/2 high, and 12 braccia long. Fix these to your walls, and place them with a knife edge so that they are stronger, and spaced one braccia apart. Then you will make a clay square, worked in your style, 1 and 1/2 braccia in size, and on top of that you will make a plaster mold. Then you will make a quantity of stucco, made with glue, flour, and wood sawdust; and make it hard, like softened wax. Then heat the plaster mold and soak it in black, melted pitch, and let it dry. Then incinerate it and shape it with sponge, hollowing it out like squares, and let it dry in the wind on a flat surface, leaving a final thickness of about 1.5 yards per face. Then paint it and attach it to the ceiling with 6 nails and a bolt in the middle. Then place the running boards on top, followed by the squares. This stucco is good for making chests and many other things. Plaster, sawdust, trimmings, and glue also make good stucco.

Of the sound that seems to remain in the bell after the bang.
The sound that remains, or seems to remain in the bell after it has been banged, is not in the bell itself, but rather is in the ear of the listener; which ear retains within itself the resemblance to the heard bang of a bell and gradually loses it, like the impression of the sun on the eye, which gradually fades away until it is no longer seen.
Counterproof.
If the above proposition were true in itself, you would not immediately end its sound by touching it with the palm of your hand, and especially at the beginning of its power, for indeed, once you have touched it, it would be useless to touch the bell with your hand, for the ear would equally retain it. Hence we see that, once the bang has been struck and your hand placed on the thing struck, the sound immediately ceases.

Every heavy object, unrestrained outside its natural place, desires to descend more in a straight line than in an arc.
This is evident because every body, whatever its nature, being outside its natural place, which is its preservation, desires to regain its original perfection in the shortest possible time; and because a chord is described in a shorter time than the arc of the same chord, it follows that every body outside its natural place desires to descend more by a chord than by an arc. From this, three things follow. The first is that the motion of gravity in the balance is not simply natural. This is evident because the arms of the balance, in descending, describe an arc and consequently curved lines. The second is that the heavy motion in the descending arm of the balance is not simply violent, because in this way natural motion is acquired by its descent. The third is that the heavy motion in the balance is intermediate between natural and violent. This is manifested by every natural motion, whether violent or beyond nature.

A point in itself is an indivisible part, being separate and similar to all and capable of all, and all indivisibles similar to one and capable of containing all in it. Of the Circles of the Moon.

I find that those circles of varying sizes and redness which appear to surround the moon at night are caused by varying degrees of the thickness of the humours, which are situated at various heights between the moon and our eyes. And that larger and less red circle is the first, lower part of these humours; the second, smaller, circle is higher and appears redder because it is seen through two humours. And so, the higher they are, the smaller and redder they will appear, because between the eye and that there will be more solid humours. Thus it is proven that where the greatest redness appears, there is greater quantity of humours.

Profile of a breaking wave:

Water falls along some line from the crest of its wave, and moves faster where its fall is least oblique, and breaks into foam where it encounters greater resistance. Therefore, from what has been said, waves break against the flow of the river and never against its current, because water falling against the current cannot generate a leap over something that is fleeing and does not receive a shock. Every impression is reserved for a certain time in its sensible object, and the one which was of greater power will be reserved for the most part in its object; and so will the less so in the one which was of less power. - In this case I call a sensible object that which is moved by some impression from what it was before; an insensible object is one which, even though it is moved from its first being, does not retain within itself any impression of the thing which moved it. The sensible impression is that of a blow received by a sonorous object, such as bells and similar things, and like a voice in the ear, which, if it did not retain impressions of the voices, a single song would never be graceful, because when jumping from the first to the fifth voice, it is as if one heard both voices at the same time, and one feels the true consonance that the first makes with the fifth; and if the impression of the first did not remain in the ear for some time, the fifth that follows immediately after the first would seem alone, and a single voice would not make any consonance, and so any song sung alone would seem to be without grace. Again, the brilliance of the sun or other luminous object remains for some time in the eye after it has been seen; and in motion a single stick of fire, moved rapidly in a circle, makes that circle appear to be of continuous and equal burning; the grains of rainwater appear to be continuous lines descending from their clouds; and thus it is shown that the eye retains the impressions of the things it sees in motion. Insensible objects that do not retain the impressions of opposite things are mirrors and any shiny object which, when removed immediately before the thing that is imprinted on it, is immediately completely deprived of that impression. We would therefore conclude that "the motion of the mover impressed upon the body moved by it is that which moves the body through the medium by which it moves." Since the ship was then ready, I wrote several times to Your Lordship and to M. Girolamo da Cusano, who has the document of this donation, and I also wrote to Corigero, but never received a reply. Now I am sending Salaì, my disciple, there to bear this gift, so that Your Lordship can tell him personally everything that happened; about which I beg Your Excellency.

I believe I will be there this Easter, nearing the end of my journey, and I will bring with me two paintings of Our Lady that I began and have brought to very good fruition in the time that remains. Nothing else happens to me, except for the following:

Magnificent Sir, the love Your Excellency has always shown me, and the benefits I have received from you, are continually before my mind.

I suspect that the small remuneration for the great benefits I have received from Your Excellency has made you somewhat disturbed with me; and this is because I have never received a reply to several letters I have written to Your Excellency. Now I am sending Salaì there to let Your Lordship know that I am almost at the end of my quarrel with my brothers, and that I believe I will be there this Easter and that I am bringing with me two paintings of two Our Lady of various sizes, which I have begun for the most Christian King or for whomever you please. I would be very pleased to know, upon my return there, where I am to stay for the purpose, because I would not want to cause further trouble to Your Lordship; and also, having worked for the most Christian King, whether my provision is going to run or not. I am writing to the president of the water the King gave me, which I was not given possession of because there was a shortage of it in the Navilio due to the large droughts and because its outlets were not regulated; but he promised me that, once such regulation was made, I would be given possession of it. Therefore, I beg you, if you should encounter this president, not to be displeased, but, now that these outlets are regulated, to remind the said president to give me possession of the water, which I understood to be largely his. Nothing else happens to me. I am always at your command.

Good morning, Sir Francesco, can God grant that you have never answered all the letters I have written to you? Now wait until I come there, for God's sake, and I will have you write so many times that perhaps you will be displeased.

My dear Sir Francesco, I am sending Salaì there to learn from the magnificence of the president what the purpose of the water regulation that was ordered for my departure at the mouths of the Navilio has been, because the magnificent president promised me that, as soon as this regulation was carried out, I would be dispatched. Now it has been some time since I heard that the Navilio was being repaired and likewise its mouths, and I immediately wrote to the president and to you, and then I replied but never received a reply. Therefore, you will deign to answer me what followed and, since it is not about to be dispatched, do not be sorry, for my sake, to urge the president a little about it and also Sir Girolamo da Cusano, to whom you will recommend me, and offer me to his magnificence.

On adjusting the poles.
On ensuring that the poles wear equally when placed on a straight line.

How the concavity that accommodates the pole of convoluted poles must be protected against its expansion. This will be discussed in the book on friction.
What motion most destroys the equality of the poles? How the concavity that accommodates the pole wears more than the pole itself. What toothed wheels wear more than the concavities that accommodate the poles? If wheels moved by strings wear the concavities of the poles more or less than wheels moved by the teeth of their pinions. The thinnest pole wears more than the concavity that accommodates it, since they are of equal weight. The concavity that receives the pole is worn away by an oblique line from the side from which its circumvolutionary motion declines.
What are the materials that most resist friction: dense with dense, or rare with rare, or rare with dense? In instruments where many wheels are in motion, perfection cannot premanence except for a brief period of time; and this arises because the wheels are not equal in weight, nor in poles, nor in motion, nor in force.

Main Column.

Of the Poles. Of adjusting the poles of the wheels.

In things that have circumvolutionary motion, certainly the circumvolutionary poles of these poles, through their precise equality, are the cause of the perfection of the aforementioned motions. Therefore, this equality will be discussed below.
What motion most destroys the mother of the pole?
There are three positions in the poles: equi-jacent, straight, and oblique. But the [straight] pole consumes the mother more than the equi-jacent one; and this arises from the fourth of this, which says: "Of poles of equal weight, the one that touches the least consumes its female most." Therefore, the pole placed upright occupies less space with its front than with its sides, except if the mother supporting it were very narrow, because she would quickly cut that pole.
On which side is the mother consumed by the pole?
The mother is consumed on the side from which its pole declines its motion, because that pole continually moves toward that side, always moving away from the opposite side.

In what aspect is the mother consumed?
From the rubbing of its pole.
The concavity made by the part in the mother by the rubbing made in it by its pole is oblique. It is proved by the fourth of this which says: "Every friction caused by the revolution of the equidistant poles on the same site will consume that site with an oblique concavity." And this is caused by the disposition of the two motions, one of which is caused by the heavy object that weighs toward the center of the universe, the second by the friction caused by the pole on that wall where it comes closest to the part that declines in its revolution mentioned above.

Figure of an equidistant pole and a wheel, with:

c a b – g h - d
What revolution of the equidistant pole is that which creates a perpendicular concavity?
The equilateral revolution of the pole which will be effected by the cord wound around that pole, as is seen done by jewelers, will always follow the path of its consummation along a line perpendicular to the center of the wheel, where the driving cord of that pole is wound. This is proved by the fifth of this, where it says: "That thing which is tied between the opposite ends of the cords that bind it, cannot approach the ends of these cords." Therefore the pole a, which is turned by means of the two equal cords b h and c g, will not be able to consume its mother except along the perpendicular line of the pole, where its wheel stops, that is, along the line a d and not along the line a h, because the cord b g pulls it towards itself in the direction g and does not allow it to rub in the direction b. And you will experience this with the pole cut around using a file or a file on a soft stone wheel.
