Main column.

Of the poles.
Of the matter that resists friction the most.
Friction occurs in three ways: hard on hard, soft on soft, and soft on hard. Of these three ways, contact varies in two ways: the first is simple contact between the rubbed bodies, and the second is compound contact. In simple contact, no matter is inserted, but only their surfaces that touch each other; but in compound contact, different materials are placed between the surfaces of the rubbed bodies, and the rougher they are, the more they wear down the aforementioned bodies. But if the rubbed bodies are of varying hardness, the softer one wears down the harder one, and this arises from the roughness of the interposed material, which is inserted into the less hard material and, having remained there, acts like a file, with which it then wears down the harder material.
But if the materials are of equal hardness, then the intervening material grinds itself, if it is less hard than the rubbed objects; but if it is harder, it wears out the friction just as two files of equal strength rub against each other.
Which pole is worn out more, the larger or the smaller one.
The larger the pole, the more it wears out in the same number of revolutions. Prove it with the fourth, where it says: "That thing wears out more, whose friction takes a longer path." Therefore our purpose is concluded, because a point marked on the pole of greater circumference takes a longer path than the point marked on the smaller circumference and consequently wears out more in its friction, etc.
If the pyramidal pole wears out equally.
The pyramidal pole placed upright is consumed, but with a pyramidal consumption, which pyramid is of the same proportion as the pole itself. Prove it by the third, which says: "That part of the pyramidal pole placed upright is consumed most in its revolution, which is of greater thickness." Prove it, and let the thickness of the pole at the head be four and at the feet two. By the fifth of the Elements: "The proportion from circumference to circumference is as from diameter to diameter," therefore the greater circumference is double the smaller. I say that the entire revolution of the pole will not be consumed equally, but rather more from the head than from the feet, in proportion as the point marked on the circumference at the head will simultaneously make a longer and faster motion than the point marked on the circumference by the feet. Therefore this consumption is not parallel, as the opponent claims, but is pyramidal.

Figures of Circular Tubes Variously Cut and Bent:

A pipe of uniform width, curved into a circular shape, placed with its diameter straight at the center of the world, will carry water with equal opposing weights around the diameter of the circular pipe.
The same will happen if the circular pipe is bent in any direction, that is, the weight of the opposing water will always be divided equally by the aforementioned diameter of the circular pipe. If the circular pipe is divided and the separate ends do not collide with each other in any part, then if the pipe is placed obliquely, the center of gravity of the water that fills the pipe will be outside the center of the circle, toward the lowest end of the pipe.
The center of gravity of the water enclosed in the oblique circular tube will be as much further from the diameter of that circle as the ends of the cut tube are lower than each other.

- I have methods of very light and strong bridges, suitable for carrying very easily and with them to follow and sometimes (as the needs arise) to flee the enemy, and other methods that are safe and inoffensive from fire and battle, easy and convenient to raise and lower; and methods of burning and destroying those of the enemy.

3.- If, due to the height of the embankment or the fortress of the place and site, it is not possible to use the role of bombardment during the invasion of a land, I have ways of ruining any (strong) fortress or other fortress, if it was not already founded on the rock, etc.

4.           - I also have ways of making bombards very convenient and easy to carry and throw with them in minutes (almost similar) of a storm, and with the smoke from it giving great fright to the enemy with serious damage and confusion etc.

9.             - And if it happens that I am at sea, I have many very effective instruments for attack and defense, and ships that will resist the fire of any heavy bombardment, gunpowder, and smoke.

- I have methods for tunnels and secret and twisted paths, made without any noise, to reach a (certain) and designated [place], even if it is necessary to pass under ditches or some river.
- I will make covered wagons that are safe and inoffensive, and which, entering among the enemy with their artillery, there is not so great a multitude of men-at-arms that they will not destroy, and behind these, a large number of infantry will be able to follow, unharmed and without any hindrance.
- If the need arises, I will make bombards, mortars, and passavolne of beautiful and useful designs, outside of common use.
Wherever the operation of the bombards is lacking, I will construct briccole, mangonels, trebuchets, and other instruments of admirable effectiveness and beyond the usual ones, and in short, according to the variety of circumstances, I will construct various and infinite things for attack and defense.

10. In times of peace, I believe I can satisfy anyone else in architecture, in the design of buildings, both public and private, and in conducting water from one place to another (suitable for attack and defense). I will also perform sculpture in marble, bronze, and clay; likewise, in painting whatever can be done, in comparison with anything else, and be it who wishes.
Work can also be done on the bronze horse, which will be an immortal and eternal glory to the happy memory of your father and of the illustrious House of Sforza. And if any of the above-mentioned things seem impossible or impracticable to anyone, I am most willing to experiment with them in your park or in any place Your Excellency pleases, and I humbly recommend myself as much as I can, etc.

When the eye moves from the sunlit white to a place of lesser light, everything appears dark. And this happens because the eye that is next to that sunlit white has its pupils contracted to such a degree that if they were previously visually present, they are now missing more than three-quarters of its quantity, and by lacking quantity, they are lacking power. Although you might say to me: a small bird would see very little at night, and because of its small pupils, the white would appear black to it. To this I would reply that here we are dealing with the proportion of the sum of that part of the brain dedicated to visual power and nothing else. Or to return: this pupil of ours grows and diminishes according to the brightness or darkness of its object, and because with time it does grow and diminish, it does not see as quickly when leaving the light and going into the dark, and similarly from the dark to the bright. In wanting to empty a pond that pours into the sea, without a doubt it is higher than the sea itself, because the water would not pour into it if it had no motion, and consequently it would not have motion if it did not descend, and it would not descend if it did not move from a place higher than that in which it moves: therefore let the mouth of the pond that pours into the sea be closed, and the river, which enters that pond in a turbid state, (n) finding that pond with little motion, will discharge its turbulence at the bottom of that pond, and thus in a short time will have filled a large part of its depth so that then, by opening the dam (above) already made at the confines of the sea, the water will depart and leave its bottom exposed to the air, in which, once it has dried up somewhat, we will be able to make the channel for the river that previously made that pond, and use the land for useful cultivation. And if the river were near the pond, we would embank the river with a sufficiently large embankment and give it a fall into the sea or near the sea. And since the end of the incident motion is lower, being on the sea, than any part of the river or the sea, the pond would open out at that place with a small and narrow channel of water, and thus the pond would come to equalize its surface down to the depth of the incident motion we mentioned of the river. And the way to prevent the sea from harming us in its growth is by means of a sluice gate, which shuts in the pond such sea ebbs, and this would not be done where the sea exhibits great variations in its rising and falling.

It seems so, and that the moon is surrounded by its elements, just as our earth is. If this were not the case, the water would divest the moon and descend to clothe the earth along with our sea. Not only the water of the moon, but the entire moon along with the water would descend, as a heavy thing, to the center of the world. If you say that the water that flows from the veins is water collected in the caves of the mountains, the answer to this will be that the water that is generated in these caves either has a greater inflow than a greater outflow, or a greater outflow than a greater inflow, or the outflow will be equal to the inflow. If the water enters the cave more than its outflow, the cave will fill completely and will expel all the air. If the water fills the entire mouth of the outlet, no more water will be able to descend, because the air will not be able to restore the vacuum that the water would create if it left the cave partially empty. Therefore, if the cave were always full of water, the same amount of water would fill the vein that supplies the water to the cave when the mouth that pours the water out of the cave would empty. This motion would therefore always be continuous and equal, which is never seen, because in all the veins that pour water out of the mountains, water diminishes and is lacking in summer, and becomes abundant in winter. And if the outlet is larger than the inlet, then the water will be lacking in the outlet until it becomes equal to the inlet. And if the inlet is made equal to the outlet, then the motion will be equal at all times. Some say that rainwater is the cause of the increase in the veins that pour water into rivers: this can be denied by the example of city ditches, which, being empty of water and a little earth, I have often seen dry and parched under the mud. But it could well be said that in such ditches the density of the clay prevents and prohibits the penetration of water beneath it, as is seen in the citerns made in salt water, which are surrounded, outside their walls and sand, with this earth, from which the vessels are worked, very fine, and the power of the salt water can never penetrate it, and so the water is always kept fresh in the citerns. But in the mountains where the sides of the stones are placed obliquely and vertically, these sides being covered with little earth, the rainwater immediately penetrates this earth, and flows between the cracks of the stones, and incorporates itself and fills the veins and cavernous places; Even the snow that settles slowly in the Alps, held back by the interposition of the roots and leaves of the small grasses of the meadows, penetrates more easily between the cracks in the rocks than it does through the aforementioned grass roots. Therefore, in addition to the settled snow that swells the rivers in summer, a large part of it penetrates through the aforementioned cracks in the rocks that make up the mountains. Here I will continue and make a little discussion about finding waters, although they seem somewhat outside our order, and then I will place them in order in their places in the extension of the work. I say that the same water penetrates the same terrain more where it is more level, and penetrates less where it is less oblique. Again, (where) on the same level, that terrain will be penetrated more where it is less dense and less rich; and so conversely. And where the stones are exposed by their edges, or a few are slanted toward the sky, there will be great penetration of water, especially when such stones are interspersed with slabs of limestone; and the layers that are interspersed with rich clay will penetrate little. And if the stones, which are exposed to the sky with their faces, are slabs of small thickness, these will drink a lot of rainwater, which will all drain away at the first bend of the slabs. Where the slabs are thicker, even if they stand upright, there the water penetrates less; and where they are thinner, more, as I said, the water will penetrate. Where the soil is sandy, there will be an abundance of water. Where there is coarse gravel, the water will be drunk everywhere, and will quickly escape from its bottom. There are the waters of the Adige, of which the varieties will be described, according to the soil, kidney, and gravel.

On the Color of the Air

I say that the blue in which the air appears is not its own color, but is caused by warm humidity, vaporized in minute and imperceptible moments, which, after being struck by the solar rays, becomes luminous under the darkness of the immense gloom of the region of fire, which covers it above. And this will be seen, as I saw, over Mount Boso, a ridge of the Alps that divide France from Italy, a mountain at its base that gives birth to four rivers that flow through all of Europe in four opposite directions; and no mountain has its base at such a height. This mountain rises to such a height that it almost passes all the clouds, and snow rarely falls there, but only hail in summer, when the clouds are at their highest. and this hail is preserved there in such a way that, if it were not for the [rare]ity of clouds falling and rising there, which does not happen (of itself) twice in an age, there would be a very large quantity of ice raised by the degrees of hail, which I found there in mid-July very thick; and I saw the air above me dark, and the sun, striking the mountain, to be much brighter there than in the low plains, because a lesser thickness of air intervened between the summit of the mountain and the sun. Again, as an example of the color of the air, we would cite the smoke produced by dry and old wood, which, coming out of chimneys, appears to be very blue (e) when it is between the eye and the dark place, but, when it rises high and comes between the eye and the illuminated air, it immediately appears to be an ashen color; and this happens because there is no longer darkness behind it, but in place of it the luminous air; and if this smoke is from green and young wood, then (tre n) it will not be blue, (but) because, not being transparent, and full of excess humidity, it acts as a condensed cloud, which takes on lights and shadows as if it were a solid body. And the air does the same, for too much humidity makes it white, and too little, infused with heat, makes it dark, a dark blue color; and this (p) is sufficient for us as regards the definition of the color of air. Although it could also be said that, if the air (as) had for its natural color this transparent blue (no), it would follow that, where a greater quantity of air were interposed between the eye and the element of the fire, that its blue would be composed there with greater darkness, as is seen in blue glass and sapphires, which appear darker the larger they are. And the air (does the opposite to us) in this case acts in the exact opposite way, since, where a greater quantity is interposed between the eye and the sphere of the fire, there (s) it appears to us more white, and this happens towards the horizon; and the smaller the amount of air is interposed between the eye and the sphere of the fire, the darker the blue appears to us even if we are in the low plains. Therefore, what I say follows: the air takes on its blue color through the corpuscles of humidity, which capture the sun's luminous rays. The difference is also seen in the particles of dust or in the particles of smoke, in the solar rays that pass through the spiracles of the walls in dark places, one ray appearing ashen, while the other, made of thin smoke, appears a beautiful blue. Furthermore, in the dark shadows of mountains remote from the eye, the air between the eye and such shadows appears very blue, and in the luminous part of such mountains it does not vary much from its original color; but whoever wants to see the final proof should paint a board with different colours, among which a very fine black should be placed, and on top of all of them a thin and transparent white lead should be applied: then it will be seen that the clarity of this white lead does not appear on any colour of a more beautiful blue than on black, but it should be thin and well ground.

Of the moon.

No opaque body is compressed by the solar ray with equal illumination, but the light will be more powerful the more that body receives the solar ray at more equal angles, thus remaining unevenly illuminated. And here the moon, being a spherical and opaque body, remains, in its parts capable of receiving light, of equal brightness; and this, from what was said above, could not exist if it were not water; since water, being spherical, it cannot capture the solar ray and return it by reflection to our eyes, except in the incident ray, which is small compared to the quantity of the lunar body; where it is necessary to concede, the sea waves, and each one by itself, catches a solar ray, and the darkness interposed between the peaks of the waves is infused among the luminous species, and does not render such clarity, [He continues, occupying the main column:] as it would do if its water were without the waves, because, if that were the case, a part of the moon would be of as great splendor, as if it were the sun itself, and it would do as is seen in our waters without the waves, in which the simulacrum of the sun is seen mirrored in such a way, that it seems that it does not otherwise impede human eyes, but that the true sun is created; which would happen similarly if the moon's water had no waves: (We see in water without waves a single image of the sun reflected, no more luminous than the true sun; and we see in an innumerable quantity of waves of water innumerable (suns) images of the sun reflected, and through the innumerable intervals of the waves, which do not receive such an image and remain dark, that multitude of such obscurities mix among the said images of the sun and are confused together because of their diminution, caused by long distance from our eye: they diminish in such a way, that the form of the shadowy and luminous wave is lost, from which remains such a brightness, that the eye can then better sustain it. Of ebb and flow.

All seas have their ebb and flow at the same time, but it appears to vary, because the days do not begin at the same time throughout the universe. And if the swiftest stream were thicker than each of the others which converge more slowly on the same spot, then the swifter stream would strike more of the converging waters; hence the concurrent stream which is more in a straight line with the current of the swifter stream will offer more resistance to that part of the swift stream which strikes it, so that, of necessity, the swift stream will bend more toward its perpendicular than the remainder of the swift stream did in striking the opposing stream [Fig. 12.a] which is in a less straight line. Propositions 38.

The riverbeds vary, after their flooding, in as many places as there are sites where their obstacles vary. What has been said happens because the obstacles of the water are those that cause the riverbeds to fill or empty; for if the water strikes the obstacles and does not overcome them, it erodes the land in front of them and fills the rear; and if the water strikes the obstacle and overcomes it, it erodes the land in front and behind it; and if it overcomes and surrounds it, it erodes the land on every side, except on that side where it is very oblique, because it has not fallen in that place; and it will deepen even more where the percussion of the water or its current is more powerful. The immovable obstacles of rivers are the cause of maintaining the islands, the shoals, and their depths, because they always act as a firm shield against the inflow of the waters. If the obstacle has a great obliquity against the inflow of the waters, (then) [Fig.1.a] both to the side and behind it is straight, then, being overcome by the waves, (it) the river will not remove land in front of it, but to the side and behind it. And if the obstacle is straight in front (and behind) and oblique in the back, the water, which overcomes it, will make great concavities in the back and not in the back. The bank will come to ruin more quickly, which has the falls or currents of the water closest to it. And the bank will be more permanent, which has the currents or falls of the river furthest from it. In rivers that are forded so that, due to their turbulence, the bottom cannot be seen, you will always pass at the beginning of the current. Of the objects that completely cross rivers, the shorter their length, the stronger they are. Of the shapes of obstacles, with which the banks of rivers are protected from the inundation of their waters. How the currents should be maintained in the middle of rivers. How the lowest level of water is maintained towards the banks of rivers. Where the walls (a) built for banks will fall towards the river. Where the walls built for banks will fall away from the river. Where the banks of rivers will not fall either towards the river or in the opposite direction, but will collapse halfway along their lengths. Where the current is directed towards the impact of the bank, there future ruin is destined. When the river overflows its banks, it is a sign of the bank's imminent collapse. It is a vain act to place obstacles in the way of the water's flow in its great depths, because where there is depth, the water is seen to flow strongly at the bottom. That part of the river will be filled with matter that is further from its main current. No obstacle should be placed in front of the water's approach. Propositions 23.

When the water levels are created along the banks of rivers with equal force, it will be a sign that the river is straight in that part, and its greatest depth will be at the middle of its width, that is, beneath the principal current of its waters: in A, 89. The principal current of rivers will be where the motions of the refracted waters collide together. The greatest depth of rivers will be beneath the current created by the refracted motions: in A, 89. The straight current of rivers will be bent by other rivers that strike it transversely. The currents of smaller rivers, which flow into larger ones, cause the opposite banks of the larger rivers to break: in A, 89. The islands of the rivers have heavier things on them towards the confluence of the waters than in the opposite place: in A, 88. Where the two currents collide together and follow the current together for a while, they hollow out the bottom beneath their conjunction. But those rivers, which after their collision emerge in opposite places, have the place of their conjunction beneath them a great concavity in the shape of a ship. The depth of the river beds, which is generated under the collision of the currents, will be greater than the length, the more acute the angle found within the conjunction of these currents is; and so, conversely, (will be) the depth, created under the collision of the currents of the rivers, will be shorter and deeper, the greater the angle of the two currents is. But if the two currents combine to form a dead sea, no depth will be created beneath this conjunction, because there will be no percussion. The islands that are first exposed when the rivers ebb and flow suddenly drain their waters into the lateral waters of the islands, and there they wash the gravel and strip it bare and stripped of its backs, which are then carried away by the river current. But if the island which is discovered in the middle of the river drains its waters into dead seas, then the sand and earth carried by these waters will stop in the aforementioned seas (and banks) and will fill their depths: in A, 88. When two currents collide together, and one, before the collision, has struck the bank of the river, the depth created by the said collision will be below the side which did not strike the bank: in A, 87. Conception: The water which flows more is more powerful and wears down its bottom more. Conception: The water which is slower, discharges more of the things which it carried with it, before it is slowed down. When two currents join together, the slower one (lasci) slows down even further, thus discharging more of the matter that was muddying it. This matter, the more powerful branch, immediately carries away with it the things that border it in its course; and thus a sudden depth is created from the bottom of the slow river to the bottom of the swift one. Conception: The running water digs out its bottom, and the lazy one fills it. Always, in front of the obstacle, the water slows down, and the sand at the bottom floods: 74 in A. When the waves refracted by the banks collide in the middle of the current, they will give birth to a third refracted motion, which rises up, and, in falling, falls in a motion participating in the length and latitude of the river: in A, at 75. But, when the refracted motions, which rise from the banks, vary, as happens continuously, that is, from greater to lesser power, then its third refracted motion, which takes place in the middle of the river, will fall now to the right and now to the left, that is, always in the opposite direction to the previous weaker refracted motion: in A, 75. When the water of the current strikes the bottom and rises up above the common course of the river, it is no longer pushed or carried by the event of the river, because it is in the air, where, its base being carried away, to be united with the flowing water, and because of this, the wave, which was in the air, comes to fall backwards. A small pole, fixed in the bottom of the current, will cause the river to be concave for a long space by the aforementioned current: in A, at 74.

Of the universal earth.

The universal earth should be the kind used to make squares, mixed with cow dung and woollen trimmings.

On grooming the male.

The male should first be placed in the pit with hooks as shown above; then coat it inch by inch, until it is the color of a square; then go over it with a small stick, gently striking it side by side; and where you hear it ring, tie it with wire. But to avoid mistakes, you can wrap it all over.

The male.

The male's tail should finally be covered with eggs, powdered squares, and ash mixed with salt water. Also good, and even better, is cow dung ash mixed with salt water.

On the frames.

The cornices should be made almost to the top with a top-like cord, and above that, finish the cornices with fine earth and clean them with the said tallow and tar. The ornaments should be made of wax.

The tallow should be mixed with blacksmith's filige and, as finely as possible, with bovine ash.

The fine earth of the bombards.

Take the trimming earth and stick it to the wall in thin slabs so that it dries well. Then pound and sift it into a fine powder; and to 50 parts of this powder, add 10 parts of not-overcooked, well-pounded and sifted square wood; also a little fine trimmings, cloth, or fustian; and to this mixture, add 6 parts of ash, which you will sift by diluting with well-salted water. Apply this liquid, thin layer two or three times with a whitewash brush, letting it dry without heating each time.

It would also be good to apply, before this, ash from burnt boar dung, dissolved in salt water.

How to increase the melting point.

You will increase the melting point when two-thirds of the copper is immersed in water. Then, using a thick chestnut stick, you will remove the remaining copper, still intact, from the melted part.

When tin should be mixed with copper.

The tin should be added to the copper once the copper has been immersed in water.

About melting the metal.

The metal should generally be made in bombards with a 6 or even 8 percent ratio: that is, 6 percent tin to 100 percent copper. And the less you add, the safer the bombard will be.

What wood is good?

Wood is good when it is young willow; or, if you cannot have willow, you should use alder. And each wood should be young and very dry.

To understand the layout of the fire.

You will know when the fire is good and useful by having clear flames; And if you see the tips of these flames disturbed and ending with a lot of smoke, don't trust them, especially when you're almost bathing in water.

The cause of freezing.

I say the cause of this freezing often comes from too much heat and even from poorly dried wood.

On restoring the metal when you want to cool it.

When you see the bronze starting to freeze, take some finely chopped willow sticks and light a fire with them.

On soaking the inside of the furnace.

The furnace must, before you put the metal in it, be soaked with Valencian earth; and on top of that, add ashes.
On the thickness of the crosspieces.

The thickness of the crosspieces at the front must not exceed half to a third of the diameter of the ballast, and the length must not exceed 30 to 36 ballasts.

On the length of the bombard's shaft.

If you want to cast a stone ballast, make the shaft's length 6 or up to 7 ballasts. And if the ballast were made of iron, make the shaft up to 12 ballasts. And if the ballast were made of lead, make it up to 18 ballasts. I mean when the bombard has a mouth capable of holding 600 pounds of stone ballast or more.

On the thickness of the bombard.

The bombard must be 600 pounds of ballast or more, with this rule: you will measure the diameter of the ballast, and divide it into 6 parts; and one of these parts will be the front thickness, and the other half will be the back thickness. And if the ball weighs 700 pounds, 1/7 of the ball's diameter will be its front thickness. And if the ball weighs 800 pounds, 1/8 of its front diameter. And if 900 pounds, 1/8 and 1/2. And if 1000 pounds, 1/9.

On the thickness of the chimney.

The chimney should not exceed two fingers' thickness, and should be buried four times in the thin earth and then well reinforced. And it should only be annealed on the inside, and then covered with a thin layer of beef ash.

The furnace must be built between four well-founded pillars.

On joining the lead to the other metal.

If you want to carefully mix lead with the metal to make up for the amount of tin required in the metal, first combine the lead with the tin, and then add the molten copper.

How to break a large mass of bronze.

If you want to break a large mass of bronze, first suspend it; then build a trough-like wall of bricks on four sides, and light a strong fire. And when it is very red, strike it with a heavy weight lifted high with great force.

How the axis that forms the bombard should be positioned.

The guiding axis of the bombard's mold should be made of pearwood and doubled from the middle to the width of a thick board, so that it does not twist. And where you leave a space in it for the impression of the frames and the shape of the bombard, it should be a surface, not an edge. And when you apply the tallow with it, burnish the surface with a hog's tooth so that it is smooth. and the tallow should be poured thinly, so that it does not leave marks when turning.
If you had to cast a large piece.

If you had to cast a hundred thousand pounds, do it with five furnaces, each holding 2,000 pounds, or up to 3,000 pounds at most.

To prepare the copper for cooling in the furnace.

When the copper cools in the furnace, immediately upon noticing it, cut it with the scrapers while it is in the furnace, or, if it is completely cooled, cut it as you would lead with large, thick chisels.

Ease of casting.

First attach a portion of the metal to the sleeve; then place it in the furnace, and this will begin its melting process with its bath.

How to remove the curls from bronze.

Make an iron rod that fits a large chisel, and use it to rub over the ridges of bronze that remain above the mortar castings, which emerge from the mold's grooves. But make sure the rod is well-weighted, and the blows are long and hard.

Make a bundle of iron wire as thick as string, and rub it with water, keeping a tub underneath to prevent mud from building up underneath.

Nature of the effect of the sound of the bombard.

The noise of the bombard is caused by the impetuous fury of the flame reflected in the resisting air; and this effect is produced by the quantity of powder ignited in the body of the bombard. Not feeling a place capable of its growth, nature directs it to furiously seek the place capable of receiving its growth; and by breaking or clearing away the weakest obstacle, it reaches the spacious air, which, being unable to escape with the speed it is assailed by, because fire is thinner than air, must necessarily be that, since the air is not of the same thinness as the fire, it cannot give way with the speed and rapidity that the fire assails it, hence resistance. And this resistance is the cause of the great noise and noise of the bombard.

But if you fired the bombard against the approach of a strong wind, you would feel a greater roar because of the greater resistance of the air against the flame; and so it would make less noise when fired against the wind, because there would be less resistance. In marshy places or other thick air, the bombard will make a greater noise from nearby, and will be heard less from a distance than on mountains and other places of thin air. If the air is equally thick or thin and without the movement of wind, the noise will be equally felt around its source and will spread from circle to circle, similar to the circles of water caused by throwing a stone into it. And in the place where similar instruments are fired, the nearby air will break or move all objects of weak resistance. All large vases with wide mouths, paper windows, and similar objects will be broken; If hay is moved, all the roofs visible from their supports will be moved; and this will happen when many windows and doors are open, and the thin and unprotected walls will pose a danger. This happens because the air deflates and rushes and tries to escape in all directions. As for the movement, hay is moved, doors, windows, trees, and the like. And if you place a loosely packed arrow with a small stone over a distance of six miles, it will fall due to the movement of the air.

Summary drawing of a river, of which a section is marked with

a b braccia 100 m o

If you wanted to know how much a river drops per mile without using another level, you would do this: be sure to choose a section of the river that most closely matches the general flow of the course whose drop you want to know, and from that you will take 100 braccia of bank, marking their beginning and end with two commas, as shown above in a b. Place a viscous or gall or a small piece of cork at the beginning, and note how many musical beats it takes for this thing, moving with the declining waves, to reach the end of the 100 braccia course. And then measure many others of slower and even faster courses. And then measure the drop of 100 braccia with the level. And with this reasoning, having measured various waters, you will then be able to tell, just by taking 100 paces from a bank, and noting how many times your vessel1 has taken that course, you will be able to tell with truth the decrease it makes per mile2.

What is the sound produced by the blow?

The time in which the blow is generated is the briefest thing that can be done by man. And there is no body so large, being suspended, that with a brief blow it does not immediately cause motion; which motion reverberates in the air, and the air resounds when it touches the thing moved.

If the noise is in the hammer or in the anvil, I say: because the anvil is not suspended, it cannot resonate; the hammer resonates in the bounce it makes after the blow. And if the anvil were to sound, the sound produced in it by each small hammer, just as the bell has the same pitch for each different thing that strikes it, so would the anvil struck by each different hammer. And if you hear different sounds from different sizes of hammers, therefore the sound is in the hammer and not in the anvil.

For the thing not suspended does not sound; Being suspended, even the slightest contact robs it of sound.

A struck bell immediately produces a tremor; the sudden tremor immediately strikes the surrounding air, which immediately resonates; being impeded by even the slightest contact, the air neither trembles nor strikes nor resonates.

If the bird that suddenly strikes the air, should it resonate or not?

I say no, because the air that penetrates through the thing that strikes it does not receive a blow, and therefore cannot produce sound.

1) On this first page of the Codex Trivulziano, only signatures are placed: in the center, a large S, identified as the signature of the Biblioteca Ambrosiana, dating back to the time when the Codex became part of it through a donation by Galeazzo Arconati. In the upper right corner, the number .1. is the first of the first sixteenth-century folio numbering system added to the Codex; further to the right, another 1, in red ink, is the first digit of the page numbering system of the third and final numbering system of the Codex. Finally, approximately halfway along the same upper edge, a third number .10. is believed to have been added towards the end of the sixteenth century, according to André Corbeau (an opinion I also share), by Pompeo Leoni when, having come into possession of Leonardo's codices, he carried out a complete survey and cataloguing of them. This number .10. is to be connected to the abbreviation «Ge.55», placed on p. 102, the page that closes the Codex.

If you are attacked at night in your quarters, or if you are in doubt, use traps that throw iron caltrops. And if you are attacked, draw them among the enemy and you will have time to organize your men against the attackers and the deceived enemy, who, due to the pain of their wounded feet, will be of little use. And you will arrange your attack as follows: divide your men into two squadrons and place the enemy between them, but make sure your men have the soles of their shoes, and likewise the horses their shoes, as I said before; otherwise, the caltrops will not recognize yours from the enemy. And make sure that each overflow throws a cartload of said caltrops.

Protect yourself from caltrops.

If you wear a cloth pad woven from cotton cords about a finger thick between your foot and the bottom of your shoe, you'll be safe from thistles, as they won't get stuck in your feet.

If you want to be sure of soft sand on your sandals, keep coarse river sand scattered along the path and where you'll be standing, and the pitch will hold it in place. And always keep bags of it ready for when you need it.

You will have these caltrops cast in the ironworks, using three-piece molds, and then the points will be filed.

Below is a drawing of three caltrops and, after a space between them, a fourth with two points, under which is written:

double caltrops1

These caltrops are to be used in a leather pouch beside each person, so that, if the expected forward movement2 were to turn into a retreat due to the enemy's strength, these, scattered behind them, would slow the horses' speed and produce an unexpected forward movement.

But to prevent this seed from being a cause of similar deception, you will first have prepared the horses' shoes in the shape depicted below. Let a steel plate, as thick and wide as the horse's shoe, be nailed between the horseshoe and the foot.

And likewise, let the infantrymen on foot be fitted with loose iron plates just above their shoes so that they can easily lift their heels, take steps, and run as needed without any obstruction. And their loosening will be as shown below.

Furthermore, if each combatant sailor has a small bag of these, and if they throw hay by hand onto the opposing galleys or ships, they will be the seed of imminent victory. But you should have your shoes ironed as described above, and filled underneath with small stitches, so that, when soft soap is thrown onto your ship, you can stand on your feet.

Again, if the enemy were to throw mortar into powder so thick that its thickness would obstruct the air that enters your lungs through your breath, you would place four posts in four spaces along the length of your ship, four per post. Each batch should have a small barrel of water and large spouts that force the water out through many small holes so that the water, converted to smoke, will join with the smoke from the mortar and draw it downward.

On the teeth of the wheels.

The toothed wheels do not exert the same force in turning as they exert on their wheels. For sometimes they exert force with the bottoms of their teeth on the end of the tooth of the wheel, and sometimes they exert force with the ends of their teeth on the bottoms of the teeth of that wheel. Therefore, since the force of the wheel is used at various distances from its center, it operates with varying powers. And for this reason, the time of clocks, even if the wheels were perfectly guided, will not be such a time of equal motion.

Of wheel, cord, and teeth.

Some motions are used with teeth, some with cords, some with contacts. Of these, those of the teeth are the most powerful. After these are those of the cords. The third weakest is that of contact. Of teeth, it occurs in clocks and similar instruments. Of cords, spinning wheels and the like. Of contact, as in silk twisting machines.

Because when the teeth of the motor touch the ends of the teeth of its carriage, the motor feels more fatigue than when the opposite occurs, that is, when the ends of the carriage's teeth touch the ends of the teeth of its motor, because it has less relief. I have learned from the lathe makers that the momentum of their lathes retains within itself some of the nature of the motion given to them by these lathes. And for this reason I have judged it possible to make the same water that grinds a mill also grind 2. For when the 32 teeth of a half wheel have been made to rotate four times around a wheel with eight teeth, that wheel can rotate four more times by itself, almost at the same speed as when it was pushed by its wheel. And in the time it leaves one wheel, it rejoins the other, as you see in the drawing.

If I had thus made two half wheels toothed to the style, or shaft, as I did on the other paper, certain by the suddenness that the wheels take to give that half rotation, they would have great difficulty in returning backward, as happens in this instrument, and they would stop for a while before they could resume their second motion. Therefore, I thought it better for such wheels to rotate a sixth time rather than a half, because in this sixth circular motion, the wheel, or lift, takes less flight than in a half-circle, so it more easily resumes the opposite motion, and is better.

For first you found it without any motion, and then you found it having within itself the motion of inspiration. Therefore, the second three times it gives by itself will be much faster than the first three times it gives by itself. And if you return to give it another three times and then let it follow by itself with its other three, these will be as much faster than the second ones as the second ones were faster than the first ones. Instrument for testing how many times a pound of lead lifts itself in water. That is, let's say, a lead measure for how many measures of water it pushes out of its level, lifting them upwards. And first you will make the plinth, the lead, and the reed of equal thickness, and note how many times the height of the lead enters into the height of the water that rises above the water level of the plinth. Then you will make the plinth and the lead of equal thickness, and the reed by half. Then the reed by a quarter.[4] Then the reed and plinth of equal thickness, and the lead by half. Then the lead by a quarter, always increasing in length what is lacking in thickness. Furthermore, make the lead wider than the plinth and the reed. And thus, by noting each quality, you will then be able to correctly judge the power of each aquatic instrument.

Remember to test in this case the weight of each quality of metal, stone, earth, and similarly wood. And you will do the same in the loot with silver and any liquid body capable of rising. And similarly, the difference is in leaving air between the lead and the water, and also in making this water touch the lead that precedes it.

If you wanted to see how many measures of water a measure of lead needs as its counterweight, you would do this: wrap a piece of lead one ounce thick around it. And grease it with soap and dip it five or six times in a bath of wax, so as to make a firm covering of equal height to the lead. Then take out the lead and make enough measures of water or wine to balance it with the said lead. And thus you will make a good and true rule, always beating the weight of the wax with the weights.

Method of simply loading heavy objects onto carts. And it is done in this way near the Lombards. A question I ask of my readers.

I want you to grant me that the line from the object to the eye through the same quality of air is straight.

If I propose plane lines for different qualities of obliquity, I understand them to be straight. If I speak of round bodies

moving on planes, let them be understood as perfect.

(Mid-page:)

I have found, among the other superfluous and impossible credulity of men, the search for continuous motion, which some call a perpetual wheel. This has lasted for many centuries, with long research and experimentation and great expense, occupied by almost all those men who delight in waterworks and wars and other subtle ingenuities. And in the end it always happened to them as it did to the archmists, that for a small part the whole was lost. Now I intend to give this alms to this sect of investigators, that is, to give them as much peace in this research as this little work of mine lasts. And beyond this, whatever they promise of themselves to others will have their desired end, and they will not always have to remain in flight, because of the impossible things promised to princes and rulers of peoples. I remember seeing many, and from various countries, childishly credulous, come to the city of Venice, with great hopes of provisions, and operate a mill in dead water. Not being able to move such a machine after much expense, they were forced to move themselves with great fury from that air.

(Mid-page:)

That is, to remove with instruments this water, as from a swamp, well, or sea, and to use this water, removed from its descent, to do what other water does to mills. Either fools or truly unnatural men... you will.

(Towards the bottom:)

Whoever denies the reason for things publishes his ignorance.

If it were possible to make a bombard, let the world be its ball, and just as a bombard throws a ball of one arm three miles, so one can measure its course as 9,000 arm lengths, that is, 9,000 ball. We can therefore say that such a bombard would throw our world nine thousand times the size of the diameter of that world away from itself. Seven thousand miles per world would be good, that would be 63 thousand miles.

(At the bottom of the page:)

If you do not want to make them of bronze, so that they are not taken, know that all the good things of Rome were plundered from cities and lands conquered by the Romans. And it was not enough to be of miraculous weights, such as the needle and two horses. And if you have it made so clumsy that it cannot be carried away, it will be made into walls and mortar. Do as you please, for everything has its own demise. And if I tell you that you do not want to do anything that gives more honor to the craftsman than to the one who spends, know that most things give more honor to their maker than to the payer.
For the sixth, take the wax and oil.

Here the question arises as to which line will make this antenna move more easily for its mover: either along the equidistinct line f m, or along the oblique line n m, or at any degree between the two lines.

It is clearly demonstrated by the 60th of the 7th that the equidicent string feels less strain from the weight it moves than by any line that weight were pulled. For the equidistinct string f m is strained only by the friction that this weight makes with the earth from which it moves. And as the said friction is lightened in n by this motion, so much does it increase in m, so that it always gives the same effort to the string f m, nor does the effort of said friction ever increase or decrease, at any degree of motion. This friction is much less than the weight of the beam, as I demonstrated in chapter 5 of chapter 9. Now it remains for us to say what difference in effort the mover of said antenna would have if he were to pull it along the oblique line n m. Certainly he would feel much more weight of said antenna when he pulled along this line than in any other assigned method. For the more it lacks the friction of the first method, the more weight it acquires of said antenna, so that in the end the antenna is supported entirely on the string that moves it. Thus, by the given reasons, it is concluded that the motion of any weight is easier along an equidistricted line than along an oblique line...

Each degree of motion along an oblique line changes degrees of weight. And along an equidistricted line, each degree of motion maintains the same weight, whether the weights are made together, or changed into n, m, and 220, when combined, because the more weight there is in n, the more weight there is in m.

Let p q be a window through which a piece of wood the thickness of a man's leg or more is inserted. When you have the stirrup b up, the person on top will hold the rope m with their hand, and you, the person on the bottom, will stop on the foot that is at b. And the stirrup a will remain weightless at this time. Then the person on top will pull the rope a with their other hand and will raise the stirrup a as much above b as b was previously above a. Then you, from below, will withdraw onto the foot that is at a and will leave b weightless. Then the person on top will similarly pull the rope m b with their other hand as much above a as a was above b, that is, one arm's length. Why are the hours sometimes long and sometimes short?

This happens because, as the air thickens due to the humidity of low temperatures, the clocks' time finds more resistance in it, so the longer it runs, the longer the hour. And if you want to be clear about this, consider the strings of the counterweights of these clocks, which thicken in such humid temperatures, and their centers become further from their bearings, which should make the hour shorter. Yet the hours in humid temperatures are longer. Therefore, this length of hours arises from this clock time and from no other cause.

The ratio of one density or rarity to the other is the same as the stroke made by the same arrow, the same distance and force, more so in one than in the other. Therefore, measure the motion of an arrow through the air, and then shoot the same one through water. But first test it in different airs, namely, foggy, rainy, and clear, mountainous and valley. Then shoot the same arrow through different muds, earths, stones, and woods, and other materials that are not sinewy. And measure the strokes made by the same arrow and by the same crossbow, which is not tired. And whatever the length of the stroke, so will be the density of the material passed. Then test and compare the nebulous things themselves, such as wood, bread, wool, cotton, sponges, linen, and the like, and then proportion.

Of all primary motions created by equal power, the one that takes the longest path will push the thing moved furthest from itself.

The halfway point of the ballista's string that is pulled to the place where it is released, as are the degrees of its motion, so will be the degrees of the diminution of its angles.

The power of the mover that pulls the ballista's string increases as the angle created at the halfway point of that string decreases.

Just as if the proportions are equal, the motions will be equal.

The motion made by the thing drawn by the ballista will be as great as the angle of the cord that propelled it[12] and as great as the motion that created that[13] angle[14] and, similarly, the[15] power of the force or weight that pulled that cord to the creation of that angle. Since all the said[16] things are of equal proportion, it is also necessary that the weight of the thing propelled by the cord, and similarly the air through which it moves, be equal in its proportion, as were the other aforementioned proportions.

That is, the motion of the thing propelled, the motion of the cord that is loaded, the thickness[17] of the angles made by that cord when it is loaded, the weight or force that pulls the middle of that cord, the weight of the thing propelled, and the quality of the air through which the thing propelled must pass.

Strength is primary and derivative. Primary force arises from abundance or scarcity, that is, an increase or decrease in its cause, such as the multiplication of air that arises from the dissolution of clouds caused by the wind, which bends plants and strengthens them. It also occurs in the muscles or tendons of animals, where the vital spirits, as they swell, contract and draw their limbs with them, giving them more power than their own weight, in proportion as the power of the created force exceeds the resistance of the weight of those limbs. That is, if the created force is 10, and the ordinary weight of the member where it is born is one, this created force exceeds 9289 and will be consumed precisely when 9 is added to that member, and one that member weighs, which makes 10. From which it is clearly manifest that 10 of potency, against 10 of resistance, consume one another, because neither more potency nor more resistance is found.

The derivative force is that which is born from the motion of the aforementioned primary, and at the same time that the primary is born. The derivative can never surpass it, but it can certainly reach its equality. But much greater potency can be achieved when, with an equal motion to the primary, this derivative is persisted for a long time. That is, if the power of the derivative force is in proportion to the power of its primary, it will be in proportion to the times with which the primary generates the derivative. That is, if the primary force originates in one degree of time and uses two times to generate the derivative, the derivative force will be double the power of the primary, and thus the derivative will subsequently increase with the time the primary generates it.

When the primary force has the same motion as the derivative, it will also have the same power. But if the motion of the primary force is less than the derivative, these forces will together have the same proportion as the length of their motions.

The motion of the primary or derivative force that is longer will be proportionally stronger.

Force, weight, impact, and material motion are equally the cause and generator of each other, and each arises through violence.

Force and weight are many cases so similar that they almost seem to be the same thing, and many other operations are so dissimilar and varied that they can be designated by two names. And where they are found to be similar is when you want to push or pull, which is as much force as weight. And where they differ is that force is consumed by itself, as is seen in crossbows that remain bent by force for a long time. Weight in the air is always equal. Gravity has weight. Force is spiritual, because a crossbow weighs as much when under its force as when unloaded. The desire of weight is toward the center, and force is to return along the line from which it was created.

If the force and the weight are of equal motion, and the force is the cause of the weight, then the power of the weight will certainly never exceed that of the force, but will be less or equal. If it is less, this will happen when you bend a tree and attach a small weight to it, which, in rising, would pull the weight with it. And the motion made by the weight would be the same as that of the tree that pulls it with it in its rising. If this force is equal to the weight, this would happen when the tree, after some motion in rising, remains bent, and the weight holding it remains suspended in the air. Then these two powers are certainly equal, because the weight cannot return to its base and the tree cannot rise. If the weight is the cause of the force, since the one has the same motion as the other, the force will never be able to exceed that weight, but will be less, or rather equal. If it is less, this will happen when a great weight is attached to a thin bond or rod, which, unable to resist so much power, bends with a motion equal to that of the weight attached to it and accompanies that weight until it comes to rest on the ground. Here the weight remains lighter than before, the more weight opposes the force of the bent bond. Hence we will overturn the above-mentioned sentence, and say better: If the force and the weight have equal motion, they will always be of equal power, even though they are interchangeably the cause of each other.

A question I ask of my readers.

I want you to grant me that the line from the object to the eye through the same quality of air is straight.

If I propose plane lines for different qualities of obliquity, I understand them to be straight. If I speak of round bodies

moving on planes, let them be understood as perfect.

(Mid-page:)

I have found, among the other superfluous and impossible credulity of men, the search for continuous motion, which some call a perpetual wheel. This has lasted for many centuries, with long research and experimentation and great expense, occupied by almost all those men who delight in waterworks and wars and other subtle ingenuities. And in the end it always happened to them as it did to the archmists, that for a small part the whole was lost. Now I intend to give this alms to this sect of investigators, that is, to give them as much peace in this research as this little work of mine lasts. And beyond this, whatever they promise of themselves to others will have their desired end, and they will not always have to remain in flight, because of the impossible things promised to princes and rulers of peoples. I remember seeing many, and from various countries, childishly credulous, come to the city of Venice, with great hopes of provisions, and operate a mill in dead water. Not being able to move such a machine after much expense, they were forced to move themselves with great fury from that air.

(Mid-page:)

That is, to remove with instruments this water, as from a swamp, well, or sea, and to use this water, removed from its descent, to do what other water does to mills. Either fools or truly unnatural men... you will.

(Towards the bottom:)

Whoever denies the reason for things publishes his ignorance.

If it were possible to make a bombard, let the world be its ball, and just as a bombard throws a ball of one arm three miles, so one can measure its course as 9,000 arm lengths, that is, 9,000 ball. We can therefore say that such a bombard would throw our world nine thousand times the size of the diameter of that world away from itself. Seven thousand miles per world would be good, that would be 63 thousand miles.

(At the bottom of the page:)

If you do not want to make them of bronze, so that they are not taken, know that all the good things of Rome were plundered from cities and lands conquered by the Romans. And it was not enough to be of miraculous weights, such as the needle and two horses. And if you have it made so clumsy that it cannot be carried away, it will be made into walls and mortar. Do as you please, for everything has its own demise. And if I tell you that you do not want to do anything that gives more honor to the craftsman than to the one who spends, know that most things give more honor to their maker than to the payer.

If the ball is drawn upward, it will travel further along that line than along any other line of motion. This happens for two reasons. The first is that the fire that moves the ball moves upward more easily than along any other line, and upward it follows its motion more evenly. The second reason is that if you draw it sideways, you encounter the same quality and resistance of air. The fire that moved the ball turns toward the sky and ceases to propel the ball. And if you draw it upward, the higher the air rises, the thinner it is, and the thinner it is, the less resistance it provides. Therefore, this ball moves upward, due to the increase in the fire that is directed upward and accompanies this motion, and due to the increase in the air, which the higher it rises, the thinner it becomes and the less resistant it becomes, this ball will make a greater lateral course than by any other path.

The water falling on the wheels of mills produces as much force in the movement of that wheel as the simple weight of the water itself. This is said only to make you understand that it is not the impact but the weight that is used in this action, since you will find only the impact at the first arrival of the water on the wheel and not otherwise. This is clearly demonstrated by the penultimate section on motion and resistance, where the action of percussion is said to be performed in indivisible time, since it is performed on the surface of its agents. And since the surface is indivisible, that part of the motion and time that creates the sound of percussion can also be said to be indivisible. And if you wanted to argue in this case that the sound of such a percussion is a continuous action, which is a continuous percussion, because when water falls on something it always makes a noise, here the water fallen through a pipe is alleged to perform its function of pushing the place where it rests, and not to make any noise. And if it were to fall from a reed of a constant thickness, as it does from that reed, after the first blow upon the object, it would not make any further noise. But when the water is surrounded by air in its descent, it causes various tortures within itself, and various thicknesses due to its intersections, because it often changes from the surface to the center. And when it reaches such humps upon the object, all the water that is supported upon that hump makes a sound above the place where these humps strike.

Of water.

It is asked why the movement of water under water does not produce the same sound that air does under air when it is driven by a whistle or a pipe, or similar instruments. That is, if you put a whistle in the mouth of a small canister filled with air, the whistle will sound with the air that passes through it. And if you fill this canister with water, and push it completely under water, together with the pipe, the canister must be joined to its mouth, as you did before with the air, and the pipe must be forcibly closed, so that the driven water passes with force through the pipe, as the air did before.

Here, in this proposition, it was meant to be said that if a ball of fresh earth is dropped on another similar one, the position of each of them, when struck together, will be equally depressed. So, the two balls, when they come into contact, will form two equal spheres, perfectly flat, being, as said, of equal materials.

But if this ball falls on a large mass of earth, even if the materials are equal, the agent will be embedded in that mass and will be damaged less than the patient, and their contacts will not remain flat.

And if the larger piece falls on the smaller one, the smaller one will not be damaged, except on the side where it lands. And the other side will be embedded in the mass it strikes, and their contact will be curved.

If you make a pile of small balls of equal size and material, and on the upper side, on the first ball, you will apply such a weight that it presses firmly against the others, which will support it. Then let them dry, and then lift them, and see which balls are those that have been damaged after the first. And consider the manner of this damage, and in what part of it, and note the location where each one is found. And thus you will be able to make a general rule of the nature of the weight; in what way it presses the place that supports it, and how its thrust decreases, and along what lines it does less harm, and where more. Again, if you make slabs of earth, of equal thickness, and place one perpendicularly on top of the other, a cubit high, and place a weight in the middle, you will be able to clearly see the manner of their subsidence, how it decreases from step to step, and how it widens from the feet.

On the percussion of dense bodies.

It seems that percussion, being made in an indivisible time, cannot pass into the space or body that receives it without divisible time. For it is said to be indivisible when it is created on the surface of bodies, that is, in their contact. But we call it divisible when such a power penetrates through the body that receives it, because it is gradually distinguished throughout all the parts of that body. And the more it is removed from its origin, the more it diminishes, because it is divided into more parts. And certainly the part is smaller than its whole. And the more parts there are, the more they are removed from the primary power. Thus, the longer and thicker the bodies that receive it, the less damage they will cause to the place that supports them when they are struck by the blow. And, conversely, the smaller the bodies struck. And for this reason, if you strike with the same hammer two nails of different sizes and of equal sharpness and contact on the wood where they are to be struck, certainly the nail that is of smaller shape will drive much deeper than the larger nail. But if said smaller nail is pointed at the front of the hammer with a little bit of a band, and the blow is struck with the point of that nail on said wood, that nail will have a marvelous penetration. So in this respect, short poles are better than long ones. It is true that they suffer from another defect, namely that they wear out the place where they exert force together with themselves all the more, so that the wear and tear of the short pole will be in a greater proportion to the wear and tear of the long one, as will be the proportion between the lengths of their contacts. I have found that all poles, of any metal, which are longer than their supports, or are of equal length, wear away in such a way that the part of their length closest to the middle becomes thinner, and conversely, the part furthest from this middle becomes thicker, so that where a pole was composed of straight lines, it now has curved lines. And the reason for this is that these poles are always aided in the friction of their contacts, when they are turned around, with some grease or other liquid. And if it is water, as happens at the poles of mill wheels, this water always beats and drips onto that pole, and the minute filings that these poles make as they wear away are deposited in the wood that supports it, and become fixed and act as a file or emery, and are removed from that pole. And because of the lines found in the wood, whether rarer or denser, harder or softer, this filings are deposited more in one than in the other. Hence this pole also wears away at the linings, so that it often appears that they are full of minute linings that surround it like various frames. But where the water is closest to the end of the wood that supports the pole, it more easily escapes from under the pole and carries away the filings with it. Therefore, in the middle, it cannot carry them away in this way, because it is further from its ends, it stops more, and the more it stops, the more it wears away the pole. This same thing also happens with iron poles that are supported by other iron or other metal. These are greased with olive oil or pork marrow grease. And since these filings cannot stay or support the weight that the pole gives them, they also flee towards the end of the pole, and it stops, already swollen by the mixture it has made with the part of the worn pole, in a place where the pole no longer touches it and no longer gives it weight, so it no longer pushes it. And for this reason there is no wear in these poles, but rather simple iron is placed oppositely to the middle of their lengths. And iron with iron wears out more than iron with grease thickened by polishing the poles.

This is the method some masters use to divide wheels and find their teeth.

If the wheel is pulled by its carriage, and you want to find out how thick you should make the carriage to cut 62 teeth, take the sixth tooth measurement of three teeth at their starting point, and this measurement will be the diameter of the said carriage.

But if the carriage is pulled by the wheel, then the sixth tooth must be narrowed by half a tooth, and this sixth tooth opening will be the diameter of that carriage, and this measurement will serve for the six-tooth carriage.

Also, if the wheel has an eight-tooth carriage, you will do the same as above, increasing or decreasing one half tooth. And you will do the same on every wheel where these two aforementioned carriages are used. And this increase or decrease of said half tooth occurs because the pulling tooth approaches one side of the wheel being pulled and moves away from the other side. And if the wheel being pulled then drives the other, these teeth will have the opposite effect. In toothed rods, that is, straight teeth, such as the scales of jacks, none of the aforementioned rules are observed; indeed, the divisions are always made in the teeth of the scale like those of the teeth of its carriage. And this is done only because its motions are in every direction.

The teeth, when whipped, do not diminish the rule of their function, since the wheels have to move in only one direction. But they would then not be useful for turning in the other direction. Of teeth and toothed wheels and of the pinion.

The moving tooth always follows the tooth that is broken, from the beginning of contact to the end. But if they collide, tip to tip, before they have reached the centers of their wheels, then the motion of that wheel will have no effect. Likewise, if these teeth collide, tip to tip, at the beginning of their contact, the motion will immediately cease and will be unable to have any effect. When the teeth of the wheels are smaller, and the ends of the hollows are further from the poles of their wheels, their contact will last a short time and be good. And if these teeth are large, they will be deeper than small ones, and their every effect will be contrary to small ones; it is true that they are more durable. On clock counterweights.

If a clock counterweight lowers 100 arm lengths and unwinds or draws with it 100 arm lengths of string, and you want these 100 arm lengths of string to be unwound with the motion of one arm, caused by its counterweight, you must increase its weight by the same amount as its motion, and it will cause a force and a motion in the clock equal to the previous one.

This increase in weight of the counterweight of the clock as much as its motion is lacking is understood. If previously with a single pound the counterweight descended 100 arms and drew with it 100 arms of rope, if you want the counterweight to descend no more than one arm, you know that it is lacking to produce the same motion as before. It is lacking 99 arms. Therefore, increase the counterweight by 99 pounds and you will have the same motion, weight, and force in the clock that you had before.

You see what a marvelous thing it is to consider how this nature operates in all its things and with what laws it has defined the effects of all causes, which it is impossible to change in the slightest degree. You see, this counterweight, which, if one pound of counterweight were to support the motion of 99 arms, requires adding 99 pounds of weight to it, if it were to perform the same function in its clock. And this happens because the instrument initially had only one line of string, and then 99 lines of that string were added to it, so that each line weighs one pound. And these lines are each shorter than the first, the more numerous they are.

You see, if the lines of the strings are initially zero and then become one arm each, since 100 are made, they must derive from the hundred arm lengths of string wound around the clock's spool.

Although this case should not be listed among the precepts of painting, I do not want to omit it because it is necessary for speculators. I say therefore that (every object of the eye is everywhere and everywhere on the surface of the aforementioned eyeball.) When the aforementioned eyeball is very bright, the eyeball, unable to tolerate it, becomes so much smaller that the similarity of that bright object to the eyeball is diminished no less in brightness than in magnitude. By this diminution, the senses can tolerate the opposite brightness.

The example of what is said above is demonstrated and will be manifest when one of the largest stars is seen through a small hole made in a paper placed near the eyeball: you will see that star greatly diminished. And this arises because the entire pupil is not used in this vision, but is used less completely, the less the star appears smaller than it did before. And this is not because this hole cuts off any part of the star seen from the eye, since through this hole passes, in addition to the quantity of the star's species, a large part of the cycle that surrounds it. A second example can also be demonstrated in another way, which helps to confirm the same conclusion, and that is: the light of a candle is placed in front of the eye, and within that candlelight, or at its outer edges, the said star is seen. Then the star will appear smaller, the smaller the pupil is, the more light it has been placed in front of it.
