Proportion is to be considered among 2323 quantities of the same kind, which quantities will be greater or lesser, or equal to one another. And of these quantities, two are unequal and can be shown to equate one to the other in two ways: that is, by referring the greater, and from this arises superposition, or the lesser to the greater, and then the second species is born, called supposition. And if you refer something equal to something equal, the third species will arise, called equiparantia, and in no other way can proportion occur.

Proportion has these various names: relation, habit, respect, mean.

Proportion is divided into two members: community and proper. A so-called cumuniter is one that uses the same term to compare two things that are not of the same genus, such as saying a mouth is sweeter than honey, or a voice is sharper than a knife. We will not speak further of this proportion, but will follow the proper proportion, which applies between things of the same genus.

Proportion properly speaking is divided into three members: arithmetric, geometric, and harmonic.

In arithmetric, or discrete quantity, one must consider and find only rational proportion. And in geometric proportion, rational and irrational proportions are indifferent. Harmonic proportion only applies to the notes of various instruments and tenses and is a mixture of continuous and discrete quantity. And we will leave this harmonic and speak of the other two.

Geometric proportion is that which compares one continuous quantity to another continuous quantity. Arithmetic proportion compares the excesses of numerical and rational quantities.

Geometric proportion is continuous and discontinuous: 1-2-2-2-4. Continuous is when the first term is to the second as the second is to the third, and so on throughout. This proceeds from the least among three terms, that is, its proportionality.

Discontinuous proportionality requires at least four terms, in which the first is to the second as the third is to the fourth, that is, 1-2-2 3-2-6, and so on to infinity.

And this discontinuous way of speaking is always understood in proportionality and not in proportion.
(from top to bottom:)

The arithmetic proportion is also divided into continuous and discontinuous. And the continuous is that which, at least, falls between three terms, such as the first to the second, as the second to the third, that is, in the excesses 1 2 3. See here the proportionality of equivalence, that is, that unity is that by which 2 exceeds 1 and 3 exceeds 2. The discontinuous arithmetic proportion is this: 1-2, 5-6, 8-9. These parts are interpolated and discontinuous. Nevertheless, their excesses are in the proportion of equivalence.

Geometric quantities commensurable with one another are those in which the same line measures both of them to one point, without any excess, as is the line of a foot, which measures to one point a line of 2 and 4 feet, and so in arithmetic, 2 measures to one point 4 and 8.

Inconmeasurable quantities are those between which there is no common measure that can equally accurately measure both, as occurs between the diameter of a square and its edge, between which no measure will ever be found that precisely measures both, as is demonstrated in the third part of the seventh part of the tenth of Euclid. Therefore, the silent roots are inconmesurable and incommunicable.

And for this reason, geometric proportion is shown to require greater abstraction and consideration than arithmetric proportion. See, it considers the rational and irrational, as has been said, and arithmetric proportion only the rational, which can be named for some number. It is entirely deprived of the other, as is demonstrated by that found between two unvoiced roots, or one unvoiced root and the other known, such as that of the diameter of a square and its cost. If the cost is 10, the diameter will be said to be the root of 200.

Equality and inequality.

Rational proportion is divided into two parts, because all quantities in the world are either equal to them, or they are unequal. If they are equal among themselves, the proportion of equality arises, and if they are unequal, the proportion of inequality arises among them.

Greater and lesser inequality.

When you make a comparison from the greater to the lesser inequality, the proportion of greater inequality will arise. And if you make a comparison from the lesser to the greater inequality, the proportion of lesser inequality will arise.

Simple and composite.

The greater inequality is divided into two members, namely, simple and composite. And the similar is understood to be of the lesser inequality, because what is or will be said of the one, also of the other.
(from top to bottom:)

Single inequality.

Single inequality is divided into 3345 members, namely, multiple, superparticular, and superpartient.

Multiple.

Single multiples arise when the larger term contains the smaller term precisely multiple times, such as dupla, tripla, quadrupla, and similar terms.

Single superparticular.

Single superparticular is when the larger term contains the smaller term once and also some part of it that is an aliquot of it, that is, multiplicative over a part properly called, namely, sexquialtera 3350 – 2; and sexquitertia 4 – 3; and sesquiquarta 5 – 4... and so on to infinity.

Single superpartient.

The superpartient simple arises when the greater term contains the lesser term only once, and in addition to this, a non-aliquot part of the lesser term. This non-aliquot part is composed of an aliquot part of the lesser term, such as 5, which contains 3 once and is left over by 2. This 2 is not an aliquot part of 3 but is composed of an aliquot part of 3, that is, 2 units.

Now we must see how many parts of the lesser term that non-aliquot part contains, that is, if it contains 2, it will be called superbipartiens, such as 5 to 3, for 3 enters into 5 once and 2/3 times.

And if that non-aliquot part were composed of three aliquot parts of the smaller number, it would be called supertripartiens, such as 8 to 5, which is one and 3/5.

And if it contains four, it would be called superquadripartiens, such as 9 to 5, which is one and 4/5, and so on to infinity.

Composite inequality.

The species of the greater composite inequality are two, namely, superparticular multiples and superpartient multiples.

Superparticular multiples.

Superparticular multiples arise when the greater term contains the smaller number more than once and, in addition to this, some aliquot part of the smaller number, as if the greater number contained the smaller number twice and, in addition to this, an aliquot part of the smaller number, which was half of the smaller number. Then the species called dupla sesquialtera arises, as from 5 to 2. And if the greater contains the lesser 2 and 1/3 times, it is called dupla sexquitertia, as356 7 to 3. And if the greater contains the lesser357 3 and 1/4 times, it is called tripla se[s]quiquarta, and so on to infinity.
(from top to bottom:)

Summary over noting.

Every larger quantity compared to a smaller one that is in rational proportion and contains multiple times and has no broken parts left over, will be called a multiple, and will be called a dupla or tripla, etc.

And if the larger contains the smaller one once, and there will be some broken parts left, and this broken part can be an aliquot or non-aliquot part of the smaller. And if it is an aliquot part, then it will be called a superparticular. And if it is not an alicundous part of the smaller but contains equal aliquot parts of the smaller, then it will be called a superparticular.

And if the greater contains the lesser more than once and some part more, that greater or lesser part is an aliquot or non-aliquot part of the lesser, being alicuta, and will be called a superparticular multiple. And if it is not an aliquot, it will be called a superpartient multiple.

And wishing to name the species of lesser inequality, where a comparison is made from the lesser to the greater, you will add the syllable called sub, and they will all be formed with this sub, just as adding sub to multiples will call them submultiples, and so on with all the above-mentioned species, which are as many of the lesser inequality as those of the greater.

The light of the eye increases and decreases slowly when seeing dark or bright things. Why does the eye, placed in a bright place, see darkness inside every dwelling, which, being inside, would then appear very bright to it?

Of birds.

If the weight of the bird is to be borne on its feet, it will exert force with those feet equal to the weight resting on them. And if that weight is not placed on the said feet, but rather on the place where the bird sits, then the legs of that bird will be left with the power of as much force as the weight that was previously supported by them. And if you were to return the weight to them, they would lack the force equal to the sum of the weight that has increased on them, so that both the first and the second method are the same. Now we will turn to the instrument, and make its mover use the force in the first degree of its power, with light and counter-light forces manageable and suitable for all its needs; Let them be prepared and swiftly moved and removed, according to the will of their mover.

Of the fury and power of birds' wings in the air.

Men will never, once they have attached the wings of birds to some swift instrument, produce the same noise or clamor that was seen to be made by the same wings when they were moved with speed by their birds.

A goat-bird is seen flying around the banks of Tesino, dropping for some distance toward the ground, and then, with such speed, bringing its wings so close that they are immediately restored to the original height from which they descended. And this motion between up and down is almost perpendicular. And it is such a vigorous movement that the beating of its wings in the air produces a noise that sounds like the voice of a kid. And it is surprising that, although it is not the size of a thrush, its voice can be heard more than a mile away. The merlin, a bird of no great size, can be seen making a very loud noise in the air when it flies with fury. And it could be said of many that they make a very loud noise when they want to pursue their prey or flee from their predator. What is said about the sound of wings on the air arises from the fact that this motion, in striking the air, is of quadrupled speed, through the 4310 joints of the wings, so that when the first moves the entire wing, the second moves its remainder with the same speed, and the third does the same with its remainder, and the fourth observes the same rule. And so, the first moving quickly, the second doubles that speed in the same time, in which time the other two follow a doubling of motion. And this is the cause of this speed, which is of such speed that the air has no time to escape from under the wings except as long as it is pushed by them. So that it comes to condense and become resistant to the wings where it is located, and which take the leap and make the bird move, as has been said above.

According to Palladius and Pliny, timber for building should be cut down to the core and left standing in the woods, on their trunks, so that their sap can drain. And this first cut should be made in the middle of the autumn. And they should be cut from the trunks in midwinter. But Vetruvius wants them to be cut at the beginning of the autumn, before the west wind, that is, the Favonian wind, begins to prevail.

The woods that thrive under water are: willow, larch, alder, oak, sessile oak, and olive. And these are the best. But they must be placed under water, or underground, so that they are green, so that they do not remain dry. And they will be better preserved if peeled and burned on the surface than in any other way.

The woods that are kept covered in the air are chestnut, beech, hornbeam, black hornbeam, lime, fir, and ash. They are also good for keys and wall chains.

The rooms on the south side should face south, and those on the north side south, because the places of regions that are hot or cold are tempered by their opposites. And the stale ones facing north should be vaulted in southern sites. The houses should be divided into two parts, one for summer and the other for winter, and all vaulted, if possible. And the winter stables should be small and face south, and those of the summer should be large and face north or north.

Walls that have to resist heat must be much thicker than those that resist cold. Because heat disintegrates the air and penetrates the pores of walls, and cold condenses and thickens the air, so that it does not spread easily through the passages and pores of walls.

Houses should not be made too high or too low, because the air on flat surfaces is thick, and in mountains it is thin. Therefore, aim for a medium height and keep warm. And if you are on a mountain, you live low down, and if you are on a plain, you live high up, that is, in the lowest or highest level of the house.

Alberese lime should be quenched as soon as it is drawn from the furnace, with a large amount of water, because even a little ignites it and makes it resemble sand and is not very tenacious.

Alberese lime should be mixed with two parts river sand and one part lime; with other limes, three parts sand and one part lime. Lime from black tuvert or other spongy stone is better for plastering and plastering walls than any other lime. Lime from large river jars is thick and sticky, and equally useful in hot and humid environments.

Flex stone, with which the ancient Romans paved their streets, makes better lime than any of the aforementioned, and there is plenty of it in the mountains of Radicofani. If a third of ancient, crushed stones or tiles are added to each mortar mixed with river or sea sand, this is an excellent mixture. Two parts of mortar and five parts of coarse, rough sand should be added to the plastering and walls of cisterns.

If the mortar is then slaked, reduced to a pile, and then well covered with sand, the longer it sits, the more perfect it becomes. The Romans had a law that it could not be used unless it had been covered for three years. And in our day, in Rome, on Via di Papa, 20 feet underground, a mountain of mortar was found that had been covered for hundreds of years. Nevertheless, it was perfectly perfect.

Sand is worthless unless it is rough and dry, so that when pressed together by hand, it does not stick together in any part, and shaking the cloth where it was placed does not leave any part of it stained.

Sea sand is not good for vaults because of its saltiness, which always leaks, and the vault becomes full of cracks. And if it is used for walls, it is made at various times, because the rain cleanses its saltiness.

Of the common parts of fortresses, which are 14.

The less difficult and simpler the thing that leads to the desired goal, the more powerful it should be considered. The members of fortresses are 18. The first of these is a well or cistern, located in the keep or room of the castellan, so that he can take it from others, and not others from him. And it must have passages through which he can reach the soldiers' quarters. Second, there must be a mill and grinders for the cannon powder. Third, there must be an oven, with the things necessary for baking bread. Fourth, the route of rescue must be safe and cannot be taken away without great difficulty. Fifth, that the castellan's tower be stronger and more prominent than the others, so that it can attack the rest of the fortress and not be attacked. Sixth, that if several castellans are placed in several towers in the same fortress, the relief routes should be so adapted that one castellan can neither attract nor place soldiers without the permission of the other castellan. Seventh, that the fortress should have as small a perimeter as possible, maintaining the due proportion. The eighth is that the walls of the circuit should be high in themselves, but low in place, and should be sloped to two-thirds of their height, with machicolations between the corbels. The ninth is that the towers should be attached to the walls individually, or with wings of angled walls, as high as the walls, with attacks on their flanks. The tenth is that in front of the gate there be a ravelin, made in a shape that offends and cannot be offended, and that it serve as a sufficient shield at the entrance to the fortress. The eleventh is that the ditches be wide and deep, with high embankments towards the bottom of the ditch. And the openings should be smooth and oblique, so that the soldiers cannot use them as a shield against the fortress. The twelfth is that the entrances be reversed, with the paths covered. The thirteenth is that the ditches be nearby. The fourteenth is that the family dwellings be poorly built within the circuit, in a place that can easily be destroyed by the main tower. The fifteenth is that the towers be round, because they resist more and absorb every shock less, and the walls should be angular and never round, because the attacks of the towers on the sides of the walls are little exposed, due to their curvature. Therefore, if one tower wanted to defend the other, it would be necessary to make them thick, with great expense and little utility. The sixteenth is that the corners

The last is that the foundations should be built on a stable and firm site. The stability of a foundation is determined by placing a vessel full of water on it. Once it is firmly in place, the ground is struck on its side. If the spot is not stable under the impact, the blow will reverberate upward, causing the water to tremble and make it jump out of the vessel. If the water does not spill, the ground is stable and free of concavities.

The aforementioned trembling of the struck foundation arises because such foundations often expose a seam of tuff or stone about a foot thick, and beneath that lies the weak and feeble soil. Due to the weight of the walls built on top of it, this seam breaks, and with it the buildings built on top.

Therefore, you will build on solid rock, or tuff, or on tenacious and solid earth. If the rock is crumbling, make sure that the lines of its steps are not oblique. And if they are oblique, they must not be cut for a distance of a thousand cubits near your foundation, by some stone quarry or other mountain breach.

But if you don't find solid ground, use piles and then fill them with clay and mortar, and then continue your wall on top of them. These should first be well connected at their ends so that the excess weight does not open them and spread them laterally at their extremities.

The wood used to brace the corners of the walls must be burnt a little on their surfaces, and then covered with black pitch, so that the corrosive humidity of the lime does not consume them.

Having completed the common parts, we will descend to the particular ones, of which there are seven.

There are seven particular parts of fortresses. First, let us discuss what is required from the nature of the ditches. Second, how the ravelins should be formed. Third, the parts suitable for the towers outside the walls. Fourth, the towers, or defenses built in the ditches, so that artillery cannot damage them. Fifth, the quality of the walls. Sixth, the drawbridges and passageways. Seventh, the main towers of the castellans.

First: the ditches are better the wider and deeper they are. But their depth is from 40 to 50 feet, and their width from 80 to 100 feet. The highest point of the ditch's embankment must not end above the ditch, so that the earth, falling, does not fill the ditch. And then it follows that as it is moved further away, it rises higher and covers more of the walls for its defenders. This great height must not exceed eighteen or even twenty feet.

Away from the embankment, a road four to five arm lengths wide should also be built within the highest point of the embankment, which should be lower than the top of the embankment by up to three and a half arm lengths, so that men can move around the ditch without being harmed by enemies. Again at the top of the embankment, let a gorge be made, with a channel underneath, so that no one can digress into the ditch without perceiving it, as shown in a. And let the gorge be 6 to 8 feet high. Fourthly, in the middle of the ditch, let a wall be built, 5 feet thick and 25 feet high. And let the top be made pointed, with a gorge on either side, as shown in b. Furthermore, let us build a road between the said wall and the fortress wall, along which one can reach the defense of the ditch and draw back the enemies fallen there, through the crossbows of the wall built in the middle of the ditch. These enemies cannot climb up, nor descend from the middle wall, nor return to where they fall, because of the chamfer and the ravines beneath them.

The sixth species is called basalisk, and is 22 to 25 feet long; its stone is made of iron, weighing approximately 20 pounds. The seventh is the blowpipe, which is 8 to 10 feet long; the lead ball is 2 to 3 pounds. The eighth is the spingarda, 8 feet long; the stone ball is 10 to 15 pounds. The ninth is the arcobuso, 3 to 4 feet long; the lead ball is 6 ounces. The tenth and last is the scoppietto, 2 to 3 feet long; the lead ball, 4 drachmas to 6. In all the aforementioned species, conditions are sought, and the first is that the alloy of their material does not exceed 3, or even 4, parts of tin to 100 parts of fine copper. The second is that the material is well condensed. Third, that the hollowness of their pipes, or trumpets, is of uniform width. Fourth, that the hole through which they are fired is small, and as close to the end of the hollowness of the tail as possible. The fifth, and last, is that the hollowness of these tails is uniformly narrowed towards its base, that is, that it is narrower at the bottom than at the mouth.

Make sure you can remove all the beams that span the frame from the hood, so you can better pile the earth that underlies the shape of the horse.

cast medals.

Take some powdered sand, not too fine, and moisten the ricotta you have with your salt water or salted brandy or turpentine, which will then retain its viscous moisture. Once you have done this, dust your molds, both pressed and flattened, with very fine ash, which will be made either of iron flakes, or burnt bone, or burnt walnut leaves, or cow dung, or calcined tin, or palpyre, or silkworm, or turmeric smoke, or vitrified and powdered valence earth, or anything subtle, so long as it does not soil the medal and that, in addition to being very subtle and almost impalpable, it is placed very thinly on the sandy and arid earth. And this is done so that the wind that is enclosed between the metal and the mold can pass through this veil of fine earth and then exhale among the coarse sand. It is present on your medal up to half its thickness. Then, dust a thin layer of earth over the medal, if the medal is a little damp, so that the thin earth will settle on it. Once this is done, remove the sand and place the second mold over the medal and finish. Then heat the mold and cast your orichalcum or copper with tin, and it's perfect.

To cast medals.

Take some scagliola plaster and coat your medal with liquid. Then immediately cover with the other plaster, which will be composed of 12 parts watch gravel and one part plaster. And make everything liquid, cast, and then recast. And then do the same on the opposite side of the medal, but grease it first so that the plaster doesn't stick to the plaster.
(from top to bottom:)

Of the joints.

The joints covered by the sheet should be caulked on the sides with a small square moistened with brandy, then with plaster and hemp.

Of the form: to be left lying down or upside down.

If it is left lying down when the bronze has been filled up to the legs, the bronze poured to fill the rump will not be able to lift it, because the legs, being thicker for their filling, will have to be very careful about the rise of the back, because the legs are firm. The bronze of the back will have to serve to fill the large weight of the legs, and for this reason I think it is useful to cast it upside down.

Of casting it upside down.

In this way, there is a risk that the weight of the bronze filling the legs will not pick up the pieces from underneath the horse's body and lift them upward.

How to unstop the furnace when any piece of bronze is obstructing the exit.

You will perform this task with wood or chestnut sticks, because if you were to make it with iron, it would be dangerous for the bronze to stick to the iron.

The place where the mold is to be reheated.

Because the mold will be of a marvelous weight, reheat it in the pit.
(from top to bottom:)

When the metal-alloying furnace has performed well, you place the appropriate number of furnaces in the same mold, and in each furnace, let the metal be alloyed. Do this primarily to shorten the alloying time, which is much quicker with five or six furnaces at a time than one at a time. The other is that if I always alloyed with a single furnace, it would become frustrated and dangerous in the final casting. Furnaces are also better for the second and third casting than for the first, so since all furnaces are used for casting several times, they will ultimately provide a more useful and safer test, that is, for the horse casting.

To stop the joints of the mold.

Once the mold is annealed and you want to rejoin it, grease the joints with a paste made with turpentine, linseed oil, or egg white mixed with abrasive dust. Once you have covered the joints, press the mold firmly with your iron cones.

To place the irons on the annealed side of the mold, turn back.

Take as much clay as you want the thickness of your mold to be, that is, 1/3 of a braccio, and anneal it and see how far it goes in. And where you see the topping protects itself from the fire, at that distance you can place your irons in the mold. And know that those irons that are under the annealed clay are more harmful than useful, so if they want to be between the earth and the topping.

On soldering the joints with holes.

So that the bronze entering through the joints doesn't disturb the plaster with which I want to fill the joints of the mold with holes, I decided to make a dovetailed cavity in the area of ​​the holes of that joint, three fingers deep and wide, and fill it with fresh plaster and then close the holes with clay.

On the last clays of the mold.

You will make from the third of the holes of the mold, or the first fourth, with clay mixed with boar hair. When you are at the last, take boar hair and hemp and clay with some glue, and give each piece of clay a piece of hemp, sometimes straight and sometimes crosswise, and then add the clays and other irons.

Of the last, that it will not fall off the horse when it is made.

First, make it all the thickness that extends from the irons inward. And before you put the irons in, you will cut it into as many pieces as you like and prop up the parts that will fall. But before you begin the last, mark the shape and the direction of the cuts with nails, and leave as many nails as you want the last to be thick when it is cut.
(from top to bottom:)

On casting.

When casting, each man should hold his furnace alight with a red-hot bronze spoon. And at the same time, unplug it and put your hand on the thin bronze spoon, so that no piece of unmelted bronze gets stuck in the place where the bronze comes from. And make sure you have four red-hot bronze spoons for the necessary number, so that if one breaks, there will be others ready.

On soaking the mold.

As soon as you have annealed the mold, while still hot, soak it with Greek pitch, or linseed oil, or turpentine, or tallow; but do everything, test first and choose the best.

To heat the mold while casting.

If you apply a coat of Greek pitch to the entire mold, mixed with brandy or turpentine, the flame that rises above the firm bronze will always heat the mold, but they are tested.

Of the earth that touches the mold from outside.

This should be dry earth from the castellaccio, pulverized, moistened with vinegar, or linseed oil, and then well-crushed, and this should be two fingers thick.
(from top to bottom:)

On distributing the bronze for the mold.

Determine the quantity of bronze each part of the mold should contain. And you will give that much bronze to the furnace that will correspond there. And you will know this by weighing the earth in the place where the furnace will correspond with its quantity. And this is done so that the furnace of the back legs, even though it has these legs, does not have its bronze touching the head, which would not be possible.

On the wood.

Test by attaching which wood is best: willow, alder, or fir.

On protecting the furnace from the cold.

Keep thin, very dry fir wood ready, and add this when the bronze is not very hot when casting.

Of lifting the head from the horse.

You can take the cinder alone. Also cinder and slag and heat it after the second coat of earth, so that the slag comes out of the cinder, so that the cinder does not remain tenacious and leaving it will have an effect. Also cinder and forge dust. And plain cinder is good, but I wanted to first apply two coats of earth on it and force the fire so that the diluted cinder penetrates between the two earths that place it in the middle, and leaves the space where it leaves empty, but test it first.
(from top to bottom:)

Construction of the inside of the mold.

Mix river sand, ash, pounded brick, egg whites, and vinegar with your clay. Test it first.

To handle the mold.

For this part, you will need to make the model of the small mold, and for that, make a small space, with its small holes, so you can see how to arrange the pieces of the mold.

The mouths for throwing hay.

The mouths for throwing hay, made of wire or rods, above the horse before starting the mold.

On making simple and quick throws.

These hay, made in a box of river sand, moistened with vinegar.

On the horse's door.

The horse's door will be thrown at the same time as the horse.

Of the thickness of the bronze.

You will make this out of bowl clay, except for the legs, which will be of rough clay.

Of the time of attaching.

When attaching, note how many hours are per hundred.

Of the quantity of wood.

Note how many woods are per mile when attaching.

If the mold cracks during the annealing.

Then make sure that the part of the mold that needs to be annealed is composed of clay that slightly diminishes during the annealing. This will be done with crushed square, ash, and coarse earth from Santa Maria della Rovera. You could also add river sand.

Regarding the peeling of the cape from the horse.

This first peeling of the cape from the horse will be done equally, for every 2 or 3 arm lengths of the joint of the mold, because if the legs are fixed at the feet and the peeling begins from above, it would have to make a sex, and the part under the body and further inside the foot, that is, the ankle, would have to rise and would exert pressure on the body and would break. The method of opening the joints will be with cones, light or screw.

Regarding filling the concrete and its nature.

The concrete should be filled with quarry dust, or ash, or plaster, or better still, lime powder, moistened slightly with linseed oil, so that the pile remains with the pressed earth. Furthermore, you will need to fill the concrete well inside and out, for I remind you that any little moisture would be a cause of serious error.

To fill the earth under the beams, the framework of the roof.

To pile the earth between the beams and under the mould, you will dig the trench as deep as a man can sit under it, having first built three walls, one in the middle and two at the ends covered with planks, and then oil and lime to prevent moisture. Then build a solid wall all around, and lay the wall 2/3 thick, and pile the earth across the mould.

First, make a piece of clay to use as a mold. Once annealed, coat it with pitch or oil. Then, let it sit underground for three days. Then, pour in your bronze. Again, test with plaster, and coat it as I said above.

To seal the joints of the cap.

Before you join the parts of the cap together for the last time, grease the edges of the joint with soft soap mixed with sifted ash, or ash dust, to seal it well and replace the clay that has become sawdust. And make it soft, like trimming earth, and then tighten it.

Of molten bronze.

When bronze is molten and boils, it fights with its opposite, and when it stops, it has won, similar to oil, which, boiling in a pan, finally cries out as it expels all the moisture.

Where it melts better than in the furnace.

You will find it melts better at the mouths where the flames come from than in any other part of the furnace.

When tin must be added to copper to make its alloy.

When you see that the copper is brought to a boil, add its tin and you will immediately see it melt together.

Of heating the bottom of the furnace.

Remember that when baking, the largest pieces should be placed at the bottom, on top of some wood, so that the fire heats the bottom. And since the bottom is made of thin pieces of bronze, they won't melt on the bottom, which isn't very hot.

On the price of casting.

The canopies and bonbardes are of little workmanship because they are made on the lathe, and once they come off the lathe, their mastery and craftsmanship are perfect. The shapes of the figures are of great workmanship, because the figure requires great care and ingenuity in its maker. Furthermore, the shape, with various humps, is of great workmanship and dangerous to cast due to the various paths and lengths created by the bronze, which does not occur in the canopies and bonbardes. After this, the cleaning, beating, filing, scraping, and polishing must be done with great diligence, because they are things performed on the surface of the work, which surface contains within itself the quality and quality of the work.

And moving along a transverse and flat path, the motion would be slow, and if it were slow, it could cool and block the passage of the other one that comes. Of the casting channel.

Once you have finished the bulk of your mold, you will also make the shape of the channel from which the bronze entering the mold will exit. And make sure that this channel is completely finished and reinforced with iron, so that it can be separated from the mold, handled, annealed, and completely finished. And make this channel separate from the mold so that it can be annealed well, because the time it takes to bury the mold and melt it would be short for such a long manufacturing and annealing process. And even if it were not annealed, the bronze could cool inside it, as has been seen on other occasions.

Of the bronze falling into its mold.

If by experience you find that all the bronze that is touched crosswise, pouring from different places, rises at the same level, you will make sure that each furnace has the same seal and the same output at the same time, except those at the base which are previously distolated, and this will be useful.
(from top to bottom:)

About baking the mold between the ovens.

I see no other way than to lower the ground so that the ovens, with their height, go under the earth, and then fill and fill between the ovens. And on this level, handle and bake your mold, and in the meantime your ovens will be placed in their stable places. And when the mold is ready, lower it between the earth below and into its place, otherwise you would not be able to handle it due to the low ceiling. And I take this as the last and best solution, making beams above the ovens, covered with earth so they do not get damaged.

About calculating the weight of the mold, to determine with what force it should be handled.

When you make the cap, use the scales and weigh the earth that goes on each piece of the mold. That is, if you are going to give a foundation to the shape of the neck and head, first weigh the earth you have prepared for that foundation. And once this foundation is filled, weigh the remaining earth that is left in the bowl, and keep a good record of this in a book. And if you do this, your drafts and handling will be well foreseen and ordered. And you will have the advantage of the water that goes up in smoke.

Regarding unstopping the furnace.

When unstopping, remember that the mouth of the mold is larger than that of the furnace, because at the mouth of the mold the bronze expands much more than when it comes out of the furnace.
(from top to bottom:)

What shape should be given to the ricotta.

When it is hardened and a mould has been made, take some cow dung and burn it; this ash is perfect for shaping it.

On the pieces of the mould.

If you shape each round part of any limb into three pieces, you will separate it from the clay much more easily than if you made it yourself into two pieces.

On handling in narrow furnaces.

When you are hardening, try to make a furnace on a beam so that you can handle it and shape it to your purposes.

On the distribution of the bronze for the limbs.

I remind you that if you throw the horse upside down, that you weigh the belt or earth that goes from the back to the top of the head, and that you place cannon powder near the place where the neck joins the back, so that when the melted bronze has almost filled the neck, the flame of this powder will demonstrate it. And once this demonstration has been made, immediately have the other furnaces moved. And this is done so that the falling bronze stops where it falls and does not have a path to run crosswise into the places lower than its impact. And make sure that the furnaces in front of the neck are filled, so that they can also fill the entire front part, because the bronze in the other furnaces would be cold before you had helped them.
(from top to bottom:)

Test the material of the mold.

You will see if the fresh plaster, softened with vinegar, or wine, or brandy, or lye, holds up to the casting, and do what you can [test] this because if it were possible to avoid the reheating of the mold, it would be useful, because it would not burn the trimming or other connections.

Proof and conclusion: that the horse does not throw itself into the water. If the horse threw itself into the water, its massive legs would hold the molten bronze much more than the mouths that face it. It would happen that the mouths would already be congealed and would have sunk, while the legs would still be in the water and, while congealing, would want to reduce their proper suction, they would have no one to fill them and restore the bronze cast. And the legs would remain imperfect, with a part missing along their entire length.

On applying the ash.

When you have applied two coats of ash and want to begin the coat, rub your hand lightly over the dry ash in the usual way, so that the coat does not obscure the brushstrokes of the ash.

On holding the bowls.

Each bowl you apply to the horse's body will have its own amount of bronze. And so much more do those who fill the body and legs. And so much more does the one who fills the neck, head, chest, and legs, and this happens when throwing with the feet up.

Of the mass.

Remember to leave a vent in the core through which the trapped air or humidity can escape, so that once the bronze has surrounded the core, the humidity, smoking and multiplying, does not pass through the bronze, causing it to boil and explode.

Of the melting.

Remember when the furnaces are made, to keep their bottoms very hot for 6 or 8 days, so that the bronze does not cool. And in addition, do not raise the metal in it too much.

Of the shape of the furnace.

Divide the bottom into two parts, that is, its diameter. The middle of this diameter will be the greatest height from the middle of the vault to the middle of the bottom. And in addition to this, you will draw the angles that the vault makes where it joins its bottom, because in that place the flame is not used and it is somewhat cold, and the bronze is thick there from the beginning to the freezing point and not in the middle. What should be added to the bronze when it begins to soak in the furnace?

When the bronze begins to soak, sprinkle common salt on top of it.

When one piece doesn't melt.

When a large piece is the last to melt, move it from its place because the cold bottom won't let it melt with the other.

Always make sure that the tongues of fire that come out of the furnace's chimneys are the same height. And besides this, it's better to fire in one place rather than in two, because one mixes up with the other.

When casting.

If you throw clay from a vessel onto the bronze as it comes out of the furnace and is about to enter the mold, a steady throw of the clay on top will be useful and will keep the metal liquid.

What should be thrown directly onto the metal as it falls into the mold?

You want to throw either silk or clay directly onto the bronze as it enters the mold.

What should be added to the clay?

From fine clay, with the same amount of liquid clay, and when the first is over, add the second, then let it dry.
(from top to bottom:)

How much bronze is needed per pound of dry earth? 100 pounds of metal goes on 16 pounds of dry earth.

How much bronze is needed per pound of dry earth? 100 pounds of metal goes on 20 pounds of well-soaked earth, and although the earth receives 4 pounds of water, the water nonetheless only occupies the porosity of the earth. And when this body of earth is removed, its size is not diminished; on the contrary, the porosity that was occupied by the water, when the water is removed, fills with air.

How much metal is needed per ounce of wax? One ounce of wax, in large objects, yields one pound of metal.

How much metal is needed per ounce of plaster? Two ounces of plaster yields one pound of metal.

How much bronze is needed per ounce of hard wood? For each ounce of hard wood, such as walnut and similar, you need one pound of metal.

To prepare the salt to be used in the molds.

Take the salt and cook it in a furnace, then dissolve it in clear water and use it to soften your earth, which should be sandy, especially the first, second, and third layers. And add it in such a way that there is as much trimming as there is earth.
(from top to bottom:)

How alkaline salt melts.

And how wood for melting must be dry and not rotten and crushed so as not to produce smoke. Willow is also good.

Perspective is demonstrative reason, by which experience confirms that all things send their images to the eye along pyramidal lines. By pyramidal lines, I mean those that start from the superficial edges of bodies and lead through distant convergence to a single point, which point, in this case, I shall demonstrate to be in the eye, the universal judge of all bodies.

I shall call the point that which cannot be divided into any parts.  Therefore, since this point located in the vision is indivisible, no1 body is seen by the eye unless it is greater than this point.  Being thus,2 the lines that come from the body to the point must necessarily be3 pyramidal; and if anyone wanted to prove that the visual virtue did not consist in this point4 and, indeed, that it were not5 that black point you see in the middle of the pupil, to these one could respond that6 a small thing such as a grain of millet or panic-seed, or another similar thing, could never diminish over any distance, nor could something greater than this point ever be seen entirely, as appears in the proof below.7

9) When an object comes very close to the eye, there is a point at which the extreme edges of the object cannot converge into the eye, thus, the less of it is seen.  The more the object passes away from this point (“the more it passes it”), the more the true size of the object is seen.  A flat piece of paper would be a planar object exemplifying this proposition.
No object that is farther away1 can be so much lower than a nearer object,2 with the eye being positioned above, that the farther object will not appear3 to it to be higher.

And that farther object can never be so much higher than the nearer object, with the eye being positioned below, that the farther object will not appear to be below the nearer object.

If the eye looks at a farther square through the center4 of a smaller, closer one, it will appear to it that the farther, larger one is surrounded by the smaller one.

Written near the center of the folio, quite close to the subsequent line of text, the second heading is separated from the line following it by a faint stroke of the pen.

Proposition.

The objects farther away are never so large that the smaller, nearer ones do not cover them over or surround them.

Definition.

This proposition5 is proven by experience, since if you look through a small aperture, there is nothing so large6 that you cannot view7 it through the hole; and the thing seen will appear to be surrounded and bounded by the extreme sides of this opening. And if you plug it up, that small plug will be what blocks8 the view of the large thing.

Here a certain rule is made, for designating names for angles according to their variety, because in the ancient writings,4 only two names are found for angles other than the right angle, namely, the "acute" and the "obtuse" angles.  But they didn't set the degrees, as the musicians did for human voices.  So because of this, as I see it necessary to give names that are different, corresponding to the diversity of the angles that are greater or smaller than a right angle, I have designated, above here, degrees for the acute and the obtuse angles.  From a to d6 will be all the lines arising from the obtuse angles positioned at point b, and likewise at b will be all the acute angles arising from the circle between d and c. On the cold.

I say that the cold arises from two causes: the first is from air5 that has no heat and the second is from the movement of air. Air, of itself, is cold and dry,6 and devoid of any material or vapor, and is converted readily7 into — or rather, it infuses within itself8 — the nature and likeness of those things that touch it and that it has as objects.9 When something touches it — for example, something odoriferous, such as musk, or sulfur, or another potent odor — it immediately becomes infused with this. Again, when a luminous body is placed within it, all the surrounding air becomes illuminated. Now to return to the cold, I say, just as the many rays of a concave mirror converging to one point make an extreme heat, so do many bellows blowing on the same point make an extreme cold.

No lifeless thing can push or pull5 without accompanying the thing being pushed, and what pushes cannot be other than force or weight.  If it is weight that pushes or pulls, it makes this motion in the thing only because it desires stability, and when it has stability, nothing displaced by its falling movement will ever be sufficient to return it6 to its previous height. Therefore the motion is stopped.

And if what moves the other thing is force, this force, as well, accompanies the thing displaced by it; and as much as it moves it, so much does it, itself, become consumed; once it has been consumed, nothing displaced by it will be capable of causing it again.  Therefore, nothing being moved can have a long operation, because if the causes do not exist, then the effects do not exist.

An object of any sort on a smooth7 and perfect plane, and whose pivot is not located between parts of equal weight, will never come to a stop. The example is seen in those who slip8 on the ice, who never stop unless their parts return to be equidistant about their center.

On the way one deceives oneself in the judging of limbs.

The painter who has ungainly hands will make similar hands in his works; and that same effect will intervene in any limb, if this is not prevented by a long study. Therefore, painter, look well at the part you have that is ugliest in your person and make good defense against that with your study; since if you are beastly, your figures will appear the same,4 and without skill;5 and similarly, every part you have in yourself6 that is good or unfortunate7 will be shown, in part, in your figures.

On the blow.

If ten8 blows of one pound per blow9 fall on top of a spot from a height of one arm, will they drive in a nail of one arm as much as would a united weight of ten pounds? This shows that they will not, since if you tried to drive in a nail using the weight of another similar nail, this would be impossible, because if you struck ten thousand such blows on top of this, they would all amount to nothing. And if you took twenty such weights, that would give a blow of the right proportion to the nail you want to drive in.

On the voice.

Do many small voices, joined together, make a noise like a large voice? I say10 not, since if you took the voices of ten thousand flies, joined together, they would not be heard from as far a distance as would the voice of a man; and if a man's voice were divided into ten thousand parts, none of these parts would be equal to the magnitude of the voice of a fly.

Experiment.

If you want to prove how much faster a one-ounce weight falls than a two-ounce weight falling from the same height, proceed as follows: Take two pieces of cork of the same width and of duplicate length, that is, the one that weighs two ounces is twice as long as the other, and have someone drop them from the top of a bell tower at the same time, and keep your eye on the smaller one that remains behind, noting with your eye the markings or stones along the wall where it passes. And when you hear the two-ounce one hit the ground,2 note what stone of the bell tower the one-ounce weight has reached, and then measure how far the ounce had traveled when the two ounces hit the ground.

* A movement made through the air is as much swifter than5 one made in the water, even though6 both are caused by equal forces, as air is thinner than water. And you can prove this with a sword.

* Where a weight has much contact with the ground, there is much resistance.7 You can see this by experience, with a large rope extended over the ground, which, when grasped by one of the ends, will resist the force of the motor.8 And if it is reduced down to a ball, it will be moved9 with a small force.

What is force?

I say that force is a spiritual virtue, an invisible power, which, by accidental, external violence, is caused by motion and placed and infused into bodies, which are retracted and bent from their natural use, giving them an active life of marvelous power. It forces all created things to change shape and location. It rushes furiously toward its desired death and varies according to causes. Slowness makes it great, and swiftness makes it weak. It is born through violence and dies through freedom. And the greater it is, the faster it is consumed. It furiously drives away whatever opposes its destruction. It desires to overcome its opposition, to kill its cause, and in conquering, it kills itself. It becomes more powerful where it encounters greater opposition. Everything willingly flees its death, being forced, it forces everything else. Nothing moves without it. The body where it is born grows neither in weight nor in shape. No motion produced by it will be lasting. It increases with fatigue and diminishes with rest. The body where it is constrained is free, and often generates new force through motion.

Force is caused by motion and infused into weight, and similarly the impact is caused by motion and infused into weight.

Force is the cause of motion, and motion is the cause of force, and motion infuses force and the impact into the weight through the object.

Force, in some effect, when it is dissolved, transfers itself to the body that flees before it, and through motion generates the most effective impact, and afterward causes ruin, as is seen in the motion of the bullet that is driven by the force of the bombard.

Force is exerted only in three functions, each containing an infinite number of forces: these three functions are to pull, to push, and to stop. And this force can arise in two different ways. The first is the sudden growth of a rare body in a dense one, like the multiplication of fire in a bombard, which, not finding itself in a vacuum to contain its growth, rushes with fury to a wider space, driving away every obstacle that opposes its desire. And the same thing happens with the flow of water and wind, which drives away every obstacle that opposes it. The second is that which occurs in bent and twisted bodies due to their nature, such as a crossbow or other similar machines, which reluctantly allow themselves to be bent, and once loaded, desire to straighten themselves, and as soon as they are given freedom, they furiously drive away whatever was opposing their course.

The shock arises from the dying of motion, and motion from the dying of force.
Violence is composed of four things, that is, 1 weight, force, 2 motion, and blow. And some say that violence is composed of three passions, that is, force, motion, and blow; and the one that is the most powerful has the shortest life, that is, the blow. The second is force; the third for weakness would be motion; and, if weight were to be accepted among this number, it is weaker and longer lasting than any of those mentioned above.

** Weight is all throughout its perpendicular opposition, and it is entire at each degree3 of that.

** An oblique and free opposition will not resist the descending of a weight, indeed it will fall together with it.

Every weight desires to descend to the center by the shortest path;4 and where there is greater heaviness, there is greater desire. And something that weighs more5 falls more quickly when it is free; and an opposition that is less oblique resists it more. But weight, by nature, passes throughout its support, and thus penetrating6 from support to support, it passes through and becomes heavier7 in body after body as it nears8 its desire. Necessity draws it and abundance chases it away; and it is all throughout its perpendicular opposition, and it is entire at every degree of that. And the opposition that is most oblique will not resist its descending, but will fall together with it when it is free. In its office of pressing, the increasing of weight is the same as force.  Weight is won by force, as force is by weight. Weight, by itself, can be seen without force, yet force cannot be seen without weight. If weight has no neighbor, he seeks one with fury; and force chases it away with fury. If weight desires an unchangeable site, force willingly flees it. If weight desires stability, force is always desiring flight. Weight is, of itself, without exertion; and force is never without these.9  The more weight falls, the more it increases; and the more10 force falls, the more it diminishes. If the one is eternal, the other is mortal. Weight is natural, and force is accidental.  Weight desires stability and permanence; and force11 desires flight and its own death. Weight, force, and blow, in pressing, have similarity to one another.

On weight, force, motion, and blow.

Weight always presses on its supports and penetrates and passes naturally from the supports1 to their bases; and it is all throughout the support and all throughout the base of this support, and all throughout the support of the base, and it penetrates2 from support to support all the way to the center of the world.

Weight always presses on its support; force is lacking in the body where it originates;3 motion is weakened and consumed in its course; the blow dies as soon as it is born, leaving its causes bruised.

Weight, which operates eternally in its pressing, is of less power than the other three passions in it, that is, force, 4 motion, and blow. The second thing, with the second most permanence, is force. It is more powerful than weight, although its office is less lasting.  The third for permanence is motion, which is of greater power than force, and it is generated by this force. The fourth, 5 and the least in permanence, is the blow, which is the child of motion and the grandchild of force. And all are born from weight.

On the disposition of motion, that is, of the thing moved.

The less resistance a thing finds while moving through the air, the further it will go. And a long, acute body of pyramidal proportions will go farther than a round body2 of equal weight.

On the cause of motion.

The faster the3 cause that moves, the farther from itself it drives the thing moved; and a medium4 speed, even though it is very vigorous, will drive its weight the same distance that a weak and rapid force will drive its proportional weight.

On the disposition of the blow.

A blow made by the same weight, motion, and force:  the one making the louder report will do less harm to its object. Take the example of the sword, which, if smacked flat on top of a table, will make a great noise5 and do little damage, while one that is hit edgewise will make little noise and6 do a good deal of damage.

On the disposition of the thing struck.

Something that makes more resistance to a blow7 will be damaged by it more, since if the thing moves when it is struck, it accompanies the course of the thing that strikes, and it is not harmed in any part. Take the example of the ax: when you want to cut the very top parts8 of trees, they bend and are not harmed, but if these tops are cut on top of a stump,9 they are divided immediately. Thus, the haymaker's sickle does not cut grasses at their tops; it cuts them at their bases.

On the blow.

Beginning1 of perspective.

All things send their images to the eye by pyramids, and the nearer to the eye these are intersected, the smaller2 will the images appear than their causes.3 Thus, you will be intersecting the pyramid with the perspective screen touching the base of that pyramid, as is demonstrated at perspective screen a n.

Eye f and eye t are one and the same thing, but eye f4 denotes the distance, meaning how far you stand away to see an object, and eye t demonstrates the straightness, meaning whether you are at the middle of, or by the side of, or standing apart from the thing you are looking at; and remember that eye f and eye t are always situated at the same height as one another.

Verbs gratia. If you lower or raise the eye for distance, f, make sure you do the same to t, the eye for the straightness;5 and although point6 f shows how far the eye is from the square, it does not show with what part it is aligned; and similarly, although point t shows the alignment, it will not show the distance. Therefore, to know both the one and the other, you must do both together, and they will indicate the same identical thing.7

If eye f observes a perfect square, each of whose sides8 is equal to the distance between S and c, and at the beginning of the side nearest this eye you fix a staff or some other straight object in a perpendicular line, as appears at r S, then I say that when you observe the side of the square nearest you, it will strike at the base of perspective screen r S; and if you look at the9 farther, opposite side, that will appear for you to rise to the height10 of point n on the perspective screen. Therefore, by this demonstration you can understand that if the eye is higher than an infinite11 number of things located, one after the other,12 on a plain, then the farther they are away, the more they will rise,13 up until the point of their meeting the height of the eye,14 and no higher. This is because — if this plain where you rest your feet is flat, even if it were infinite — the things placed on the plain15 will never rise higher than the level of the eye, because the eye16 has within itself that point to which all the pyramids bearing species of objects to the eye direct themselves and conjoin. And this point is always in a line with the point of diminution, which appears at the end of all things seen. And from the base of the first pyramid on to the point of diminution, … 417

If you want to depict something as being nearby that will produce the same effect that natural things do, it will be impossible for your perspective not to appear faulty, with all the deceptive demonstrations and discordant proportions that could be imagined in a sorry work, unless the person viewing this perspective positions himself, and his viewpoint,3 at the same distance, height, and straightness of eye, or better, at the same point at which you were situated when making this perspective — so that you would need to make a window the size of your face, or better, a hole through which to regard this work.  And without any doubt,4 if you do so, this work of yours, being well accompanied by shadows and lights, will make the same effect that the natural makes, and you will not be able to persuade yourself that these things are painted.  Otherwise do not get involved with it, unless you start by taking your viewpoint from at least twenty times as far away as is the greatest width or height of the thing you are depicting.  And this will satisfy any viewer of this work located at any point of observation.

If you want to see the proof quickly, get a piece of staff, like a small column, eight times as high as it is wide, like a column without base or capital.  Then mark out forty equal spaces on a flat wall, conforming to the spaces that there would be5 between forty columns like your little column.  Then position6 a thin band of iron four arms away from the wall, to match up with the middles of these spaces, that has a little round hole at the middle, the size of a large pearl, and to this7 hole, join a light that touches.  Then proceed by putting your column up at each sign on the wall, and indicate the umbra and then the penumbra, and look at them through this hole in the iron.

On the voice.

Does an instrument1 that is twice the size of another one have a voice twice the size?

On the voice.

Is a voice that is twice the size of another one heard twice as far?  I say it does not, since if it were so, two men shouting would be heard twice as far as a single one.  Nonetheless, experience does not confirm this.

On statues.2

If you want to make a marble figure, first make one out of clay.  When this is finished and dry, put it into a box that is large enough3 also to contain — after the clay figure has been removed — the piece of marble4 within which you want to reveal5 a figure resembling the clay one.  Then, once you have put the clay figure into the box, get some sticks that just enter through the box's holes, and push them in, so much6 for each hole, that each white stick touches the figure at different places; and tint with black the parts of these sticks remaining outside of the box, and make a countersign on each stick and on its hole so that they match up where you put them in.7  Then take the clay figure out of the box and put your piece of marble in, and take enough off from the marble so that all your sticks can be hidden up to their signs at the given holes.  And to be able to do this better, make it so that the whole box can be lifted up while the bottom of the box stays under the marble.  And in this way you can remove from it using your tools, with great facility.8

The reason for this is that, when the weight departs from the force of its motor, although this departure is at the first degree of its power, (nonetheless, finding the air without motion), the weight finds the air at the first degree of resistance.  (And although the air has a greater sum of resistance than the power of the weight being thrust into it), nevertheless, in striking only a small part of the air, the weight comes to finish as the victor).  So the weight drives the air from its site and, in driving the air, it impedes its own velocity somewhat.  (Therefore, as this air is pushed, that pushes and drives other air, generating circular4 movements behind itself, and for these circles the weight moved therein is always the center, just as for circles made in the water, which have the place struck by the stone as their center.  And so, because one circle drives another, the air that is in front of its motor — all along that line — is prepared for movement, and this effect increases the more, the more the weight driving the air presses the air.  So this weight finds less resistance in the air and redoubles its course, with more velocity, like a boat being drawn through the water, which is moved with difficulty in its beginning motion, even though its motor is at its most potent strength.5 And when this water begins to take motion, with arched waves, the boat finds little resistance in following that motion, so it moves with greater facility. Then, as it changes course, the escape prepared before it by the fleeing air it is no longer of any use,7 and the more it the reason of the eighth proposition,10 that the part of the motion found between the initial resistance of the air and the beginning of its decline is of the greatest power, and this is the middle portion of the path, which is made through the air in a straight and direct line.

Preparation for an experiment regarding the pressing force of weight, labeled experiment.  Two pieces of staff with different weights loaded onto their tops, braced upright within two holes along a horizontal plank, their bases pressing into a quantity of earth. Labels:

If a one-pound weight causes a support to penetrate one inch into the ground, how much will a two-pound weight cause another such support to penetrate into soil of the same quality, during the same amount of time?  Make the proof1 in this manner:

Take a piece2 of staff and saw it in half, as exactly as you can.  Then, with wax, equalize their weights in the balances by attaching some wax to the one that weighs less.  Then take earth, of the sort used for making jugs, and work it3 so that it acquires a consistent softness and tenderness.  Then flatten it4 by hitting it against a flat place, and take the two pieces of the staff and set them upright, making them touch the earth with those parts that were previously united, or rather where the saw divided them, so that these are of equal width, and fix them above by making them pass through two equal holes in a thin board that are a thread wider than the width of the staff.5  Then load the first with one pound of weight and the other with two, and let them stand for an hour, placing them with attention6 and removing them at the same time; then measure the holes that were made.  But before you make a general rule from this case, try it two or three times and see whether the trials produce the same results.

Preparation for an experiment regarding the load-bearing capacity of iron wires. Groups of one, two and eight iron wires, labeled 1, 2, and 8, are fixed upright between two braces; the groups of two and eight wires are bound with sparse, diagonal windings; each of the columns of wires is loaded regularly with a weight at the top, resembling an inverted cup with weighted rings around the mouth. A plumb line hangs between the single and doubled wires. Labels:

Below the braces, a plan view of the single and doubled square wires:  a simple square and two adjacent squares.  Labels:

You will do the experiment in this manner:  Get a few7 iron wires, drawn by a square wire-drawing machine, and fix one at the end with two attachments and load it at the top with an equal weight, and note when it just starts to take a bend, verifying this by a wire with a counterweight at its end, and note how much weight causes it to start this bend.  Then double them into two doubles8 and bind them by wrapping thin silk around, and you will see by experience that this experiment confirms my reasons.  And try it, similarly, for four doubles, continuing by degrees to as many you will, always binding with the silk but a few times.

Two vertical, rectangular supports, both the same height, both divided into various rectangular sections.  The first, bearing a rectangular weight labeled 100, is a square column divided into eight cubes.  The second, bearing a larger, rectangular weight labeled 800, is four adjacent columns like the first one; the front and side faces of the second support show the vertical divisions between the columns, each of which is then divided into four sections, each section equivalent to two of the cubes, taken vertically, from the first column.  Labels:

A support with a diameter twice that of another one will bear eight times as much weight as the other,9 if both are of equal height.

This is clearly demonstrated, because if the first support, proportional to eight diameters, 10 will bear one hundred, the second, which is of squared doubling, contains four of these supports within itself.  And if this second support, also, were [of a height] proportionate to eight widths, it would bear four times as much as11 the first support, but since it is of four diameters,12 it diminishes its due height by half and grows stronger by as much again.  So if it previously bore in accordance with being four times the width of the first one, it will bear twice as much, for its being of doubled strength, which, all told, makes eight hundred pounds.13

On the support.

A pillar that is enlarged in width will gain as much more than1 its due strength as it remains short of its2 proportional height.

If a pillar ought to be nine arms high — meaning that if it is one arm wide, the rule3 sets it at nine arms high — and if you connect one hundred of them together, widthwise, this combination will be ten arms wide and nine high.  And if the first pillar bore ten thousand pounds, then, because this second one is about one width in height, and since eight parts of its length are lacking, it will bear eight times more; that is, each connected pillar will bear eight times more than it would when not connected.  That is, if it bore ten thousand pounds before, now it will sustain ninety thousand.

Verbs gratia.  If you take a rush4 whose height is equal to one hundred of its widths, putting it in a perpendicular line, and give it one ounce of weight, it will sustain that.  Then bind one hundred rushes together with continuous binding, so that the rushes compose a body whose height is equal to five5 of its widths.  As many times as five enters into one hundred, so many times more weight will this body sustain than if its height were of one hundred widths.  And since five enters6 twenty times into one hundred, each7 rush will sustain twenty times more weight than before because of the aforesaid binding; that is, if before it bore one ounce, then afterwards it will bear twenty.

If a lance whose length is one hundred times its 8 width bears twenty pounds, what will a lance of the same staff bear whose length is five of its widths?  As many times as five enters into one hundred, so many times less weight will the staff of one hundred widths bear than the staff of five widths.

Arches that stand through the support of chains are not permanent.

An arch is longer lasting when it has a proper opposition to its thrust.  The arch, of itself, tends to fall; and if the arch is thirty arms and the interval between the walls that support it is twenty, we know that the thirty will not pass through the twenty unless the twenty, also, becomes thirty.  So, when the arch is overcome by an excessive weight, it straightens and the poorly resisting walls open to give entry between their space, to the ruin of the arch.  But if you do not want to strengthen the arch with an iron cord, you will need to provide it with such shoulders as will make resistance to its thrust, which you will do as follows: Load spandrels21 m and n with stones22 in such a way that the lines made by their junctures are directed toward the center of the circle made by the arch.  And the reason this will make the arch permanent is as follows.  We know clearly that when the arch is loaded over quarter a b with an excessive weight, wall f g is thrust [outwards], because the arch tends to straighten itself;23 and if the other quarter, b c, were loaded, this would draw wall f g inwards, were it not for the line of stones, x y, that resists this.

The part of the foundation of a building that weighs more, penetrates more into the ground, leaving the lighter parts up higher, disunited from itself.

And the part of the ground that is pressed more - if it is porous - yields more.

You must always make foundations that extend equally beyond the load of their walls and piers, as shown at points m, a, and b.  And if you do as many do - that is, they make a foundation of equal1 width up until the surface of the earth, and on top of this they place an unequal load, as is demonstrated at b e and at e o - then part b e of the foundation will weigh more, because it is burdened with the corner pier, and it pushes its foundation down more than wall e o does, which does not entirely occupy its foundation; and indeed, this does push less and penetrates less.  So, when pier b e penetrates2 into the ground, it disunites and detaches from wall e o, as is seen in the majority of buildings, which are separated around these piers.

What the arch is.

An arch is nothing other than a strength originating from two weaknesses, since the arch of a building is composed of two quarter circles,3 and each of these quarter circles tends to fall, being very weak of itself.  As each one opposes itself to the ruin of the other, the two weaknesses are converted into a single strength.

On weights.

It is impossible to straighten a one-hundred-handed rope suspended between two pulleys that are one hundred hand apart, with each of these having a one-thousand-pound weight attached to the end.  I say that if you attach a one-hundred-pound weight to the middle of this rope, the rope2 will break before it straightens to lift its weight to a.  And it almost appears impossible to say that two thousand pounds of weight attached to the ends of the rope ought not to lift two hundred pounds, that is, the weight of the rope plus the weight attached to the middle of the rope. The reason for this is that the weight attached to the middle of the rope performs the same office, in acting as a counterweight for the one thousand pounds, as would the same amount of weight attached to the end of a lever fifty fathoms long.  Therefore, to know the truth of this effect, that is, whether it is possible for the two-thousand-pound weight to straighten this rope, measure the diameter of the solid part of the pulley that supports the one-thousand-pound weight, and note how many times half of this diameter will enter into the distance from the middle of the pulley to the middle of the hundred-pound weight, measuring along line or r a; and as many times as this part of the diameter, meaning or, enters into r a, so many times will half of the weight attached to the middle of the rope be lifted.  Now then, let us say that or enters two hundred times up until over the middle of the rope, and so many times does the other half, which says "four hundred."  Therefore say, "four hundred times one hundred make forty thousand," and then there is the weight of the rope, the rule for whose weight is below.3  In effect, a rope that is very long will not straighten without breaking.

On weights.

When unequal weights are positioned at unequal distances on the balance so that it remains flat, and then moved apart by equal distances, the balance will tip toward the part having the greater weight.

That is, if weight b weighs one pound, it will be counterweighted by three pounds at c.  The reason is that, if b is three inches away from the pivot and c is one inch away, it is necessary to restore it so that each part on either side of the pivot is of equal numbers.  That is, if c is four, that is, three pounds of weight and one of space, which make four, similarly, b will be three spaces and one pound, which make four.  Therefore, since there are four on each side, considering the pounds and the spaces together, the balance stays level.

Now, if you want to move the two weights[1] by the same distance from their locations, the greater weight will draw the arm of the balance downward.  And the reason is that if you pull b toward a and, similarly, c toward d, the distances from the pivot to the weights depart from their previous proportion.  This is because you entered three times into o b previously, and when you move the weights to a and to d, then d o enters into o a only two times, and not three times, as before.  In order to equalize the balance again, it would be necessary for the weight of three to become two, and then that would stand well.  Otherwise, the three would go down.

One end of a horse's bone propped up on a wisp of straw, on top of a block.  A circle at the middle of the bone shows the point of impact of the sheaf.

If you support the end of a horse's bone one-fourth of an arm above the head of an axe, making a prop for it out of a wisp of straw, and give a blow onto the middle of it, with your fist or with a tight sheaf of straw, you will see the bone break under the blow given it from above.

On the blow and motion made by weight or force.

I say that motion made by a falling weight is equal to motion made by force.

A hammer striking onto a brick held in a man's hand.

The body that receives a blow is not damaged on its opposite side as it is struck on the side.  The experience appears in the stone that is struck in the hands of a man:  his hand is not hurt as much when he holds the stone being struck as it would be if receiving the blow itself.
