Beginning of the treatise on water.

Man is said by the ancients to be a lesser world,1 and to be sure, the use of this name is well employed, since, insofar as man is composed of earth, water, air, and fire, this body of the earth is his likeness. If man has bones as the support and framework for his flesh, the world has stones2 that support the earth.  If man has a lake of blood within himself, where his lung grows and diminishes with his breathing, the body of the earth has its Ocean Sea,3 which also grows and diminishes every six hours, with the breathing of the world. If veins derive from this lake of blood, which branch throughout the human body, similarly,4 the Ocean Sea fills the body of the earth with infinite veins5 of water.  The body of the earth lacks sinews, which are not there,6 because sinews are made for the purpose of movement; and as the world is in perpetual stability, no movement occurs to it; and as no movement occurs to it, sinews are not necessary for it.  But in all other things, they are very similar.

On the veins7 of water on mountain tops.

It is clearly apparent that the whole8 surface of the Ocean is of an equal distance from the center of the earth, when there are no storms9, and that the tops of the mountains10 are as much farther away from this center11 as they rise above the surface of this sea.  Therefore, if the body of the earth were not similar to that of man, it would be impossible for the water of the sea, which is so much lower than the mountains, to be able to rise naturally to the tops of these mountains.  So it ought to be believed that the cause that keeps the blood at the top of a man's head is the same one that keeps water at the tops of mountains.

On the heat in the world.12

Where there is life, there13 is heat; and where there is vital heat, there are movements of humors.14  This is proven, since it is seen, by effect, that the heat from the element of fire always draws moist vapors, dense fogs, and thick15 clouds to itself, which rise from the seas and other marshes,16 rivers, and wet valleys.  And as these draw, little by little, up to the cold region, that first part stops, because the hot and humid is not suited to the cold and dry.  So, once the first part has stopped, it orders the other parts there,17 and thus, part joining with part, it becomes thick, dark clouds.  And often these are moved18 and carried by winds from one region to another, where, because of their density, they make such a thick heaviness that they fall in dense rain.  And if the heat from the sun is added to the power of the element of fire, the clouds are drawn higher and find more cold, so that they freeze and tempestuous hail is caused.  Now, that same heat that holds such a great weight of water, as is seen raining from the clouds, wrests19 the waters from down at the bases of the mountains up upward, and it leads them into and holds them20 at the tops of the mountains, where, finding various fissures, they continue.  These waters cause rivers when they flow out.21

I say that, just as natural heat keeps the blood in the veins7 at the top of a man, when the man8 is dead, this cold blood is reduced to the low places.  And when9 the sun heats the man's head,10 this effect multiplies, causing the sudden arrival of much blood, with humors, so that in forcing the veins, this often generates pains in the head.  , the body of the earth has veins that branch throughout, and because of the natural heat dispersed throughout its containing body, the water remains in the elevated veins at the similarly high tops of mountains.  And water flowing through a conduit, walled within the body of this mountain, as a dead thing, will not depart from its original lowness, unless it is heated by the vital heat of the first vein.  Again, the heat of the element of fire and, during the day, the heat of the sun, have the power to awaken the humidity of the low places of mountains11 and to draw this upward, in the same way that it12 draws the clouds and awakens their humidity from the bed of the sea.13

On the blood at the top of the head.

It would appear to be so, because of a simple one,9 that when someone breaks the top of a man's head, what comes out is none other than that blood that is found between his lips.  Since every weighty thing seeks low places, and blood has weight, it appears impossible for it to rise upward of itself, like a light and airy thing.  And if you wanted to say that the expansions10 that the lung makes in its lake of blood — when the lung fills itself with air in the gathering of the breath, or deflates, driving the blood of the lake fleeing through the veins — that those are what cause the increasing and the inflating, and that this inflation causes the blood to escape from the above-mentioned break at the top of the head, then this opinion is quickly reproved, since the veins are well capable and suited to accommodate the increasing of the blood, without its having to overflow through the break in the head, as it would if they could receive but little support.

Why this blood escapes through the top of the head.

The spiritual parts have the power to move and accompany11 materials with their course.

We see that fire, by means of its spiritual heat, sends up through the chimney, as a vaporing smokiness, material12 that is terrestrial and weighty, as is seen in the soot you see returning into ashes when you burn.  Thus, the heat that is mixed in with the blood, finding that it can evaporate through the break in the head and desiring to return to its element, bears in company with itself the blood with which this heat13 is infused and mixed.  The reason that the smoke rises upwards with such fury and carries earthen matter with it, is that the fire that attaches onto the wood nourishes and feeds itself on a fine moisture.  But the coarser moisture cannot be consumed by the heat14 of the fire found therein, so the fire, …415

On the movement of the sea every six hours.

If the heat6 moves humors, the cold stops them, and where there is greater coldness, there is greater stability of humors.7

If someone wanted to allege that the moon, which is something that increases the cold, were what made the sea grow and diminish every six hours,8 for the reasons assigned above, this would appear to be impossible, since something that is similar to another does not draw by similarity, but rather it draws through want of conformity.  You will not see the hot and dry fire drawing9 fire to itself, rather it will draw the cold and humid; you do not see water drawing other water to itself.

How water is lighter than the earth.

Any liquid body is penetrated by a heavier body placed on top of it, and a heavy10 and porous body will be penetrated by liquids and subtle bodies.

If you mix earth with water, you will see the earth penetrate the water, becoming a bed for it.  And if water thrown onto the earth is often seen to penetrate and seep down into this earth, this occurs because the porosity of the earth provides a pathway for the water arriving on top of it.11  It was filled with air, and since the air is unable to remain under the water, it immediately abandons that earthen porosity.  And because nothing can remain vacant, the water enters and fills the places abandoned by the air.12

Because the movement of water, although it is slower than that of a man, always appears to be faster.

The reason for this is that if you look at the movement of water your eye cannot stop, but rather it does as when viewing things in your shadow when you are walking, where, if the eye attempts to comprehend the quality of the shadow, the wisps of straw or other things contained in this shadow appear to have rapid motion, and it will appear that those are much faster in fleeing out from this shadow than the shadow is in proceeding forward.

On the center of the Ocean Sea.

The center of the sphere of water is the true center of the orb1 of our world, which is composed of water and land in a spherical form.  But if you wanted to find the center of the element of the earth, this would be located equidistant from the surface of the Ocean Sea, and not equidistant from the surface of the land;2 because it is clearly understood that this ball of the earth has no perfect rotundity except at that part where there is sea or marsh or other stagnant water, and any part of the earth that juts out beyond the sea goes farther away from its center.3

Proof of how the earth is not spherical, and not being spherical, it cannot have a common center.

We see the Nile start off from the southern regions and stream across4 various provinces, flowing northward over a distance of three thousand miles, to empty into the Mediterranean waves at the shores of Egypt.5  And if we want to indicate this descent as being ten arms per mile, which are commonly granted as being universal for the courses of rivers,6 we will find that the Nile has its mouth ten miles lower than its source.  Also, we see the Rhine, the Rhone, and the Danube depart from the Germanic territories, which are practically at the center of Europe, and one to the east, another to the north, and the last to the southern seas, makes its course.  If you consider it well, you will find that the plains7 of Europe8 make a concourse that is much more elevated than the high peaks of the maritime mountains.  Now, just think how much higher their tops are than the marine shores.

Regarding some who say that the water is higher than the dry land.

To be sure, it is no small astonishment that the common opinion causes me, which is made, contrary to the truth, by the universal concurrence of the judgments of men.  And this is that all agree that the surface of the sea is higher than the highest peaks of the mountains, alleging many vain and childish reasons, against which I shall allege only one simple and brief reason.  We can see clearly that if you take the shores away from the sea, the sea will clothe the earth and make it perfectly spherical.  Now consider9 how much earth would have to be removed to cause the marine waves to cover the world.  Therefore, that which was to be removed must be higher than the seashore.

Because rivers change their beds and often remove and deposit1 in different locations.

The movement of the water always tends to consume its support.  And the softer part resists this less and2 departs from its location, leaving various hollows, where the water turns again on itself with various eddies, and consumes and excavates, widening these voids.3  And striking into the new banks, it leaps back, striking into the shores.  Consuming and eroding, and with ruin to what opposes it, it changes course as a result of this destruction,4 taking the lightest earth along with its course, which it then deposits in the quieter places.  By raising the river bottoms,5 it diminishes the quantity and force of the water, sending its furor to the opposite side.  And if it finds a bank,6 it erodes that and undermines the foundations until, with great ruin, it uncovers new ground.  And if it finds plains it occupies them, and, removing and excavating, it makes itself a new bed.  And if7 it finds buried stones it uncovers them and then bares their lower parts,8 which often times because of their size resist the impetuous course,9 which reflects against the opposing stones10 and bounces back to the opposite side, breaking11 and damaging the opposite banks.

What the foam of water is.

Water that falls from above, into other water, encloses within itself a certain quantity of air, which is submerged with it by means of the blow, and with a swift motion12 it surges up again, coming to the surface that it left, clothed thinly with moisture in a spherical body,13 leaving the site of the first percussion in a circular manner.

Or rather, the water that falls on top of other water starts off from its place, with various and diverse ramifications,14 bifurcated and concave, which go maneuvering and interweaving together.15 When these have struck onto the surface of the water, because of16 the power of the weight and the blow given by the said water, the air does not have enough time to escape into its element, because of the17 great rapidity; indeed, it submerges in the way noted above.

Why water digs its18 pit in a circle where it falls violently.19

The water that falls in the way noted above does not widen its pit, because its falling straight down is an indication that it has little force of water behind it to drive it forward.  Indeed, it falls, disunited20 and fine, almost in a perpendicular line.  And the air found among this disunity, having weight above itself almost equally, cannot escape so quickly, so the weight above submerges it together with the blow.  But since the air can not be disunited from its own element without violence, once it has obeyed the fury of the blow and the weight, it surges up again immediately and returns in round bubbles to the surface of the water near the place21 struck.  So, as it does not depart from the site of the first percussion, it does not harm the banks of its pit.  But when the impetuous river, swollen with the new rains, flows22 between its banks, it falls23 to the low expanses of water, with fury, and not as before, when it calmly rained on top of the other water, mixed in with air.  Indeed, united and forceful, it wounds24 and opens up the struck water,25 on down to the hard bottom.  Baring the lower parts26 of the buried stones27 and removing them, it makes a new barrier against itself with the sides28 of the previously made pit.  It strikes against this29 and yet remains vanquished, and it divides into two contrary courses at the given percussion, which part from each other … 430

The wind is entirely the same as water in its movement.

All things universally desire to be maintained in their nature,4 so the course of water that moves5 tries to maintain the power of its cause,6 and if it finds opposition standing against it,7 it completes the measure of the initiated course, with circular and eddying movements.

Overhead view of water flowing through a channel blocked on one side by a rectangular barrier, analogous to f. 58 r: 1. The flow of water produces a forceful eddy just beyond the barrier and oscillates in a succession of percussions against alternating sides of the channel.

The meandering courses of waters, which are caused by rebounds from the percussions made by the water into the banks, will deepen the bed beneath the river more than at any other part, and they strike at great depths in their percussions.1  And the water turning through2 these depths3 is cause for the hollowing and destruction of the banks that are struck.4

And it is clearly seen and recognized that the waters that strike the banks of rivers act like balls that strike against walls, which depart from those at angles equal to those of their percussions and go to strike against the opposite walls.  Thus, these waters, having made their percussion first against one bank, rebound to the opposite, and there they make a great percussion and hollowing,5 because there is a greater confluence6 of water in that place.  The reason is that the water, rebounding from one bank to the other, digs away at the bottom of the river,7 at the part that is beneath itself.  But the other water of the river, which cannot be received at this lowness, gets pushed and driven somewhat along the direction of the river;8 then, because flight is lacking in it,9 it returns to its natural course.  That is, since the bottom of the river is lower under the twisted ways made by the percussions of the waters mentioned previously, this second water,10 which has lost its accidental means of flight, resumes its natural course and falls into the low places of the river, striking the banks in the same place as the percussion of the rebounds noted before.  Since this bank is buffeted, then, by two different percussions,11 a greater concavity is caused there, because one strikes the bank up above12 and the other, of greater declination, erodes and undermines the bank at the base.  And this is the cause of the ruin and devastation13 of the banks, noted above.

What the moon is.1

The moon is not luminous of itself, but it is well suited to receive the nature of light, like a mirror, or water, or some other shining body.  And it grows larger in the east and the west, as do the sun and the other planets.  And the reason is that every luminous body grows larger, the further away it goes.  It can be clearly comprehended that any planet or star is farther from us2 in the west than when it is over our heads, by about thirty-five hundred [miles],3 by the proof indicated to the side.4  And if you see the sun or the moon reflected in water that is near you, it will appear to you to be the same size in the water as it appears to you in the sky.  And if you go a mile away, it will appear one hundred times greater.  And if you see it reflected in the sea at sunset, the reflected sun5 will appear to be more than ten miles long, because it will cover more than ten miles of the sea with its reflection.6  And if you were where the moon is, the sun would appear to reflect in as much of the sea as it illuminates during the day,7 and the land among the waters would appear like the dark stains appearing on the moon, which appear to the men8 standing on the earth exactly as our world would to men who lived on the moon.

On the quality of the moon.

When the moon is completely illuminated in our sight, we see its full day,9 and then its Ocean casts us less humidity, because of the reflection of the sun's rays that strike on it and rebound to us.  And the less light, the more it damages.

Proof9 of the growth of the sun in the west.

Certain mathematicians demonstrate that the sun grows larger in the west because the eye always sees it through air of a greater density, alleging that things appear greater when seen in the fog and in water.10  To these I respond that this is not so, since things seen in the fog are equal in color to things that are distant, but not being equally diminished, they appear to be of greater size.  Also, nothing seems larger in level water, and you can make the proof of this in tracing on a board that is half under water.11  But the reason12 the sun grows larger is Every luminous body appears larger, the farther away it is.13

Because oftentimes effects show the nature of their causes, I will use those to describe the nature of the eye, and in what way it receives the species of objects into itself. We see with our eyes those things that are situated along the line of the nape of the neck. This would, therefore, demonstrate that these things are seen from the surface of the eye, if it were not for a certain experiment that contradicts this.

Push your eyeball upward from below with your finger. It will appear to you that the thing seen makes contrary movement, from above downward.  Therefore, this visual virtue appears on the opposite side of the pupil. Being thus, the things positioned at the back of the line of the pupils cannot be at the given site.  So, with these two contrary arguments, it is necessary to admit, since the eye sees straight on to its center things that are at the back of itself,2 that the lines of the species bend. Which proof will be made with good experience, and you will proceed in the following manner:

Something that sends its image through the air, passing from air into denser air, bends its line when it enters the denser air. And when it passes from this denser air into the bottom of some water, which is denser, there the line will bend a second time.  The species from objects pass through three degrees of bodies, each denser than the other, namely, the air, the subtle humor within the pupil, called crystalline, and the cornea.  And the crystalline humor is as much denser than the air as the cornea is denser than that humor, therefore the angles at which the lines break are equal.  And if the line of the species did not make these breaks, you would not be able to see things that are to the side. And since these things can be seen, the species must necessarily converge to a single point.

This type of effect happens because, when the eye is moved with the finger upwards from below or downwards from above, it moves by moving4 or pushing the eyelids, which join within their origins to the surface skin of the eye.  And if you push the lower eyelid upward, it pulls behind the eye and lifts the pupil upward; and the part of the eye from the center backwards will make contrary movement; and the movement will be contrary to the images of the objects impressed on that posterior part of the eye, where the virtue of the imprensiva5 is based.  And this effect occurs when keeping both eyes open, because the eye that is not moved sees the thing in its site,6 while the one that has been moved will move the image of the object that it has impressed on its imprehensibility. And the thing seen by the moved eye is never of the distinct form that was sent, which is what is seen by an eye that is not moved, since, when it is moved, it does not see the image of the object along that central line where it can best judge things, but rather it sees from those parts which are about that center, and because they are of a less transparent humor, the things are seen in a more confused manner.

It would be impossible for the eye to send the visual virtue7 out beyond itself by means of visual rays, because, in its opening,8 that first part that started going out and that had to go to the object9 could not do this without time.  Thus being, in a month it could not go to the height of the sun when the eye wanted to see it; and if it did arrive there,10 it would be necessary for it11 to be continuous all along the whole path12 between the eye and the sun, and it would become ever wider, so that13 the base and tip of a pyramid were composed between the sun and the eye.  If this were the case, there would not be enough — even though the eye were for a million worlds14 — for all of that virtue not to become consumed.  And if, indeed, this virtue had to proceed through the air as does an odor,15 the winds would bend it and carry it to another location.  And we see the body of the sun with that16 same rapidity that we see at a distance of one arm, and it does not change17 for the blowing of the winds, nor for any other accident.

On the nature of the folds in drapery.4

The part of the fold farthest from its constrained edges will reduce most into its original nature.5

Everything desires, by nature, to be maintained as it is.

The cloth tends to stay flat because it is of equal density and thickness, both on the reverse side and on the front side; so when it is constrained by some fold or pleat to depart from this flatness, observe6 the nature of the force at the part where it is most constrained, and you will find the farthest part from this constraint to reduce itself most to its original nature, that is, that of staying extended and wide.7

Let a b c be the fold in the cloth mentioned above, and let a and c8 be the places where this folded cloth is constrained.  I proposed to you that the part of the cloth9 farthest from the constrained extremes reduces most into its original nature.

Therefore, since b is farthest10 from a and c, fold a b c is wider there than in any other location on it.

A board positioned upright before a fire. The board bends noticeably, with the concave side toward the flames.

Example in regards to the above.

I told you that something wide whose front side has as much latitude as its reverse side cannot by nature stand, unless flat, and thus, the contrary follows for unequal surfaces.  Therefore, take a board and fasten it on one of its sides:  you will immediately see it become concave and curved,11 with convex torsion towards the fire, and this derives because the heat12 moves the humidity. Since every body is united together by the humidity infused into it, 13 part of this humidity escapes from the surface facing the fire, and part penetrates into the opposite surface.  The part that escapes towards the fire leaves that surface diminished, while the other part escaping to the opposite surface remains there, and, in remaining, causes that to grow and expand14; so this makes these two surfaces unequal and curved in such a way that the greater bends about the lesser.

Every pyramid composed of a long concourse of rays contains within itself an infinite number of pyramids; and each one has power for all, and all for each one.

The equidistant circuit of the pyramidal concourse gives equal qualities of angles to its objects, and the thing is received by its object as equal in size.

Every opaque body fills the surrounding air with an infinite number of images of itself, which, by means of an infinite number of pyramids infused throughout that, represent1 this body all throughout and entirely at every part.2

** Every radiant pyramid, of long…

The body of air is filled with an infinite number of pyramids composed of radiant and straight lines, which originate from the superficial extremes of the opaque bodies placed within it.  And the further they go from their cause, the more acute they become; and although their passage is intersected and interwoven, nevertheless, they do not become confused for one another.  And they proceed along a divergent course, amplifying and infusing themselves throughout all the surrounding air;3 and they are of equal power4 among themselves, and all are equivalent to each one, and each one is equivalent to every other.  And through these, the image of the body5 is borne all throughout and entirely at the part.  And each pyramid, for itself, receives the entire form of its cause in each of the smallest parts of itself.

All colors in distant shadows

are unknown and indiscernible.

All colors in the distance are unknown in the shadows, because anything not touched by the principal light is incapable of transmitting its likeness to the eye through the more luminous air, because the lesser light is overcome by the greater. For example, we see, being in a house, that all the colors on the walls are seen clearly and easily when the windows of the house are open; and if we do not leave the house and look a little farther through the windows to see the paintings on the walls, we will instead see a continuous darkness.

That which is more similar to light in brightness will be seen from a greater distance and will have a greater form than is required for the quality of the body at that distance.

Precepts of Painting.

The painter must first accustom his hand by copying drawings by good masters, and having accomplished this accustoming with the judgment of his tutor, he must then accustom himself to portraying good reliefs according to the rules set forth below.

On portraying in relief.

The person portrayed in relief must arrange himself so that the eye of the figure being portrayed is level with the eye of the person being portrayed. This will be done on a head that you are going to portray from life, because generally, the figures or people you encounter in the street all have their eyes at your height, and if you were to make them either higher or lower, your portrait would be dissimilar.

On portraying figures

for histories.

The painter must always consider, on the wall he is to decorate, the height of the site where he wishes to place his figures, and that what he portrays from life, for this purpose, must be so much lower to the eye than the object he portrays, as the said object is placed higher than the eye of the viewer; otherwise, the work will be reprehensible.

Because painting can never appear

as distinct as natural things.

Painters often despair of imitating nature, seeing their paintings not have the relief and vivacity that objects seen in a mirror have, alleging that their colors, in brightness or darkness, far surpass the quality of the lights and shadows of the object seen in the mirror. In this case, they blame their ignorance and not reason, for their lack of knowledge. It is impossible for the painted object to appear of such relief as to resemble the objects in a mirror, although both are on the same surface, unless they are seen with a single eye. And the reason is: two eyes that see one thing after the other, as a b sees n m, m cannot completely occupy n, because the base of the visual lines is so wide that it sees the second body after the first. But if you close one eye like S, the body f will occupy r, because the visual line begins at a single point and is based on the first body, so that the second of equal size will never be seen.

Every corporeal form, as far as the eye is concerned, is divided into three parts: body, shape, and color. A corporeal resemblance extends further from its origin than does color or shape; furthermore, color extends further than shape. But this rule is not observed with luminous bodies.

The eye observing an object that is a minimal part of the horizon, with:

The above proposition is very well demonstrated and confirmed by experience, for if you see a man from close by, you will recognize the quality of his body, his shape, and similarly his color. And if he moves some distance away from you, you will not recognize who he is, because the quality of shape is lacking. If he moves even further away, you will not be able to discern his color; rather, he will appear to you as a dark body. Further away, a small, round, and dark body will appear to you: round it will appear because the distance diminishes the individual parts so much that only the greater mass appears. The reason is this. We know clearly that all the similarities of things enter the imagination through a small aperture of the eye. Therefore, if the entire horizon a b enters through a similar aperture, body b c being a very small part of that horizon, what part will it occupy in the smallest representation of such a large hemisphere? And because luminous bodies are more powerful in darkness than any other body, it is necessary that, since the aperture of sight is very dark, as is the nature of all holes, the species of distant bodies are confused in the great brightness of the sky, and if they appear at all, they appear dark and black, as does any small body seen in the brightness of the air.
All bodies together and each individually fill the surrounding air with their infinite similarities, which are all throughout and all in the part, carrying with them the quality of the body, color, and shape of their cause.

On Linear Painting.

Let the edges of any body be carefully considered, along with the manner of their meandering. Let these meanderings be judged to determine whether their vaults participate in circular curvature or angular concavity.

On Painting.

The shadows which you discern with difficulty, and whose edges you cannot know, but rather grasp with confused judgment and transfer to your work, you will not make them finite or complete, for your work will be a wooden result.

On Reverberation.

Reverberations are caused by bodies of a clear quality, with full and semi-dense surfaces, which, struck by the light, reflect it back onto the first object, similar to the bounce of a ball.

Where there cannot be...

luminous reverberation.

All dense bodies clothe their surfaces with various qualities of light and shadow.

Lights are of two natures: one is called original, the other derivative.

I define original light as that which comes from the blaze of fire or from sunlight or air; derivative light is reflected light. But to return to the promised definition, I say that luminous reflection does not come from that part of the body that faces shadowy bodies, such as dark places, meadows with varying heights of grass, green or dry woods. Although the part of each branch facing the original light is clothed in the quality of that light, nevertheless, the shadows cast by each branch on itself are so many, and so many are the shadows cast by one branch on another, that in short, such darkness results that there is no light at all; therefore, such objects cannot give any reflected light to opposing bodies.

Just as in small things one does not understand

errors as in large ones.

In things of minute form, the quality of their error cannot be understood as in large ones. And the reason is that if this small thing is made in the likeness of an acorn or other animal, its parts, due to the immense diminution, cannot be searched for with the proper purpose by its maker, which would be appropriate, therefore it remains unfinished; not being finished, you cannot understand its errors. For example: you will observe a man from a distance of 300 arms and carefully judge whether he is beautiful or ugly, or whether he is monstrous or of ordinary quality. You will see that with all your effort you will not be able to persuade yourself to make such a judgment. And the reason is that due to the aforementioned distance, this man diminishes so much that the qualities of the particles cannot be understood; And if you want to see the above-mentioned man's diminution carefully, place a finger a hand's breadth away from your eye, and raise and lower it so much that its upper tip ends under the feet of the figure you are looking at, and you will see an incredible diminution appear. And for this reason, one often doubts the shape of a friend from a distance.

Because the chapters of figures,

one above the other, is a work to be avoided.

This universal practice, which is practiced by painters on the facades of chapels, is quite reasonably to be criticized, because they paint a scene on one level with its landscape and buildings, then raise it to another level and paint a scene, varying the point of the first, and then the third and fourth, so that a facade appears to be made with four points; which is the utmost folly of such masters. We know that the point is placed at the eye of the viewer of the scene, and if you wanted to tell me how I can depict the life of a saint divided into many scenes on the same wall, I would answer that you should place the foreground with the point at the eye level of the viewer of that scene, and on that level depict the first large scene. and then, gradually decreasing the figures and buildings on various hills and plains, you will complete the entire furnishing of the scene. And the rest of the facade, at its height, you will make large trees in comparison with the figures, or angels, if they are relevant to the scene, or birds or clouds or similar things. Otherwise, do not bother with them, or all your work will be false.

Of light that operates in all its quantities

in a single luminous center.

If a large spherical light were to illuminate another spherical body much smaller than itself, it would be necessary, if the luminous rays departed from the surfaces of the light, that the smaller body would be encompassed and illuminated more than halfway. Thus, the shadow, where it was farthest from its cause, would become smaller towards its end; And experiment shows the contrary, because the lights of candles that are long and narrow, when they illuminate a small spherical body, the shadow that would be cast on the round wall would be broad and low, for this reason. Let a b, c d be the height and width of the light: if the surfaces are to operate, a b will illuminate the spherical body as much more than halfway, as it is from p n and from y s, and its shadow on the wall will appear much smaller than that on the spherical body. The surfaces of the thickness of the light at c d will illuminate the spherical body at p y, that is, in the middle; this being so, the shadow of the wall will be as broad as that of the wall. Therefore, the shadow on the ball will be large and low, and likewise that of the wall, which, since experiment has shown to be round in shape and always larger than its cause, we must nullify both the above demonstrations and admit that the center of every light is the cause of shadows.

The young man must first learn perspective, then the measurements of everything, then from the hand of a good master to become accustomed to good limbs, then from life to confirm the reasons for the things learned, then see, for a time, from the hands of different masters, then become accustomed to putting the art into practice and practicing it.

How the first painting was only a line, which surrounded the shadow of the ash cast by the sun on the walls.

How the painting should be seen from a single window, as it appears because of the bodies thus

made (small egg figure follows). If you want to make a round ball at a height, you must make it long according to this similitude, and stand so far back that when foreshortened it appears round.

How scenes should not be occupied and confused with many figures.

Just as a cloth should not be confused by too many folds, but should only be made where the hands or arms hold them, and the rest should be left to fall simply where its nature draws it, and the nakedness should not be obscured by too many lines or broken folds.

Just as cloth should be copied from nature, that is, if you want to make a woolen cloth, use the folds according to those, and whether it is silk or fine cloth or peasant cloth or linen or fleece, go about differentiating the folds for each, and do not make a dress, as many do, from patterns covered with paper or thin leather, or you would be seriously mistaken.

How old men should be depicted with lazy and slow movements, legs bent at the knees when standing still, feet evenly spaced and far apart, backs sloping low, heads bowed forward, and arms not too outstretched.

How women should be depicted with bashful gestures, legs clasped together, arms drawn together, heads lowered and bent sideways.

How old women should be depicted with bold, quick and furious movements, like those of infernal furies. And the movements should appear more rapid in the arms and heads than in the legs.

Small children with quick and crooked gestures when sitting, and timid and fearful gestures when standing.
How to represent the ages of man, that is, infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, old age, and decrepitude.

Of three kinds of perspective.

How there are three kinds of perspective. The first deals with the diminution—and is called diminutive perspective—of things that are distant from the eye. The second contains within itself the method of varying colors that are distant from the eye. The third and last deals with the declaration that things should be less finite the further they are. And these are the names: linear perspective, color perspective, and forward perspective.

Of the accentuation of colors.

Which color is more evident: the lighter thing appears further away, and the darker does the opposite.

Of making good selection.

Of the few folds in clothing.

Just as figures dressed in cloaks should not be so naked that the cloak appears to be on the flesh, unless you want the cloak to be on the flesh. For you must consider that between the cloak and the flesh there are other garments that prevent the shape of the limbs from being revealed and visible above the cloak; and those limbs you reveal, make them so thick that other garments appear beneath the cloak. But you should only reveal the almost true thickness of the limbs of a nymph or an angel, who are depicted dressed in thin garments, blown and impressed by the blowing of the winds on the limbs of said figures.

On the method of depicting

distant objects in painting.

It is clear that one air is thicker than the other, which borders on the flat earth, and the higher it rises, the thinner and more transparent it becomes. The lowness of tall and large things that are far from you will be little seen, because you see it by a line that passes through thicker and more continuous air. The summit of these heights is seen by a line which, although it originates in thicker air from your eye, nevertheless, ending at the highest height of the thing seen, ends in air much thinner than its lowness. For this reason, the further this line is from you from point to point, the more it changes quality from thin to thin air.

Therefore, painter, when you paint mountains, make sure that from hill to hill the lowness is always lighter than the height, and the further you make one from the other, the lighter the lowness; 4 - 43 and the higher it rises, the more it will reveal the truth of form and color.
How the air should become clearer,

the lower you lower it.

Because this air is thick near the earth, and the higher it rises, the thinner it becomes, when the sun is in the east and you look toward the west, which shares the south and north, you will see that thick air receive more light from the sun than the thin air, because the rays encounter more resistance. And if the sky and your vision end with the low plain, that final part of the sky will be seen through that thicker and whiter air, which will distort the true color seen through its midst, and the sky will appear whiter there than above you, because the visual line passes through a smaller quantity of air corrupted by thick humors. And if you look toward the east, the air will appear darker to you the lower it goes, because in that low air the light rays pass less.

On the Discernment of the Shadows of Places

and of the Things Placed Therein.

If the sun is in the east and you look toward the west, you will see all illuminated things entirely devoid of shadow, because you see what the sun sees. And if you look toward south and north, you will see all bodies surrounded by shadow and light, because you see what the sun sees and what it does not see; and if you look toward the sun's path, all bodies will show you their shadowed part, because that part cannot be seen by the sun.

On the Method of Figuring a Night.

That which is entirely deprived of light is all darkness. If the night is in a similar condition and you wish to depict a scene in it, you will make a large fire appear so that the object closest to it is more deeply colored by it, because the object closest to the object participates more in its nature. And by making the fire shine red, you will make all the things illuminated by it also appear red, and those farther from the fire more deeply colored by the black of the night. The figures between you and the fire will appear dark in the brightness of the fire, because that part of the object you see is colored by the darkness of the night and not by the brightness of the fire. Those on the sides will be half dark and half reddish; and those that can be seen after and at the edges of the flames will all be illuminated by a reddish light on a black background. As for actions, you will have those who are close to you shield themselves with their hands and cloaks to protect themselves from the excessive heat, and turn their faces in the opposite direction to appear to flee. Those further away4 you will have the majority of them shield their eyes with their hands, offended by the excessive brightness.
Because two things of equal size

will appear larger than the painted one in relief.

This reasoning is not as easy to demonstrate as many others, but I will nevertheless try to satisfy it, if not completely, then in some part. Diminutive perspective shows us by reason that the further things are from the eye, the more they diminish, and this reasoning is well confirmed by experience. Therefore, the visual lines that are found between the object and the eye, when they extend to the surface of the painting, all cut at the same point; and the lines that are found between the eye and the sculpture are of various points and lengths. The longest line extends over a limb that is further away than the others, and therefore that limb appears smaller, since many lines are longer than the others, and because there are many particles further apart, one from the other, being further apart, they must appear smaller; appearing smaller, they diminish the entire sum of the object; and since this does not happen in painting, because lines ending at the same distance must be without diminution.

Therefore, undiminished particles do not diminish the sum of the object, and therefore painting does not diminish like sculpture.

Just as painting surpasses all human works through the subtle speculation inherent in it, the eye, which is called the window of the soul, is the principal way through which the common sense can more copiously and magnificently contemplate the infinite works of nature. And the ear is the second, which is ennobled by the things narrated, which the eye has seen. If you historians or poets or other mathematicians had not seen things with the eye, you could poorly relate them in writing. And if you, a poet, depict a story with the painting of the pen, and the painter with the brush will make it easier to satisfy and less tedious to complete. If you call painting mute poetry, the painter will still be able to call the poet blind painting. Now consider which bite is more harmful, blind or mute. If the poet is as free in invention as the painter, his fictions are not as satisfying to men as paintings, because if poetry uses words to depict forms, actions, and places, the painter moves with the very likenesses of forms to counterfeit those forms. Now see which is closer to man, the name of man or the likeness of that man. The name of man varies in different countries, and the form is not changed except by death.
And if the poet serves the senses through the ear, the painter through the eye, a more worthy sense. But I want nothing more from these than that a good painter depict the fury of a battle, and that the poet write another, and that they be put in public company. You will see where the viewers will pause most, where they will consider most, where more praise will be given, and which will satisfy better.

Certainly, painting, far more useful and beautiful, will please more. Write the name of God in a place and place his figure opposite it: you will see which will be more revered. If painting embraces within itself all the forms of nature, you have only the names, which are not universal like the forms; if you have the effects of demonstrations, we have the demonstrations of the effects. Take a poet who describes the beauty of a woman to her lover; Take a painter to depict it: you will see which way nature will turn the enamoured judge. Certainly the testing of things should leave the verdict to experience. You have placed painting among the mechanical arts. Certainly if painters were as apt at praising their works by writing them down as you are, I doubt it would be given such a vile name. If you call it mechanical because it is manual work, since the hands depict what they find in the imagination, you writers draw with the pen manually what is found in your mind. And if you were to say it is mechanical because it is done for a price, who falls into this error, if error it can be called, more than you? If you read in the Studi, do you not go to the one who rewards you most? Do you produce any work without some reward? Although I do not say this to condemn such opinions, because every effort expects a reward. And a poet might say: I will create a fiction that signifies great things; The painter will do the same, as Apelles did in Calumny. If you were to say: poetry is more eternal, for this I will say that the works of a coppersmith, who is more preserved by time, are more eternal than your or our works; nevertheless it is of little imagination, and painting, by painting on copper with glass colors, can be made much more eternal. We can be called grandchildren of God through art. If philosophy extends to moral philosophy, and this to natural philosophy; if the former describes the operation of the mind, the latter considers what the mind operates in movements; if the former frightens people with infernal fictions, the latter does the same with the same things put into action. Let the poet set himself to represent a beauty, a pride, a nefarious and ugly thing, a monstrous thing with the painter; let him make in his own way, as he wishes, a transmutation of forms, that the painter will no longer be satisfied. Haven't we seen paintings that resemble living things so closely that they have deceived men and animals?
How white bodies should be depicted.

If you depict a white body surrounded by a lot of air, because white has no color by itself, but rather is tinted and transformed into part of the color that is its object. If you see a woman dressed in white in the countryside, the part of her that is seen by the sun will be so light in color that it will, like the sun, be partly obscure to the eye. And the part that is seen by the air will be luminous because of the sun's rays woven and penetrating it, because the air itself is blue, the part of the woman seen by that air will appear to lean blue. If there are meadows visible on the surface of the earth, and the woman stands between the meadow illuminated by the sun and the sun itself, you will see all the parts of these folds visible from the meadow become colored by rays reflected in the color of the meadow; and so they are transformed into the colors of the luminous and nonluminous nearby objects. If you know how to reason and write the demonstration of the forms, the painter will make them appear animated with shadows and lights composing the expression of the faces; which you then do not add with the pen where one adds with the brush.

What light is good for portraying from nature: high or low, large or small, powerful or small or large and weak, or small and weak.

Just as he who despises painting does not love

the philosophy of nature.

If you despise painting, which is the sole imitator of all the evident works of nature, you will certainly despise a subtle invention, which with philosophical and subtle speculation considers all the qualities of forms: air and places, plants, animals, herbs, and flowers, which are surrounded by shadow and light. And truly this is science and the legitimate daughter of nature, because painting is born of nature itself. But to put it more correctly, we would say granddaughter of nature, because all evident things were born of nature, from which things painting was born. Therefore we would rightly call it the granddaughter of nature and the relative of God.

Of the eye that, through a greater light,

cannot discern the smaller ones.

Of the positioning of the limbs.

The limbs that require effort, make them muscular, and those that are not used, you will make without muscles and soft.

Of the action of the figures.

You will draw the figures in such an attitude that it is sufficient to demonstrate what the figure has in its soul. Otherwise, your art will not be praiseworthy.
On choosing the right atmosphere for grace

If you have a courtyard that you can cover with a curtain at your discretion, this light will be good. Or when you want to portray someone, portray them in bad weather, at dusk, placing the portrait with its back against one of the courtyard walls. Observe the faces of men and women in the streets at dusk, when the weather is bad. How much grace and sweetness is seen in them! So you, painter, will have a courtyard arranged with walls painted black, with a slight overhang of roof above it. And let it be 10 braccia wide, 20 long, and 10 high. And when it is sunny, cover it with a curtain, or portray an hour at dusk, when it is cloudy or foggy. And this is perfect atmosphere.

Because faces from a distance appear dark.

We see clearly that all the resemblances of evident objects, large or small, enter the senses through the dim light of the eye. If the resemblance of the grandeur of heaven and earth passes through such a small entrance, the face of man, amidst such a great resemblance of things, is almost nothing because of the distance that diminishes it, and occupies so little of that light that it remains incomprehensible. And having to pass from the surface to the impressionable through a dark medium, that is, the hollow nerve that appears dark, that species, not being of a powerful color, is tinged in that darkness of the path, and having reached the impressionable, it appears dark. No other reason can be given, if that point is black that is in the light, and it is because it is filled with a transparent horror like air and performs the function of a hole made in a board, and when looked at, it appears black, and things seen through the light and dark air are confused in the darkness.

Like shadows at a long distance.

Shadows are lost at a long distance because the great quantity of luminous air that is found between the eye and the thing seen retains its shadows of that thing in its own color.

Because a man seen at a certain distance

is not recognized.

Diminishing perspective shows us that the further away something is, the smaller it becomes: and if you look at a man a crossbow bolt away from you, and place the window of a small needle close to your eye, you will be able to see many men sending their likenesses to your eye, and at the same time they will all fall into that window. Therefore, if the man a crossbow bolt away sends his likeness to the eye that occupies a small part of a needle window, how will you be able to discern or see the nose or mouth or any part of that body in such a small figure? And if they are not seen, you will not be able to recognize the man who does not show his limbs, which give men different shapes.

Attitude.

The fontanel of the throat falls on the foot, and by throwing an arm forward, the fontanel emerges from that foot; and if the leg goes backwards, the fontanel goes forward, and so it changes in every attitude.
How to depict a fortune.

If you want to depict a fortune well, consider and depict its effects carefully, when the wind, blowing over the surface of the sea and the land, removes and carries away those things that are not stationary with the universal mass. And to depict this fortune well, you will first make the broken and shattered clouds rise up in the wind's path, accompanied by the sandy dust lifted from the seashore, and the branches and leaves, lifted by the force of the wind's fury, scattered through the air and in company with many other light objects; the trees and grass bent to the ground as if they were trying to follow the wind's course, with their branches twisted outside their natural course and their leaves disheveled and upturned. The men who are found there, some fallen and turned over, are almost unknown because of their clothes and the dust, and those who remain standing are then hugging some tree, so that the wind does not tear them; others with their hands covered with dust, bowed to the ground, and their clothes and hair straight in the wind's flow. The troubled and stormy sea is full of churning foam among the high waves, and the wind raises in the conflicting air a finer foam like a thick and enveloping fog. The ships within are some with broken sails and its fragments flapping in the air in the company of some broken ropes, some broken masts fallen with the ship listless and broken among the stormy waves; certain men, shouting, embrace the remainder of the ship. You will make the clouds driven by the impetuous winds, battered against the high mountain peaks, resemble those wrapped back like waves struck against rocks; the air terrifying because of the dark shadows cast in the air by dust, fog, and thick clouds.

On depicting someone speaking

among many people.

You will do what you want him to do among many people: consider the subject matter he is to discuss and accommodate the actions pertaining to that subject matter. That is, if it is persuasive matter, let the actions be relevant; if it is declarative matter for various reasons, let the speaker take a finger of the left with the first two fingers of his right hand, having closed the two smaller ones, and with his face turned readily toward the people, his mouth slightly open so as to appear to be speaking. And if he were sitting, let him appear to raise himself a little upright and forward with his head; and if you make him stand, have him bow his chest and head a little toward the people. They should be depicted as silent and attentive: all looking at the orator in the face with expressions of admiration, and making the mouths of some old man in wonder at the sentences he has heard, keeping their mouths low, drawing many wrinkles back on their cheeks, and with their eyebrows high at the joints, which create many creases on the forehead; some sitting with the fingers of their hands intertwined, hold their tired knee there, others with one knee over the other, on which they hold their hand so that it receives the elbow, from which their hand goes to support the bearded chin of some bowed old man.
On aiding the false relief of painting with artificial light and shadow.

On increasing the relief of painting: you will use a line of clear light between the false figure and the visible object receiving its shadow, dividing the figure from the darkened object, and on the same object you will make two light parts that divide the shadow cast on the wall by the opposing figure. And often use a method of making those limbs that you want to be somewhat distant from their body, especially when the arms cross the chest, so that between the shadow of the arm on the chest and the arm's own shadow, there remains a little light that appears to pass between the space between the chest and the arm. And the further you want the arm to appear from the chest, the greater the light will be. and always try to arrange the bodies in fields such that the dark part of the bodies ends in a bright field, and the illuminated part of the body ends in a dark field.

On Surrounding Bodies

with Various Shade Lines.

Always try to make the shadows cast on the surfaces of bodies by vague objects waver, with various twists, through the variety of the members that cast the shadows and of the thing that receives the shadow.

On the Being of the Shadow in Its Own Right.

Shadow is of the nature of universal things, that all are more powerful at the beginning, and weaken toward the end. I speak of the beginning of every form and quality, evident and inevitable, and not of things brought from a small beginning to great growth by time, as would be a great oak tree, which had a weak beginning from a small acorn. Rather, I would say that the oak is more powerful at the birth it makes of the earth, that is, at its greatest thickness. Therefore, darkness is the first degree of shadow, and light is the last. Therefore, you, painter, will make the shadow darker near its cause, and the end ensure that it converts into light, that is, that it appears endless.

Just as shadows cast by particular lights

must be avoided, because their ends are

similar to beginnings.

The shadows cast by the sun or other particular lights are without grace for the body that is accompanied by them, because they leave the parts confusedly divided, with a clear boundary, of shadow from light, and the shadows are of equal power at the end as at the beginning.
What is shadow and light?

Shadow is the privation of light and the sole opposition of dense bodies to luminous rays. Shadow is the nature of darkness, light is the nature of light. One conceals and the other reveals; they are always joined to bodies, and shadow is more powerful than light, because it prohibits and entirely deprives bodies of light, and light can never completely banish the shadow of bodies, that is, dense bodies.

A body and two shadows:

Separate and joined shadow.

Body and light shadow:

Separate, invisible shadow.

What is the difference between a shadow joined to bodies

and a separate shadow?

A joined shadow is one that never separates from illuminated bodies, such as a ball, which, standing in the light, always has a part of itself occupied by the shadow, which is never divided by any change in location made by the ball. A separate shadow can be created by a body or not.

Let's say that the ball is one arm's length away from a wall, and the light is on the opposite side. The light will cast on the wall exactly as much shadow as is found on the side of the ball facing the wall. The part of the separate shadow that does not appear is when the light is below the ball, because its shadow goes toward the sky and, finding no resistance along the way, is lost.
