Some people believe that a triangle does not cast any shadow on

a wall.

There are some mathematicians who have held that a triangle with its base turned toward the light does not cast any shadow on a wall, which they prove by saying: no spherical body smaller than the light can reach half by shadow. Radiant lines are straight. Therefore let us assume that the light is g h, that the triangle is l m n, and that the wall is i K. Let the light g see the face of the triangle l n and the part of the wall i q, and so h sees, just as g sees the face l m, and then sees m n, and the wall p K; and if the whole wall is seen by the light g h, the triangle must be without shadow, and he who has no shadow cannot cast one; which in this case seems credible, if the triangle n p q were not seen by the two lights g, h: but i p and likewise q K, each one is not seen by itself except by a single light, that is, i p cannot be seen by h, q K will never be seen by g, therefore p q will be twice as bright as two visible spaces that hold shadow.
A Method of Increasing and Arousing the Mind

to Various Inventions.

I will not fail to include among these precepts a new speculative invention, which, although it may seem trivial and almost laughable, is nevertheless of great use in arousing the mind to various inventions. And this is: if you look at some walls smeared with various stains or stones of various mixed materials, if you were to invent some site, you will be able to see there the resemblance of different landscapes adorned with mountains, rivers, rocks, trees, large plains, valleys, and hills in various ways. You will also be able to see various battles and ready-made figures, strange expressions of faces and clothing, and an infinite number of things, which you will be able to reduce to a complete and good form. And in such walls and mixtures it happens as if the sound of bells were ringing, that in their tolling you will find every name and word you can imagine.

Of the 10 functions of the eye,

all pertaining to painting.

Painting encompasses all 10 functions of the eye: darkness, light, body and color, figure and place, relocation and proximity, motion and stillness. This little work of mine will be woven from these functions, reminding the painter of the rules and methods he should use to imitate all these things in his art, the work of nature and the ornament of the world.

How the painter should practice

color perspective.

To demonstrate this perspective of varying and losing or diminishing the true essence of colors, you will take objects placed in the countryside, at a distance of 100 yards, such as trees, houses, men, and places. And as for the first dawn, you will have a very firm glass, and so let your eye be firm; and on the said glass draw a tree over its shape, then move it so far across that the natural tree almost borders on your drawing. Then color your drawing so that in color and shape they are comparable to each other, and that both, closing one eye, appear painted on the said glass and at the same distance. And follow the same rule for the second and third trees, one hundred and one hundred braccia apart. And keep these as your guides and masters, always working on your works, wherever they belong, and they will help you to escape the work. But I find a rule that the second is 4/5 smaller than the first, when it is 20 braccia away from the first.

On the winding and balancing of figures

and other animals.

Whatever figure you make, gentle animal, remember to avoid the woody, that is, that they counterbalance and balance each other in such a way that they do not seem like a piece of wood.

Those who want to appear strong, do not make them so, except by turning their heads on their shoulders.
On Linear Perspective1.

Linear perspective, in the sphere of visual lines, attempts to prove by measurement how much the second thing is smaller than the first, and how much the third is smaller than the second, and so on, step by step, up to the end of the objects seen. I find by experience that if the second thing is as distant from the first as the first is from your eye, even though they are of equal size, the second will be equally smaller than the first. And if the third thing, of equal size to the second and the first2 in front of it, is as far from the second as the second is from the first3, it will be half the size of the second; and so, step by step, for equal distances, the second will always be half the size of the first, provided that the interval does not exceed 20 arms. And within 20 of the said braccia, the figure similar to you will lose 4/5 of its size, and within 40 it will lose 9/10, and then 19/20 in 60 braccia, and so on, gradually decreasing, making the wall distant from you twice your size, since making only one makes a great difference from the first braccia to the second.

On placing a figure first in the scene.

The first figure in the scene you will make smaller than life-size, the more braccia you depict it distant from the first line, and then place the others in comparison with it according to the rule above.

I assign the degrees of things opposite to the eye,

just as the musician assigns the degrees of voices opposite to the ear.

Although things opposite to the eye touch each other hand to hand, I will nevertheless make my rule twenty by twenty, as the musician did among the voices, who, although united and attached to each other, nevertheless placed degrees from voice to voice, calling them first, second, third, fourth, and fifth; and thus, step by step, he gave names to the varieties of raising and lowering the voice.

Method of making the shadow accompany the light and the body for figures.

When you make a figure and you want to see if the shadow is a companion of the light, that it is not more red or yellow than the nature of the being of the color you wish to shade, you will do this. Cast a shadow with your finger on the lighted part, and if the accidental shadow you cast is similar to the natural shadow cast by your finger on your work, it will be fine; and then with your finger closer or further away make darker or lighter shadows, which you always compare with yours.
How the limbs must be supported by the bending and swaying of their limbs.

Bent arm, with:

From b to is a head, and so from c to 2. And this happens when the elbow forms a right angle.

Double cone with a common base placed between two lights:

Just as two lights that place in the middle a body shaped on two sides like a pyramid of low pyramids leave it without a shadow.

Because the eye, having seen the light, the place of the middle light appears dark, and similarly, having emerged from the darkness, the place of the middle light appears very clear.

Because the thing placed close to the eye leaves its edges indiscernible.

Two 'things opposite to the eye', with:

All those things opposite to the eye, which are too close to it, must have their edges confused in discernment, as happens with things close to the light that cast a large and blurred shadow. So does this, which, when judging things in the open, in all cases of perspective, the line is similar to the light. And the reason is that the eye creates a master line, which by distance enlarges and encompasses with true knowledge large things from afar, as well as small things from nearby. But because the eye sends forth a multitude of lines surrounding this principal one in the middle, and those which are farthest from the center in its circulation are less capable of perceiving the truth, it happens that the thing placed near the eye, at that distance, is not so close to the main line as to comprehend the boundaries of that thing, it follows that these boundaries fall into lines of weak comprehension, which are to the eye's function like hunting dogs which, when they remove the prey and cannot catch it, so these cannot catch it, but are the cause of the main line turning towards the things removed from these lines. Hence the things whose boundaries are judged by these lines are confused.
On the Way to Learn Well by Heart.

When you want to know something well studied by heart, follow this method. That is, when you have drawn the same thing so many times that you feel like you have it in your head, try doing it without a model. Polish your model on a thin, flat piece of glass and place it over the thing you made without the model. Note carefully where the polish does not clash with your drawing, and where you find a mistake. Remember not to err there again; instead, return to the model and draw the incorrect part so many times that you have it firmly in your imagination. And if you cannot get flat glass to polish something, take a very thin, well-greased kid paper and then dry it. Once you have used it for one drawing, you can erase it with a sponge and make the second.

On the Way to Draw a Correct Place.

Take a glass of glass the size of a half-sheet of paper, and hold it firmly in front of your eyes, that is, between your eye and the object you wish to portray. Then place your eye two-thirds of a braccio away from the glass and steady your head with an instrument so that you cannot move your head at all. Then close or cover one eye, and with a brush and a ground pencil mark on the glass what appears through it. Then polish it with glass paper and dust it on good paper, and paint it, if you like, then using airy perspective well.

To learn how to do a good pose.

If you want to master the straight and straight poses of figures, hold a frame, or a canvas framed with a ruler, between your eye and the nude you wish to portray, and draw the same frames on the paper where you wish to portray the nude, subtly. Then place a ball of wax on one side of the net to serve as a target, which, as you look at the nude, you will always hit against the throat, and if he were facing backwards, hit against one of the knots of the neck. And these lines will show you all the parts of the body, which in each position are found under the throat, under the corners of the shoulders, under the breasts, hips, and other parts of the body, and the transverse lines of the net will show you how much higher he is when resting on one leg than the other, and likewise the hips, knees, and feet. But always hold the net perpendicularly, and in fact, all the parts you see that the nude takes from the net, make your drawn nude take from the drawn net. The drawn frames can be as much smaller than those of the net as you want your figure to be smaller than the natural one. Then, in the figures you will make, keep in mind the rule for the clash of the limbs, as the net showed you, which must be 3 and a half arms high and 3 wide, 7 arms away from you, and approximately one arm from the naked.
4 - 41 We know well that he who is practical and good will not make such errors, but rather, with good rules, will remove so little at a time that he will finish his work well. Even the sculptor, if he works in clay or wax, can remove and add; and when it is finished, he can easily cast it in bronze; and this is the last and most permanent operation that sculpture has, because that which is only marble is subject to ruin, and not bronze. Therefore, that painting done in copper which can be removed and added, as I told you about painting, is equal to bronze, because when you first made the work in wax, it could also be removed and added. If this sculpture in bronze is eternal, this one in copper and glass is most eternal. If bronze remains black and ugly, this one is full of various and beautiful colors and infinite varieties of which as above. And if you wished to speak only of painting done on panel, I am content to give the verdict on this with sculpture, saying that painting is more beautiful, more imaginative, and more copious, and sculpture more durable, and has nothing else. Sculpture shows what it is with little effort; painting seems miraculous in making impalpable things appear palpable, flat things in relief, and near things distant. In fact, painting is adorned with infinite speculations that sculpture does not employ.

Just as the mirror is the master of painters.

When you want to see if your painting as a whole conforms to what is portrayed from life, take a mirror and have the living object reflected in it, and compare the mirrored object with your painting, and consider carefully whether the subject of both similarities conforms together. And above all, the mirror must be taken as its master, that is, the flat mirror, because on its surface things have a resemblance to painting in many parts. That is, you see painting done on a flat surface showing things that appear raised, and the mirror on a flat surface does the same. Painting is a single surface, and the mirror is the same. Painting is impalpable, in that what appears round and distinct cannot be surrounded by the hands, and the mirror does the same. The mirror and painting show the resemblances of things surrounded by shadow and light; both appear far beyond their surfaces; and if you know that the mirror, by means of its lines, shadows, and lights, makes things appear distinct to you, and if you have among your colors shadows and lights that are more powerful than those of the mirror, certainly, if you know how to compose them well together, your painting will also appear like a natural thing seen in a large mirror.
Of the sad excuse made by those who falsely

and unworthily call themselves painters.

There is a certain generation of painters, who, because of their lack of study, must live under the beauty of gold and azure, who with utter foolishness allege that they fail to produce good works because of poor payments, which they would still know how to do as well as anyone else, if they were well paid. Now look at these foolish people! These people do not know how to hold up some work as good, saying: "This deserves a good reward, and this is mediocre, and this is of good quality," and show that their work deserves every reward.

Just as sculpture requires less ingenuity

than painting and lacks many natural qualities.

I apply myself no less to sculpture than to painting, and since I do both to the same degree, it seems to me with little imputation that I can judge which requires greater ingenuity, difficulty, and perfection than the other. First, sculpture is subjected to certain lights, that is, from above, and painting brings with it light and shadow everywhere: light and shadow are therefore the importance of sculpture. The sculptor in this case is aided by the nature of the relief, which generates it by itself; and the painter, by accidental art, creates it in places where nature would reasonably do so. The sculptor cannot diversify himself in the various natures of the colors of objects, painting is not lacking in any part; the perspectives of sculptors do not appear at all true, those of the painter seem hundreds of miles beyond the work; aerial perspective is distant from their work; they cannot represent transparent bodies, they cannot represent luminous ones, nor can they represent refracted lines, nor shiny bodies, such as mirrors and similar shining objects, nor fogs, nor dark times, nor an infinite number of things that must not be mentioned so as not to bore. What it has, that it is more resistant to time, although painting done on thick copper, covered with white enamel and, over that, painted with enamel colors and fired again, has similar resistance, this surpasses sculpture forever. It might be said that where they make a mistake, it is not easy to fix it: this is a sad argument for wanting to prove that an irremediable forgetfulness makes the work more worthy.

But I will say indeed that the master's ingenuity will be more difficult to fix someone who makes such errors than to repair the work spoiled by them.
On Aerial Perspective.

Buildings projecting above the line of the city walls:

Here is another perspective, which I call aerial, because through the variation of the air one can discern the different distances of various buildings whose origins lie on a single line. It would be like seeing many buildings beyond a wall, all of which appeared the same size above the edge of that wall, and you wanted to make one appear further away than the other in a painting. You must depict a somewhat thick air. You know that in such air, the furthest things seen, such as mountains, because of the great quantity of air between your eye and the mountain, the mountain appears blue, almost the color of the air, when the sun is in the east. Therefore, you will make the first building on that wall its color, and the furthest one less outlined and more blue. Whatever you want to be equally farther away, make equally bluer. Whatever you want to be five times as far away, make five times as bluer. And this rule will ensure that buildings, if they appear to be of the same size on a line, will clearly recognize which is more distant and which is larger than the others.

Just as a painter cannot be praised,

if he is not universal.

Some can clearly be said to be mistaken who call a good master a painter who only paints a head or a figure well. Certainly, it is not a great thing for a painter who studies only one thing, or his lifetime, not to achieve some perfection. But knowing that painting embraces and contains within itself all that nature produces and that the accidental action of men conducts, and ultimately what can be comprehended by the eye, it seems to me a poor master who paints only one figure well. Now don't you see how many and what kind of acts are performed by men alone? Don't you see how many different animals, trees, herbs, flowers, varieties of mountainous and plain sites, fountains, rivers, cities, public and private buildings, instruments suitable for human use, various clothes and ornaments and arts? All these things belong to being, of equal operation and quality, used by what you wish to call a good painter.

On portraiture.

Which is better, to portray from nature or from the ancient? Or which is more laborious, profiles or shadows or lights.
Of studying until you wake up,

or before you fall asleep in bed in the dark.

I have found it quite useful, when you find yourself in bed in the dark, to use your imagination to repeat the superficial outlines of forms previously studied, or other notable things understood through subtle speculation. And this is precisely a praiseworthy and useful act for confirming things in the memory.

Just as the painter must be eager to hear,

when creating his work, the judgment of every man.

Certainly, while a man paints, everyone's judgment should not be ignored, since we clearly understand that a man, even if he is not a painter, has a true understanding of the other man's form and will judge well whether he is hunchbacked, or has one shoulder high or low, or whether he has a big mouth or nose, or other defects. And if we know that men can truly judge the works of nature, how much more should we confess that they can judge our own errors, for you know how much man is mistaken in his own works; and if you do not recognize this in yourself, consider it in others, and you will profit from their errors. So be patient in listening to the opinions of others, and consider carefully whether the critic has reason to criticize you or not; and if you find so, correct it; and if you find otherwise, pretend you did not understand him, or show him by reason. If he is a man whom you esteem, reason, like him, is mistaken.

As in works of importance,

a man should not trust his memory so much

that he does not deign to draw from nature.

Any master who attempted to imagine that he could capture within himself all the forms and effects of nature would certainly seem to me to be possessed of great ignorance, since the said effects are infinite and our memory is not capable of sufficient capacity. Therefore, painter, be careful that the greed for gain does not overcome the honor of your art, for the gain of honor is much greater than the honor of riches. So for these and other reasons that could be mentioned, you will first devote yourself to drawing, with demonstrable form to the eye, the intention and invention first formed in your imagination; then proceed to subtract and place until you are satisfied; then arrange the men, clothed or naked, in the manner you have planned for the work, and make sure, through measurement and size subject to perspective, that nothing of the work appears that is not well advised by reason and natural effects. And this will be the way to gain honor for your art.

Whatever is painted in black and white will appear in better relief than anything else, and therefore I remind you, painter, to dress your figures in the lightest colors possible, for if you paint them in dark colors, they will have little relief and little clarity from a distance. And this is because the shadows of all things are dark; and if you paint a dark dress, there will be little difference between the lights and the shadows, and in light colors there will be a great difference.
On how to memorize

the shape of a face.

If you want to easily memorize the expression of a face, first memorize many heads, eyes, noses, mouths, chins, throats, necks, and shoulders. For example, noses come in 10 shapes: straight, humped, hollow, with a protrusion higher or lower than the middle, aquiline, even, sharp, round, and pointed: these are good in terms of profile. Facially, noses come in 11 shapes: even, thick in the middle, thin in the middle, with a thick tip and thin at the base, thin at the tip and thick at the base, with broad noses, narrow noses, high noses, and low noses, with open holes and holes filled by the tip. And so you will find diversity in the other details, which you must portray from life and commit to memory. Or, when you have to paint a face from memory, carry with you a small notebook where similar features are noted. And when you have glanced at the face of the person you want to portray, you will then look in part to see which nose or mouth resembles them, and make a small mark there to recognize them later at home. I won't speak of monstrous faces, because they can be easily memorized.

Of the games that designers should play.

When you, designers, want to find some useful amusement with games, you should always use things that are relevant to your profession: that is, to develop a good eye for judgment, to know how to judge the truth of the widths and lengths of things. And to accustom your mind to such things, let one of you draw a straight line at random on a wall, and each of you hold a thin twig or straw in your hand, and each cut his own to the length that seems to him to be the first line, standing 10 braccia away. Then each of you go to the model to measure his own judgemental measure against it; and the one whose measure comes closest to the length of the model will be the superior and victorious and will win the prize previously assigned by you. You should also take foreshortened measures, that is, take a dart or other reed and look in front of you at a certain distance, and each one with his own judgement estimate how many times that measure fits into that distance. Also, whoever draws a line of one braccio best will be tested with a drawn line; and similar games are an opportunity to develop good visual judgment, which is the principal act of painting.

Whether it is better to draw in company or not.

I say and confirm that drawing in company is much better than alone for many reasons. The first is that you will be ashamed of being seen in the crowd of draftsmen, being inadequate, and this shame will be a reason for good study. Secondly, good envy will spur you to be among those more praised than you, since the praise of others will spur you on. The second is that you will take on the traits of those who do better than you, and if you are better than the others, you will benefit from avoiding their shortcomings, and the praise of others will increase your virtue.
And if you want company, take it for its study. This can be beneficial to you through the enrichment that comes from various speculations. Any other company could be harmful.

When should one study the choice of things?

Young people should spend their winter vigils studying the things prepared for the summer, that is, gather together all the nudes you took in the summer and select the best limbs and bodies from them, and put them into practice and in mind.

On attitudes.

Then, the following summer, you will choose someone who is well-dressed and who has not been raised in doublets, so that his figure is not strange to his nature, and you will have him perform graceful and gallant actions. And if this does not clearly show the muscles inside the limbs, it matters nothing; it is enough to have good posture from this alone, and to reconcile the limbs with those you studied last winter.

How it is necessary for a painter to know

the intrinsic form of man.

The painter who has knowledge of the nature of nerves, muscles, and tendons will know well how many and which nerves are responsible for moving a limb, and which muscle, when deflated, causes that nerve to contract, and which cords, converted into very thin cartilage, surround and gather that muscle. And thus he will be a diverse and universal demonstrator of various muscles through the various effects of the figures, and will not do as many do, who in different poses always demonstrate the same things in the arms, backs, chests, and legs. These things should not be considered among the minor errors.

On the selection of beautiful faces.

It seems to me no small grace that of that painter who gives beautiful expressions to his figures, a grace which those who do not possess by nature can acquire through accidental study in this form. Be careful to remove the good parts of many beautiful faces, which are confirmed by public fame rather than by your own judgment, because you could deceive yourself by removing faces that had a conformity with your own, because it often seems that similar conformities please us. And if you were ugly, you would choose faces that are not beautiful and you would make ugly faces, like many painters, whose figures often resemble the master; so take the beauties, as I say, and put them in mind.
On the Way to Learn to Compose Figures Well in Stories

1.

When you have learned perspective well, and have memorized all the members and bodies of things, be often tempted, in your leisure, to see and consider the positions and actions of men as they speak, argue, laugh, or fight together; what actions they have, what actions the surrounding dividers or viewers of these things perform; and note them with brief signs (small figure of a man) in this form in a small notebook of yours, which you should always carry with you, and which should be of colored paper, so that you do not have to erase it but change from old to new; for these are not things to be erased, but rather to be preserved with great diligence, because the forms and actions of things are so infinite that the memory is not capable of retaining them. Hence you will reserve these as your masters and teachers.

How diligence must be learned first

than memory.

When you, as a designer, wish to undertake a good and useful study, practice drawing slowly and judging which and how many lights have the first degree of clarity, and similarly, among the shadows, which are darker than the others and how they blend together. Compare the quantities one with the other, and which side the lines point toward, and how much of the lines bend in one direction or another, and where more or less evident, and how broad or thin; and finally, make sure that your shadows and lights are blended without lines or smoke-like marks. And once you have trained your hand and your judgment to this diligence, you will be done so quickly that you will not even notice.

Of the painter's life in his studio.

So that the prosperity of the body does not spoil that of the mind, the painter or draftsman must be solitary, especially when he is intent on the speculation and consideration that, continually appearing before the eyes, provide material for the memory to be well reserved. And if you are alone, you will be all yours, and if you are accompanied by a single companion, you will be half yours, and the less so the greater the indiscretion of his practice; and if you are with more, you will fall into a similar inconvenience. And if you were to say: "I will do it my way, I will withdraw to be able to better speculate on the forms of natural things," I say this can be ill done, because you could not help but often lend an ear to their chatter; and if you could not serve two gentlemen, you would poorly perform the duty of the company and even worse the effect of the speculation of art. And if you say, "I will withdraw so far that their words will not reach me and will not hinder me," I tell you that in this respect you will be considered mad. But you see, by doing so, you would still be alone.
On Judging Your Painting.

We know clearly that errors are more noticeable in other people's works than in your own, and often by criticizing others' small errors, you will ignore your own major ones. And to avoid such ignorance, first make sure you are a good perspective artist, then have a thorough knowledge of the measurements of men and other animals; and also a good architect, that is, insofar as it pertains to the shape of buildings and other things on earth, which are infinite in form. The more knowledge you have, the more praiseworthy your work will be; and in those you are not experienced with, do not refuse to portray them from life. But to return to the promise above, I say that in your painting, you must hold a flat mirror and often look at your work in it, which will be seen from the opposite direction and will appear to you to be from the hand of another master, and there you will judge the errors better than otherwise. And it is also good to often get up and take a little other amusement, because in returning to things you have better judgment, whereas remaining fixed on the work makes you very deceived. It is also good to step away, because the work appears smaller and the more it is understood at a glance, the better one recognizes the discordant and disproportionate members and colors of things.

What rule should be given to child painters?

We clearly know that sight is one of the [most] rapid operations there is, and in a moment it sees infinite forms, yet it understands only one thing at a time. Let us suppose. You, reader, will look at this entire written page at a glance, and immediately judge it to be full of various letters, but you will not know at this time what letters they are or what they mean, so you must go word by word, line by line, to gain knowledge of these letters. Again, if you wish to ascend to the height of a building, you must ascend step by step; otherwise, it will be impossible to reach its height. So I say to you, whom nature directs to this art: if you wish to have a true understanding of the forms of things, begin with their details and do not proceed to the second unless you first have the first well memorized and practiced. If you do otherwise, you will waste time or indeed greatly prolong the study. And remember that you learn diligence before alacrity.
On the Convention of the Limbs.

And I also remind you to take great care in assigning limbs to figures that, after being consistent with the size of the body, also correspond to the age. That is, in young people, limbs with few muscles and veins and delicate, rounded surfaces, of a pleasing color; in men, they should be sinewy and full of muscles; in old people, they should have wrinkled, rough, and veiny surfaces, and very evident nerves.

Just as cherubs have joints

contrary to men in their thickness.

Small cherubs have all their joints thin, and the spaces between them are large. And this happens because the skin above the joints is alone without any other pulp, and is of the nature of a sinew that surrounds and binds the bones together, and the fleshy substance is found between one joint and another, enclosed between the skin and the bone. But because the bones are thicker at the joints than between the joints, as a man grows the flesh sheds that excess that was between the skin and the bone, so the skin comes closer to the bone and ends up thinning the limbs; and above the joints, because there is only the cartilaginous and sinewy skin, it cannot dry out, and by not drying out, it does not shrink; hence for these reasons children are thin at the joints and thick between the joints, as can be seen in the joints of the fingers, arms, and shoulders, which are thin and have hollow cavities; and man, on the contrary, is thick in all joints—fingers, arms, legs—and where children have holes, they have relief.

Of the different sizes that exist between children and men.

Between men and children, I find a great difference in length from one joint to the other; for a man has two heads at a time from the shoulder joint to the elbow, from the elbow to the tip of the big toe, and from one shoulder joint to the other; and a child has one, because nature assigns to us the size of the house of the intellect before that of the vital spirits.

On giving light.

First, it gives a universal shadow for the entire containing part that does not see the light, then it gives it intermediate and principal shadows in comparison with one another; and so it gives the containing light of the intermediate light, then giving it the middle and principal shadows in similar comparison.
How to make a head so that its parts

concur with the appropriate straightness.

Figure of a head divided by parallel lines:

To make a head so that its limbs concur with the rotation and bending of a head, follow these guidelines. You know that eyes, eyebrows, bridges of the nose, the edges of the mouth and the sides of the chin, jaw, cheeks, ears, and all parts of a face are placed at equal straightness on the face. Therefore, when you have made the face, draw lines that pass from one corner of the eye to the other, and so on along the straightness of each limb. And, drawing the ends of these lines from the two sides of the face, see if the space in the same parallel is equal on the right and left. But I remind you carefully that you should have these lines drawn at the point of your view.

How to represent the 18 operations of man.

Firmness, movement, course. Standing, leaning, sitting, bending, kneeling, adjacent, suspended.

Carrying, being carried, pushing, pulling, hitting, being hit, burdening, and lifting.

You will first discuss the lights emitted by windows, which you will call 'constrained air'. Then discuss the lights of the countryside, which you will call 'free light'. Next, discuss the light of luminous bodies.

How you should make a simulated animal appear natural.

You know that no animal can be made without its limbs, each of which in itself resembles some other animal. So if you want to make a simulated animal appear natural, let's say a snake, take the head of a male or a hound, the eyes of a cat, the ears of a porcupine, the nose of a greyhound, the eyebrows of a lion, the temples of an old rooster, and the neck of a water turtle.

On portraying something.

When you portray and move some beginning of line, make sure that you look throughout the body you are portraying, to see anything that clashes with the straightness of the beginning of line.
How a figure will not be praiseworthy if it does not exhibit an action that best expresses the passion of the soul.

A figure is more praiseworthy if its action best expresses the passion of its soul.

How to portray an angry figure.

You will have someone hold the angry figure by the hair, with his head bowed to the ground and one knee on his side, and with his right arm he will raise his fist high. This person will have his hair raised, his eyebrows low and close together, his teeth clenched, and the two corners of his mouth arched. His neck will be thick and wrinkled in front, from leaning toward the enemy.

How to portray a man in despair.

You will have the man in despair reach for a knife and have his clothes torn with his hands, and one of those hands will be used to tear his wound; and make it with the feet apart and the legs somewhat bent, and the body similarly facing the ground with the hair torn and scattered.

On the grace of the limbs.

The limbs of the body must be gracefully arranged to suit the effect you want the figure to achieve; and if you want to create a figure that demonstrates gracefulness, you must make the limbs graceful and relaxed, without displaying too many muscles. The few muscles that you do display for the purpose should be soft, that is, with little emphasis, with the shadows not harsh, and the limbs, especially the arms, should be disjointed (small figure of an arm), that is, so that no limb is not in a straight line with the limb that joins it. And if the hip, the pole of the man, is found, for posing, to be made so that the right is higher than the left, you will make the joint of the upper shoulder fall in a perpendicular line above the most prominent object of the hip; and let the right shoulder be lower than the left, and the fontanelle always be higher than the middle of the joint of the upper foot that is resting; the leg that is not resting should have its knee lower than the other and close to the other leg. The attitudes of the head and arms are infinite, therefore I will not abstain from giving some rules, provided that they are easy and pleasing with various twists and wriggles, with the joints disjointed for this purpose not like pieces of wood.

How a separated shadow will never be similar

in size to its cause.

If the luminous rays are, as experience confirms, caused by a single point, and in a circular course from that point they disintegrate and scatter through the air, the further they move, the more they spread; and the thing placed between the light and the wall is always cast a larger shadow, because the rays that touch it, once their confluence reaches the wall, become wider.
On the Comfort of the Limbs.

Regarding the comfort of these limbs, you should consider this: when you want to represent someone who, for some reason, must turn backward or to one side, you should not have the feet and all the limbs move in the same direction as the head. Instead, you should divide this movement into four joints: the foot and knee, the hip, and the neck. And if you stand on the right leg, you should bend the left knee inward, and the foot should be slightly raised, the left shoulder slightly lower than the right, and the nape of the neck should meet the same place where the ball of the left foot is turned, and the left shoulder should be above the tip of the right foot, a perpendicular line. And always use figures that where the head is turned, the chest does not turn, since nature, for our convenience, has made the neck easily adaptable to the different desires of the eye, to turn in various places; and the other joints are partly obedient to this same thing.

And if you make a man sitting, and his arms sometimes have to work on something transverse, make the chest turn over the hip joint.

Of the shadow cast by a body situated

between two equal lights.

Two lights equidistant from a central line:

A body placed between two equal lights will cast two equal shadows, which will be directed in a straight line toward the two lights. If you move the body and place it closer to one of the lights, the shadow directed toward the closer light will be less obscure than the shadow directed toward the farther light.

The body closest to the light

casts a larger shadow, and why?

If an object placed opposite a particular light is very close, you will see it cast a very large shadow on the opposite wall, and the further you move the object from the light, the smaller the shadow will be.

Because a shadow that is greater than its cause

is cast in discordant proportion.

The discrepancy in the proportion of the shadow, greater than its cause, arises because the light, being smaller than the object, cannot be equally distant from the object's extremity, and that part that is more distant grows more than the adjacent one, and therefore grows more.

Because the shadow is greater than its cause

has confused edges.

The air that surrounds the light is almost of the same nature as that light in brightness and heat, and the further it moves, the more it loses its resemblance. The thing that casts a large shadow is close to the light and is illuminated by the light and the luminous air, so this air leaves the edges of the shadow confused.

How high point 1 should be placed.

Point 2 should be as high as the eye of a common man, and the highest point of the plain that borders the sky should be made at the height of the boundary between the flat land and the sky, except for the mountains, which are free.

How to depict a battle.

First, you will depict the smoke from the artillery mixed in the air together with the gunpowder stirred by the movement of the cavalry and the combatants, which mixture you will use as follows. The gunpowder, because it is an earthly and weighty substance, and although due to its fineness it easily rises and mixes with the air, nevertheless willingly returns to the bottom, and its highest point is formed by the thinnest part; therefore, it will be seen less and will appear almost the color of air. The smoke that mixes with the dusty air, the higher it rises, will appear like dark clouds, and the smoke will be visible at the top more clearly than the dust. The smoke will have a somewhat blue color, and the dust will fade to its color. From the side where the light comes, this mixture of air, smoke, and dust will appear much brighter than from the opposite side. The longer the combatants are in this turbulence, the less visible they will be, and the difference between their lights and their shadows will be less. You will make the faces, the people, and the air red, and the gunners and their neighbors; and the said redness, the further it distances itself from its cause, the more it fades, and the figures that are between you and the light, being distant, will appear dark against a bright background, and the closer their legs are to the ground, the less visible they will be, because the dust is coarser and thicker there. And if you make horses running out of the crowd, make the little clouds of dust distant from each other, as far as the interval between the horse's leaps can be; and the cloud that is furthest from the said horse will be less visible, indeed it will be high, scattered and sparse, and the one closest to it will be more evident, smaller and denser. Let the air be filled with lightning of various kinds: some rising, some descending, some on a flat line, and the bullets of the guns be accompanied by some smoke in their wake; and you will make the first figures dusty, the hair and eyelashes and other flat places suitable for holding the dust. You will make the winners running with their hair and other light things scattered in the wind, with their eyelashes low3,
How small figures [should] not

be finished.

I say that things that appear minute will happen because the thing is far from the eye. This being so, there must be a lot of air between the eye and the object, and the large amount of air impedes the clarity of the form of these objects, making the minute particles of these bodies indiscernible and unrecognizable. Therefore, you, painter, will make the small figures only hinted at and not finished. If you do otherwise, you will counterfeit the effects of nature, your teacher.

The thing remains small because of the great distance between the eye and the object. The great distance encloses within itself a great deal of air. The large amount of air forms within itself a large body, which impedes and removes from the eye the minute particles of objects.

What space should the painter use

for his works?

Since experience shows that all bodies are surrounded by shadow and light, you, painter, must arrange that the illuminated part ends in something dark, and likewise the shadowed part of the body ends in something light. And this rule will greatly improve the clarity of your figures.

On portraying.

When you have to portray from life, stand away three times the size of the object you are portraying.

On depicting a wild place.

Trees and grasses that are more ramified with thin branches should have less darkness of shadow. The tree and grasses that have larger leaves will be the cause of greater shadow.

On shadow.

Where the shadow borders the light, consider where it is lighter or darker and where it is more or less smoky toward the light. And above all, I remind you not to make shadows as defined in young people as you do with stone, because the flesh retains a little transparency, as you see when looking at a hand placed between the eye and the sun, which appears red and luminous; and you will place the most colorful part between the lights and the shadows. And if you want to see what shade is needed for your flesh, cast a shadow on it with your finger and, according to whether it is lighter or darker, hold your finger closer or further from your painting, and it will imitate it.
How should one know which part of the body is more or less luminous than the others?

Head in profile with external lines converging on:

If there is light and the head, the body will be illuminated by it, and that part of the head that receives the beam above it between more equal angles will be more illuminated, and that part that receives the beams between less equal angles will be less luminous. And this light performs its function similarly to the blow, because the blow that falls between equal angles will be initially powerful, and when it falls between unequal angles, it will be less powerful than the first, the more unequal the angles are. For example: if you throw a ball at a wall, the ends of which are equidistant from you, the blow will fall between equal angles; and if you throw the ball at the said wall from one of its ends, the ball will fall at unequal angles, and the shot will not land.

How to Light Figures 1.

Light should be used according to the natural setting where you imagine your figure to be. That is, if you represent it in the sun, make the shadows dark and create large areas of light, and cast the shadows of all the surrounding bodies and their shadows on the ground. And if you represent it in bad weather, make little difference between the lights and the shadows, and do not cast any other shadows at the feet. And if you represent it indoors, make a great difference between the lights and the shadows, and a shadow on the ground; and if you represent a curtained window and a white house, make little difference between the lights and the shadows. And if it is illuminated by fire, you will make the lights reddish and powerful, and the shadows dark, and the cast of the shadows on the walls or ground be finite, and the further it is from the body, the larger and larger it becomes. And if it were illuminated partly by fire and partly by air, make the air's light more powerful, and the fire's light almost red, resembling fire. And above all, make sure that your painted figures have a strong, high light—that is, the living ones you portray—because the people you see in the streets all have the light from above, and know that no one you know so well would have difficulty recognizing them if you were to give them the light from below.

Order of portraying.

On portraying. First, portray drawings by a good master, done by art, from life, not by practice; then in relief, accompanied by the drawing drawn from that relief; then in good natural light, which you must put into use.

How high the light should be for portraying

naturally.

The light for portraying naturally should be from the north; do not change this; And if you do it at midday, keep the window covered, so that the sun shines on it all day, without making any changes. The height of the light must be so positioned that each body casts its shadow on the ground as far as its height.

Just as the beauty of color must lie in the lights.

If we see the quality of colors being recognized by the light, we can conclude that where there is more light, there the true quality of the illuminated color is more clearly seen, and where there is more darkness, the color is tinged with the color of that darkness. Therefore, you, painter, remember to show the truth of colors on the illuminated parts.
Of Shadow and Light.

Every part of the surface surrounding bodies is transformed into part of the color of the object it is placed against.

If you place a spherical body between various objects—that is, on one side is the light of the sun, on the opposite side is a wall illuminated by the sun, which may be green or another color, the plane on which it rests is red, and the two transverse sides are dark—you will see the natural color of the body participate in the colors that are its objects. The most powerful will be the luminous one; the second will be that of the illuminated wall, the third that of the shadow. Then there remains a quantity that participates in the color of the edges.

On the quality of the air, shadows, and lights.

That body will have the greatest difference between the shadows and the lights, which is seen by a greater light, such as sunlight or, at night, firelight. And this is of little use in painting, because the works remain crude and without grace.

That body found in medium light will have little difference between the lights and the shadows. And this happens at dusk or when it is cloudy; and these works are soft and graceful, every quality of face. So in everything the extremes are vicious: too much light makes one crude, too dark prevents one from seeing, the middle is good.

If you want to divide a circle into 8 equal parts without closing the sixth, you know that from 6 to 8 is a third of 6. Therefore, since the opening of the sixth with which you made the circle is a sixth part of that circle, you will divide that sixth part into 4, and 3/4 of this sixth circle will be an eighth part of the whole. To divide this sixth part into 4 parts, you will do this: once you have made your circle, without moving the sixths of its opening, place one of its points at point a, and by moving the other point, you will make the line b c; and, placing the point at c, make the line a d with the other. Then place the tip of these six points at b and draw the line d and a, then draw the line d and f, and from a [a] f there is 1/4 of the line a c. Therefore, by the reasons given above, if a c divided into 4 contains within itself the 4 twenty-fourths, similarly...3

But to better prove the above reasons, if your circle were divided into 24 parts, a c, which is the sixth part of that circle, contains within itself 4, which says: 4 times 6, 24; f c contains within itself 3, which 8 times 3 similarly makes 24. Therefore you have here 3 differences of divisions in a circle without opening or closing the sixths. Just as a f is one twenty-fourth of the circle, f c is 1/8 of the circle, a c is precisely 1/6. Method of measuring heights, widths, and distances without moving a foot. Place a perfect square on the ground, as shown above; then place your eye on the corner m and look toward the foot of the tower, from which you want to know the distance, and as much as b a enters a c, so much does m n enter n f. And if you want to know, without moving yourself or your square, the true height of the tower, you will do this. Place your eye on the corner n, and look at the top of the tower p, and as much as b c enters c n, so much does p f enter f n; And knowing by the first measurement the true distance between f and n, you will be able to know how much the tower fits inside it: that is, if b a fits three times into a m, so m n fits three times into n f, and if m n is one braccio distant, n f will be 3 braccia; and knowing this, you will then be able to know if b c fits twice into c n, so p f fits twice into f n. Now you know by the first measurement that f n is 3 braccia, and if p f fits twice into these 3 braccia, it comes to be exactly one and a half braccia. And this is a just and good rule.

Double file of horsemen across a river:

If the river is dangerous because of its course, two files of horses should be placed across the river, spaced 6 braccia apart. The horses should be placed so close together that they almost touch each other; and the line or troop of horses should be with their heads turned toward the rushing water. This is done only to push back and break the force of the water. And between the two lines, armed and unarmed soldiers pass. The upper line should consist of the largest cavalry to better break the force of the river, the lower line to support the soldiers if they fall and to provide support for them as they cross.
Of weights.

I ask: if a weight of one pound, falling two cubits, sticks a span into the ground, how much will it stick if it falls 40 cubits? Or how much will a weight of two pounds stick if it falls two cubits?

It is also asked: if this weight is a quantity wide, and if that quantity is doubled by the same weight and falls the same height, how much more will the smaller width stick than the larger, the ground being of equal resistance.

Paves are made to ward off the fury of arrows.

A defense formed by closely spaced spears:

Just as the Germans entangle and weave, closing themselves together, their long spears against the enemy, stooping and placing one of their heads on the ground, holding the rest in their hand.

River bend:

If the water is so high that infantry or cavalry cannot cross, the river should be narrowed into many streams, as Cyrus, king of the Persians, did at the conquest of Babylon on the Ganges River, which at its narrowest is 10,000 fathoms. Alexander did the same on the same river, and Caesar on the Sicuris River.

Deep stretch of river:

If the river were so deep that it could not be crossed by wading, the captain should dig many streams that take in the water and then return it below the river; in this way the river will become shallow and can be crossed easily. This is what Alexander did in India against King Porrus at the pass of the Hydaspes River; Caesar did the same in Gaul and in Spain on the Liger River. He formed two companies of cavalry and had the soldiers cross the middle. Hannibal did the same thing in the Po with the elephants.

Saddle equipped with sacks:

The Assyrians and Euboeans used to carry sacks on their horses that they could fill with wind at will, which they carried instead of the saddle packsaddle. The top and sides of the saddle are well covered with plates of baked leather, so that arrows would not pierce it, for they value safe flight no less than uncertain travel. A horse made in this way can carry four or five men at a time.
Infantry lines crossing a river:

If it happens that the infantry have to cross a river that is dangerous because of its rapid flow, this is the safest way. The soldiers should take each other's arms and form a line like a palisade, linked by their arms. These lines should be arranged to follow the water's edge, so that no one gets in its way. This is the safest way. The reason is that the first soldier on top is the one who sustains the initial impact, and if he were alone, the water would knock him down, but all the others below should sustain it and use it as their shield, thus ensuring each other's safety.

In fact, if the river flows from right to left, each row, when passing from the first to the second bank, has to receive from the right shoulder the flow of the river and its companion, from the left the right shoulder of the companion and the escape of the water.
The Assyrian boats were made of thin willow sticks woven around willow poles, shaped into small boats, and coated with fine powder soaked in oil or turpentine, roughly equivalent to mud. This resisted water and did not crack under impact because it always remained cool. Caesar dressed these boats with cowhide when crossing the Sicuris, a river in Spain, as Lucan testifies.

Willow-skin wickers and branches:

What is force?

I say that force is a spiritual, incorporeal, and invisible power, which is caused with a short life in those bodies that, by accidental violence, remain outside their natural being and rest.

I said spiritual, because in this force there is active life; I say incorporeal and invisible, because the body, where it is born, does not grow in weight or shape; of short life, because it always desires to conquer its cause, and, having conquered that, it destroys itself.

To the right of the figure.

If I wanted to know how much weight the stick of eight pounds and four cubits gives to the wall at c and how much to the point e, I do this. Divide the base of the triangle at c e by half, which will be d e, and as much of the upper part of the stick occupies as that part, that weight remains at the wall at c, and the remainder goes to e. A body whose longitude exceeds its latitude and depth must, for that reason, exert a greater load on its lower, lower portion than on its upper one.

But if the body is on the horizon with its two extremities, its two outermost extremities must be of equal weight at their contacts, when the body is of equal thickness and weight along its entire length.

Circle on a long horizontal line, with:

That body, whose continuous width is exceeded by its length, must exert an equal load on its two outermost contacts, when they are equidistant from the center, as f and e.

But when the body is on a perpendicular line, I say that the contact of the lower extremity receives upon itself all the superimposed load, and the upper one weighs nothing at its opposite contact, as appears in g and e.

But if the said body is placed with its two extremities at a discordant distance from the said center, it will be of discordant weight, because the part that is closest to them is heavier, and the farthest one becomes lighter, as appears in a e.

Therefore, if in the first proposition the said weight is shown to be distributed between its two extreme contacts f e, and similarly in the second the lower e receives everything, and the upper g nothing, then it is necessary to confess by geometric and arithmetic reasoning that the weight that is found between one and the other mode participates in the two extremes as a e 3.

If the weight a e is 4 braccia and 8 pounds, and you hang it so that it is not entirely at the point e, nor divided in half at f e, but rather is found in the middle of the line f e, that is, above the point c, I say by arithmetic reason that if the weight, standing upright, gives 8 pounds of load to the point e, and standing entirely downwards it gives 4, then take the halfway point between 4 and 8, which is 6; therefore the point e is 6, and c a is 2 between force and weight. And by arithmetic reasoning we find that if the base of the triangle a c e is taken, and that is divided in half at the point d, I always say d e is given to a c, and similarly d f is given to e; d e is similar to a b, and similarly d f is similar to b e.

These bales full of gunpowder are to be thrown inside the enemy's bastions.

A Stoclades is a one-foot bale made of hemp and glue, and is filled with gunpowder tails, the tails no longer than a finger's length. Each tail is made of thin copper covered with sinew, or glued paper, and all the tails have their own butts. They are perforated with a small hole and all rest on a copper bale, which is filled with various aberinth-like holes and filled with powder. And these are said to be full of cross-holes, which connect with the holes of the muskets, and then a fire is set like a blowpipe, which fire extends eight holes, so that no one can pick it up and drown it. And when the fire has reached the middle, immediately the muskets begin, one after the other, to spit out their deadly balls with a terrifying noise. And if you want to use it in a galley, make the muskets out of paper and fill them with pitch mixed with powdered sulfur between them, and it will perform three functions: first, it will cause damage with the muskets, second, it will set a fire that cannot be extinguished and will burn the wood, and no one can approach it because of the great stench.

These are types of bellows without leather, and are of wonderful utility and very eternal. Their function is as follows. And it would seem to many who have not seen or have not seen similar animals that one of the two could not fly, believing that if the bat has well proportioned its weight to the span of its wings, the eagle has a shortage of them. A reed and a bundle of reeds:

When a single reed has in itself the same proportion in thickness to its length as a bundle of such reeds, it will be in itself strong and resistant, as the said bundle is in itself, because if the bundle is 9 heads and supports 9 ounces, and they are 9 reeds tied together, a single one of the similar 9-headed reeds will perhaps support an ounce.

Let a dinar weight be applied to the top of a reed; you will see it bend to the ground. Take a thousand of these reeds and tie them tightly together, tie them at the feet, equalize them at the top, and load them: you will see that where by the first reason it should support about 3 1/2 pounds, it will support more than 40.

So, by this reason, the air that supports the bat, which weighs one two hundred and twentieth of the eagle's weight, were to be trampled and pressed by the beating of an eagle, it would have to be 60 times greater than its species.

Method of smashing a ship. But first they must be entangled, that is, hung together in such a way that you can break away at your own discretion, so that when the ship sinks, it doesn't drag yours down with it. And do this. Pull a weight up and then release it, and when it falls it will give a blow, like a pile in a castle. How is it possible for large rocks to be

overturned by the water.

Know that rocks are turned by water, because the water either surrounds them or overtakes them. If it surrounds them, the water follows it, intersecting with it and dislodging the earth or sand opposite the rock, and, having dislodged it, the rock itself turns. And if the water overtakes it, the water, after overcoming the rock, falls by its own accord, and by the force of the impact, penetrates from the surface to the bottom of the other water, and gnaws and dislodges, undermining the rock from its opposite supports, so that it also turns, and does so little by little until it will cover an entire river. What is water?

Among the four elements, water is the second heaviest and most volatile. It never rests until it joins its maritime element, where, unmolested by the winds, it settles and rests with its surface equidistant from the center of the universe. It is the growth and nourishment of all vital bodies. Nothing without it retains its original form. It connects and augments bodies by increasing. Nothing lighter than it can penetrate it without violence. Heat readily raises it in a thin vapor through the air. Cold freezes it, stability corrupts it. That is, heat moves it, cold freezes it. Firmness corrupts it. It takes on every odor, color, and flavor and has nothing of its own. It penetrates all porous bodies. No human defense is availible against its fury, and if it is available, it is not permanent. In its swift course, it becomes the supporter of things heavier than itself. It can rise upward by motion or leap as it sinks. In its ruin, it submerges with itself things lighter than itself. The principal of its course will sometimes be on the surface, sometimes in the middle, and sometimes at the bottom. One quantity rises above the alternating course of the other, and if this were not so, the surfaces of the flowing waters would be without globes. Every small obstacle, either on the bank or at the bottom, will cause ruin on the opposite bank or opposite bottom. Shallow water does more damage to the bank in its course than when it runs full. Its parts do not weigh on those below it. No river will ever maintain its course in a single place between its banks. Its upper parts do not burden the lower ones.

Why Nature did not create equal power in the power of vision.

Nature did not create equal power in the power of vision, but gave that power greater power the closer it approached its center. And she did this so as not to violate the law given to all other powers, which are more powerful the closer they approach that center. And this is seen in the act of percussion of any body and in the supports of the arms of a balance, where the weight, as it approaches, diminishes its gravity. It is seen in columns, walls, and pillars; it is seen in heat and in all other natural powers.

The rays that show us the edges of luminous bodies do not originate from the bodies themselves, but from their images, which are imprinted in the thickness of the lids of the eyes of the viewing bodies. Let us first prove this by a persuasive method, which teaches us: a wide-open eye does not show us such rays around luminous bodies, and if the image of a star or other light passes to the eye through a minimal pre-hole made in the paper placed in front of the eye, such luminous bodies will always be without rays. Therefore the rays that appear to extend from the luminous body upon contact with the eye that sees it, arise when the eye, almost closed, looks through the narrow slit between the lips of the eyes at a certain luminous body, the image of which is reflected in the thicknesses of the lips that terminate these lids, and after this impression is reflected to the pupil of the eye, which pupil receives three images of the same luminous body, namely two in the thicknesses of the lips that terminate the lids of the eye, and one in the pupil, and since these three images are very close to each other, it appears to the eye that they are continuous and joined to the image of the pupil. And the proof, which experience shows us to confirm our purpose, is manifested in raising or lowering the face while keeping the eye fixed on the luminous body. When the eye is raised, it will lose all the lower rays of that luminous body. This arises because, where the luminous body does not see, it cannot imprint its image there, and where the incident ray does not strike, it does not generate the refracted ray, and therefore the pupil does not receive it. And the same will happen when lowering the face, because then the thickness of the upper lid of the eye neither sees nor is seen by that luminous body. Therefore, the image, as has been said, cannot imprint itself there, and consequently the eye cannot see what is not there, but sees that image in the lower lid, which lid sees and is seen by the luminous body. On the Draining of Marshes.

The draining of marshes will be done when turbid rivers are led into them.

This is proven because where the river flows, it removes soil, and where it slows down, it leaves its turbulence there; and this is because in rivers, water is never slowed down as in marshes, where the water has an imperceptible motion. But in these marshes, the river must enter through a narrow, low, and narrow space and exit through a wide, shallow space; and this is necessary because the river's flowing water is coarser and more earthy below than above, and the slow water of marshes is similar. However, the superior lightness of marshes differs greatly from its inferior gravity, which is not the case in river currents, in which the superior lightness varies little from the inferior gravity. It is therefore concluded that the marsh will sink because it receives turbid water from below and clear water is discharged from above from the opposite part of the marsh, and for this reason the marsh will necessarily raise its bottom by means of the soil which continually discharges upon it, etc.

Of birds.

Before birds prepare for their long journeys, they await favorable winds. These favorable conditions (in various species of birds) are of various kinds, because birds that fly by jerks, or by leaps, must fly against the wind; others receive the wind on one side at different angles; others receive it from both sides. But birds that fly by jerks, such as thrushes and other similar flock-flying birds, have weak wing feathers, poorly armed with smaller feathers that cover the larger ones. Therefore, their flight must be against the wind, because the wind tightens and presses one feather against another, and thus their surfaces become smooth and slippery as they penetrate the air. The opposite would happen if the wind struck these birds on the tail, because then it would enter under each feather and turn them upside down toward the head, and thus their flight would be a confused motion, like that of a mixed leaf in the course of the wind, which continually whirls through the air in different revolutions. Furthermore, their flesh would be defenseless against the percussion of the cold winds, and to avoid such accidents they fly against the wind's course with a fresh motion, and their leaps acquire great impetus in their descent, which is made with the wings closed to leeward, and the refracted motion proceeds with the wings open against the wind, which restores the bird to the same height in the air from which it first descended, and continues in this manner until it reaches the desired place.

I say that no part of the surface of water moves by itself unless it descends. Therefore, since the sphere of water has no surface at any point that can descend, it is necessary, by the first conception, that it does not move by itself. Why are ponds formed near the sea, and why do their great expansions flow into the sea through such a narrow channel, on the sides of which such a large embankment is built between itself and the sea?

The waves of the sea throw up a great quantity of sand, which rises along the entire shore, both above the mouth of the pond and elsewhere. When the waves cease, the mouth of the pond is closed by the aforementioned material thrown up by the sea, and the water that the pond receives from the surrounding rivers, finding no further outlet, continues to rise and acquire weight and strength. Thus, either it breaks the embankment placed between itself and the sea, or it overflows and, with its spillage, consumes as much of the embankment as it touches. and it perseveres in this course so long that it clears away from itself all the matter that was preventing its necessary clearing. And it consumes only as much as is necessary; and at the beginning it widens greatly, because the water that pours over the mouth is thin; and at the end the course of this water narrows, because this course has become thicker due to the acquired depth; and this is the reason why the outlet of the ponds into the sea is always narrow.

On the friction of the heavens: whether it creates sound or not.

All sound is caused by air rebounding in a dense body, and if it is caused by two heavy bodies, it is by the air surrounding them, and this friction consumes the rubbed bodies. It would therefore follow that the heavens, in their friction, because there is no air between them, do not generate sound; and if such a friction were true, in the many centuries that the heavens are turned, they would be consumed by such an immense velocity occurring each day. And even if it did create sound, it cannot be spread, because the sound of percussion under water is barely felt, and less or not at all in dense bodies. Furthermore, in polished bodies their friction does not create sound, which would similarly happen if no sound were created by contact, or the friction, of the heavens. And if these heavens are not polished by the contact of their friction, they follow that they are globular and rough. Therefore their contact is not continuous. This being so, a vacuum is generated, which it is concluded does not exist in nature. Therefore it is concluded that friction would have worn away the edges of each heaven, and all the more so as it is faster toward the center than toward the poles, for it would be worn away more in the center than from the poles, and then it would no longer rub, sleep would cease and the dancers would stop. Except if [the] heavens [were] one to rotate toward the east and the other toward the north.
Whether the stars are illuminated by the sun or by themselves.

They claim to be illuminated by themselves, arguing that if Venus and Mercury did not have their own light, when they come between our eyes and the sun, they would obscure as much of the sun as they block out from our eyes. And this is false, because it is proven that the shadowy part of the bright part is completely surrounded and covered by the lateral rays of the rest of that light, and thus remains invisible. This is demonstrated: when the sun is seen from a long distance through the branches of leafless plants, these branches do not occupy any part of the sun as seen by our eyes. The same happens to the aforementioned planets, which, although they are without light by themselves, do not occupy, as has been said, any part of the sun as seen by our eyes.

Of the Moon's Spots.

Others said that the moon was composed of more and less transparent parts, as if one part were like alabaster and another like crystal or glass. It would follow that the sun, striking the less transparent part with its rays, would remain on the surface, and thus the denser part would remain illuminated and the transparent part would show the shadows of its dark depths; and this is how the moon's quality is composed. And this opinion has pleased many philosophers, especially Aristotle, yet it is a false opinion, because in the different aspects that the moon and the sun often find themselves in before our eyes, we see these spots vary, sometimes becoming dark and sometimes clear. They would become dark when the sun is in the west and the moon is in the middle of the sky, for then the transparent concavities would cast shadows up to the tops of the lips of such transparent concavities, because the sun could not penetrate its rays into the mouths of such concavities. These would appear bright during the full moon, when the moon in the east faces the sun in the west. Then the sun would illuminate even the depths of such transparency, and thus, since no shadows are cast, the moon would not show us the aforementioned spots at that time; and so on, now more, now less, according to the changes of the sun from the moon and the moon from our eyes, as I said above.
Of the Spots of the Moon.

They said that the spots of the moon are created in the moon itself by being of varying rarity and density; if this were the case, in a lunar eclipse the solar rays would penetrate through some part of the aforementioned rarity. Since this effect is not seen, this opinion is false.

Others say that the surface of the moon, being smooth and clean, like a mirror, receives within itself the likeness of the earth. This opinion is false, since the earth, exposed to the water in different aspects, has different shapes. Therefore, when the moon is in the east, it would reflect different spots than when it is above us or when it is in the west; which is the case with the spots of the moon, as seen during the full moon, which never vary in its motion in our hemisphere. The second reason is that the object mirrored in the convexity takes up a small portion of that mirror, as is proven by perspective. The third reason is that at full moon, the moon sees only the middle of the sphere of the illuminated earth, in which the ocean and other waters shine, and the earth makes spots in that splendor, and thus half of our earth would be seen surrounded by the splendor of the sea illuminated by the sun, and in the moon such a resemblance would be a minimal part of the moon itself. The fourth is that a splendid thing is not reflected in another splendid thing. Therefore, since the sea takes its splendor from the sun, as does the moon, no earth could be reflected in it without also seeing the body of the sun and of each star opposite it in particular.

On painting.

The most important part of painting is the fields of painted objects. In these fields, the edges of natural bodies, which have a convex curvature, are always recognized. The figures of these bodies are always recognized in these fields, even if the colors of the bodies are the same as those of the aforementioned field. This happens because the convex edges of the bodies are not illuminated in the same way as the field itself, because this edge will often be lighter or darker than the field itself. But if this edge is the same color as the field itself, this part of the painting will undoubtedly obscure the recognition of the figure of this edge; and this choice of painting is to be avoided by the minds of good painters, since the painter's intention is to make his bodies appear beyond the fields, and in the above-mentioned case the opposite occurs, not only in painting but also in works in relief.

The eyes of all animals have their own eyeballs, which themselves grow and shrink according to the intensity of sunlight or other light. But in birds it is more diverse, especially in nocturnal birds, such as owls, barn owls, and tawny owls, which are similar to the little owl. Why water is salty.

Pliny says in his second book, with 103 chapters, that seawater is salty because the sun's heat tans and dries out the moisture, which it sucks out, and this gives the sea, which expands greatly, a salty taste. But this is not true, because if the saltiness of the sea were caused by the sun's heat, there is no doubt that lakes, ponds, and marshes would be all the more salty, the less mobile and shallower their waters are. And experience shows us otherwise: such marshes show us that their waters are completely devoid of saltiness. Furthermore, Pliny assumes in the same chapter that such saltiness could arise because, once every soft and subtle part, which the heat easily draws toward itself, is removed, the rougher and coarser part remains; and for this reason, the water on the surface is sweeter than at the bottom. This is contradicted by the same arguments given above, namely, that the same would happen to marshes and other waters that dry up due to the heat. It has also been said that the saltiness of the sea is the sweat of the earth. To this it is replied that all the veins of water that penetrate the earth would be salty.
