Discourse on Painting 1.

Perspective, which is used in painting, is divided into three main parts, the first of which deals with the diminution of the quantities of bodies at different distances.

The second part deals with the diminution of the colors of these bodies.

The third is that which diminutes the perception of the shapes and boundaries of these bodies at various distances.

Perspective uses two opposing pyramids for distances: one has its angle at the eye and its base remote to the horizon; the second has its base toward the eye and its angle at the horizon. But the first is concerned with the universal, embracing all the quantities of bodies opposite the eye, as would be a large landscape seen through a narrow aperture, since the greater number of objects is seen through that aperture the more distant they are from the eye; and thus the base is generated at the horizon and the angle at the eye, as I said above.

The second pyramid extends to a particular, which appears smaller the further it is removed from the eye, and this second perspective arises from the first.

On knowing how much the ship

moves per hour.

Our ancients used various methods to determine the voyage of a ship in each hour, among which Vetruvius includes one in his architectural work, which method is as fallacious as the others. This method is a mill wheel touched by the waves at its ends, and through its entire revolutions a straight line is described, which represents the circumferential line of that wheel reduced to a straight line. But this invention is not valid except on the flat and motionless surfaces of lakes. If the water moves with the ship at the same speed, then the wheel remains motionless; and if the water moves faster or slower than the ship, the wheel does not move at the same speed as the ship, so that this invention is of little value.

Here is another method based on the experiment of a known distance from one island to another. For this, a light board is made, struck by the wind, which becomes more or less oblique as the wind strikes it more or less swiftly. And this is in Battista Alberti.

Among the accidental powers of nature, percussion greatly exceeds each of the others, which are produced by the movers of heavy bodies at the same time, with equal motion, weight, and force. This percussion is divided into simple and composite. Simple is that in which the mover is joined to the moving percussion pin at the junction of the struck place. Composite is that in which the moving percussion pin does not terminate its motion at the point of its impression, as is the case with the striking hammer of the minting die. And this compound percussion is much weaker than the simple percussion, because if the hammer mouth had attached the coin to be stamped, and I struck it on the imprint of the impression, and if in the hammer mouth the opposite concavity of the coin had been cut, then the impression would be quicker and clearer on the side struck by the simple motion than on the side of the compound percussion, as is the case with the coin that remains struck in the minting die, where the descent of the hammer has struck it, and the percussion refracts and reverberates against the front of the hammer.

On the Beginning of Bird Flight.

How a Bird Takes Flight After First

Fixing on Flat Ground.

When birds wish to begin their flight, they must adopt one of two methods. One is to lower their body to the ground, and then, with a very rapid extension of their bent legs, generate a leap into the air. At the end of this leap, the wings have completed their extensions and immediately lower them with speed toward the ground, and ascend the second level, which is oblique like the first, and thus, proceeding successively, rise to the height they desire.

Bird taking off from the ground:

Some others first raise their wings obliquely forward and then lower themselves, as far as they can, with their chest to the ground. In this position, they quickly extend their legs, leaping upward and forward obliquely. At the end of the momentum, they lower their wings obliquely downward and backward, and thus find themselves well above and ahead of the point from which they separated. At the end of the momentum, they regain some more wings, and so the motion continues.

Bird that lowers and rises again:

Other birds, after they have lowered themselves to the ground and spread their wings upward and forward, simultaneously lower their wings and extend their legs. Thus, the power of the first wingbeat, combined with the power of the leg extension, becomes very great. This combined power is the greatest that can be achieved in the initial stages of flight of these birds.

The second method used by birds in the beginning of their flight is when they descend from high to low. These birds simply launch themselves forward and simultaneously open their wings upward and forward, and in the process of leaping, lower their wings downward and backward; and thus, rowing, they continue their oblique descent.

I saw the bird turned upside down by the tired wind, which entered above the wind with tired wings.

In all birds that fly high, when their wings are raised, their wings remain pierced, as is demonstrated in its place. And when these wings descend, they remain joined, and so, since the compressed and condensed air does not yield to the descending wings with the same velocity as the wing itself, the bird must be refracted by this percussion, from which it rises, and is carried aloft by the acquired impetus for a distance of height equal to the impetus that refracts it has of life. And at this time the wings reopen and pierce the spaces between the said feathers, and then with fury it lowers the wings again, bringing the feathers together, and thus regains the impetus it had previously lost. And this is the way all birds that rise with a straight motion, such as the lark and similar birds, and those birds that do not use this expansion of their feathers, such as predatory animals, must have a dizzying elevation, that is, a spiral, or you could say, a circular motion.

Right column.

Winged insect:

The parrot and many similar insects all fly with four wings, the back ones being smaller than the front ones, and the front ones partially cover the back ones. All these kinds can rise with a straight motion, because when these wings rise, they remain perforated, holding the front wings much higher than the back ones. This holds them almost to the end of the force that pushes them upward, and then, as they lower them, the longer wings join the shorter ones, and thus, as they descend, they regain new impetus. There are also other kinds of volatile insects that fly with four equal wings, but these do not cover each other when descending or even when rising, and these cannot rise with a straight motion.

What is impetus?

Impetus is what is otherwise called derivative motion, which arises from the primary motion, that is, when the moving object was united with its mover.

Never in any part of the derivative motion will a velocity equal to that of the primary motion be found. This is proven because "with each degree of motion of the bowstring, some of the power acquired by its mover is lost." And because every effect participates in its cause, the derivative motion of the arrow gradually diminishes its power, and thus participates in the power of the bow, which, just as it was generated gradually, is also gradually destroyed, etc.

The impetus impressed by the mover on the moving object is infused into all the united parts of that mover; And this is evident because all parts of the moving body, both internal and external, have equal motion, except in circumvolution, because in that the more impetuous part always revolves around the less impetuous part, that is, those closest to the center of the moving body. And the part that moved first always remains further from the beginning of its motion, if it is not impeded; and this happens because it is more powerful in this circumvolution.

And if, for the adversary, one were to say: the impetus that moves the moving body is in the air that surrounds it from the middle to the rear, this is denied, because the air that follows the moving body is drawn by the moving body to fill the vacuum it leaves. And again, the air that condenses in front of the moving body flees backward in the opposite direction.

This is proved by the objects that are supported between the two waters, which are of equal weight to the water, and it shows well in clear waters the true motion of the water that carries them, because sometimes the fall of the wave toward the bottom carries them with it to the percussion of that bottom, and would refract with it to the surface of the water, if the flowing body were spherical; but often it does not bring it back, because it would be wider or narrower in one direction than in the other; and its unevenness is struck on the larger side by another refracted wave, which goes on turning that mobile, which moves as much as it is carried; This motion is sometimes swift, sometimes slow, sometimes to the right, sometimes to the left, sometimes up, sometimes down, twisting and turning on itself, sometimes this way, sometimes that, obeying all its motors, and in battles waged by such motors, it always falls prey to the victor.
